questions.current_path: Year 12 / The Nature of Light / Light and Special Relativity / investigate the evidence, from Einstein’s thought experiments and subsequent experimental validation, for time dilation and length contraction , and analyse quantitatively situations in which these are observed, for example: observations of cosmic-origin muons at the Earth’s surface; atomic clocks (Hafele–Keating experiment); evidence from particle accelerators; evidence from cosmological studies
questions.text:
Muons are very short-lived particles that are created when energetic protons collide with each other. A beam of muons can be produced by very-high-energy particle accelerators.
The high-speed muons produced for an experiment by the Fermilab accelerator are measured to have a lifetime of 5.0 microseconds. When these muons are brought to rest, their lifetime is measured to be 2.2 microseconds.
Name the effect demonstrated by these observations of the lifetimes of the muons.
Both lifetimes belong to the same particle, so the difference cannot be a property of the muon that changed. Ask instead what happens to the rate of a moving clock when it is compared with a stationary one.
Calculate the velocity of the muons as they leave the accelerator.
Start from $t_v = \frac{t_0}{\sqrt{1 - v^{2}/c^{2}}}$ and rearrange it so that $v$ is the subject rather than the lifetime.
Decide which of the two lifetimes is the rest lifetime before substituting: it is the one measured with the muons brought to rest, and it is the shorter of the two. Sanity-check the result at the end, because the answer cannot exceed $c$.

questions.current_path: Year 11 / Kinematics / Motion in a Straight Line / use mathematical modelling and graphs, selected from a range of technologies, to analyse and derive relationships between time, distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration in rectilinear motion, including: (ACSPH061)
questions.text:
A rocket was launched vertically to probe the upper atmosphere. The vertical velocity of the rocket as a function of time is shown in the graph.
Using either words or calculations, compare the acceleration of the rocket at $t = 20\,\mathrm{s}$ with its acceleration at $t = 100\,\mathrm{s}$.
On a velocity-time graph the acceleration is the gradient, not the value. Compare the slope of the curve at the two times - drawing a short tangent at each point is a reliable way to do it.
Account for the shape of the graph over the range of time shown.
Work along the graph in two sections, from lift-off to the peak at about $120\,\mathrm{s}$ and from the peak to the end, and account for each separately because the forces acting are not the same in both.
In the first section the thrust is roughly constant, so use $F_{net} = ma$ and ask what is happening to the mass of the rocket and to the opposing drag. In the second section ask which of those forces has stopped.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / Advanced Mechanics / Projectile Motion / analyse the motion of projectiles by resolving the motion into horizontal and vertical components, making the following assumptions: a constant vertical acceleration due to gravity; zero air resistance | Year 12 / Advanced Mechanics / Circular Motion / investigate the relationship between the total energy and work done on an object executing uniform circular motion
questions.text:
A 30 kg object, A, was fired from a cannon in projectile motion. When the projectile was at its maximum height of 25 m, its speed was 20 m s$^{-1}$. Ignore air resistance.
An identical object, B, was attached to a mechanical arm and moved at a constant speed of 20 m s$^{-1}$ in a vertical half-circle. The length of the arm was 25 m.
Calculate the force acting on object A at its maximum height.
The speed at the maximum height tells you nothing about the forces there, because a horizontal velocity does not make an object accelerate. Ask instead which forces act on the object at that instant and whether they balance.
Calculate the time it would take object A to reach the ground from its position of maximum height.
Take the fall from the maximum height as a journey of its own rather than as the second half of the whole flight. The object starts that part of its motion with zero vertical velocity, so the time follows from a displacement equation in which the initial velocity term is zero.
The horizontal speed of 20 m s$^{-1}$ is not needed for this part. Check that your answer is of order a couple of seconds, since a fall of about 25 m takes a little over two seconds.
Describe and compare the vertical forces acting on objects A and B at their maximum heights.
Both objects are moving horizontally at their maximum heights, so for B you must first supply whatever vertical acceleration its circular path requires, which is $v^{2}/r$ directed towards the pivot. Compare the resultant vertical forces on the two objects, not the individual forces.
Remember that it is the resultant that produces the acceleration, and that B has two vertical forces where A has only one. For B, decide whether the upward vertical component of the tension is greater or smaller than the weight, and use the required acceleration to decide.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / Electromagnetism / The Motor Effect / conduct a quantitative investigation to demonstrate the interaction between two parallel current-carrying wires
questions.text:
Two parallel wires are separated by a distance of 0.75 m. Wire X is 3.0 m long and carries a current of 2.0 A. Wire Y can be considered to be infinitely long and carries a current of 5.0 A. Both currents flow in the same direction along the wires.
What is the direction of the force that exists between the two wires?
The stem tells you that both currents run in the same direction. Use the standard result for what happens when the currents in two parallel wires run in the same direction. No numbers are needed here, and do not calculate a force, because only the direction is asked for.
On the axes, sketch a graph that shows how the force between the two wires would vary if the length of Wire X was increased.
Write the force in terms of the length before you draw anything: for a long straight wire Y the force on a length $L$ of wire X is $F = \frac{\mu_0 I_X I_Y L}{2\pi r}$, in which every quantity except $L$ is fixed by the stem.
Check your line by setting the length of wire X to zero and asking what the force must then be. Where the line has to start is worth a mark in its own right, so settle that before worrying about the gradient.
In your Physics course you have performed a first-hand investigation to demonstrate the motor effect. Explain how your results demonstrated that effect.
Decide what 'the motor effect' means and write it down before writing anything else: the force experienced by a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field, $F = BIl\sin\theta$. The 3 and 4 mark descriptors are only available once your results are tied back to that equation.
List what you actually varied in the investigation - current, the number of turns or the length of wire in the gap, the field strength, the orientation of the coil - and for each one name the factor of the equation it tests. Then say which way the force moved.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / The Nature of Light / Light: Wave Model / conduct investigations to analyse qualitatively the diffraction of light (ACSPH048, ACSPH076)
questions.text:
Sir William Bragg and his son Sir Lawrence Bragg shared the Nobel prize for physics in 1915 for their work on X-ray diffraction and crystal structure analysis.
Describe ONE way in which an understanding of crystal structure has impacted on science.
You need two things here: a specific piece of scientific work, and what understanding of crystal structure made possible. Naming a broad area of science on its own is not enough.
Outline the methods of X-ray diffraction used by the Braggs to determine the structure of crystals.
Set the method out as a chain: a beam of X-rays of known wavelength, a single crystal that is rotated, a record of the directions the X-rays come out in, and then the calculation that turns those angles into a distance.
The key physics is interference between rays scattered from parallel planes of atoms: those rays travel different distances so they add or cancel. Work out the condition for them to add, and be careful about which angle is being used - the one between the ray and the plane, or between the ray and the normal.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / The Nature of Light / Light: Quantum Model / analyse the photoelectric effect as it occurs in metallic elements by applying the law of conservation of energy and the photon model of light, (ACSPH119) | Year 12 / The Nature of Light / Light: Quantum Model / investigate the evidence from photoelectric effect investigations that demonstrated inconsistency with the wave model for light (ACSPH087, ACSPH123, ACSPH137)
questions.text:
A student carried out an experiment on the photoelectric effect. The frequency of the incident radiation and the energy of the photoelectrons were both determined from measurements taken during the experiment. The results obtained are shown in the table:
Graph these results on the grid, including the line of best fit.
Put the quantity the student set, the frequency, on the horizontal axis and the quantity they measured, the photoelectron energy, on the vertical axis. Both scales must be linear and carry units.
One of the six points sits well off the trend. Plot all the points, then draw a straight best-fit line that does not pass through that one - dot-to-dot joins and curves will not earn the mark.
Sanity-check your line against the photoelectric equation: its gradient should come out as Planck's constant, and its intercept on the energy axis should be minus the work function.
How could the reliability of the experiment be improved?
Reliability is about random error and scatter, so think about what happens to a spread of repeated measurements, and about how many data points the gradient of the best-fit line is being based on.

questions.current_path: Year 11 / Waves and Thermodynamics / Wave Behaviour / explain the behaviour of waves in a variety of situations by investigating the phenomena of: reflection; refraction; diffraction; wave superposition (ACSPH071, ACSPH072)
questions.text:
Geophysics. Attempt this question OR one other from Questions 27 to 31 in Section II (25 marks).
(i) is a naming question: think of the portable instrument a survey crew carries over the ground to measure $g$ locally.
(ii) needs two separate things, what the instrument actually measures and how a set of readings is turned into a picture of what lies beneath the surface. A response giving only one of these will not earn the second mark.
The diagram shows a map of the part of an ocean that includes two chains of features, a chain of islands and a chain of seamounts.
Read the *shape and the ages* of the two chains before naming anything. One chain is straight with ages increasing steadily along it; the other is curved and much older throughout.
(b)(ii) needs three things: where the magma comes from, why the volcanoes end up in a line, and what the change in trend between the two chains tells you about the plate.
Use the age labels on the map. A chain that gets steadily older in one direction can only be recording motion over time, and that is what identifies the process.
Describe how you carried out a first-hand investigation to determine the relationship between the nature of a surface and the radiation reflected from it.
Markers award marks for four separate things: what you did, what you kept constant, how many times you repeated it, and how the radiation was detected and recorded. Make sure all four appear.
The independent variable is the *nature of the surface*, so change only the surface between trials and record the reflected intensity for each. Keep the angle of incidence, the distance and the source intensity fixed.
Be explicit that the radiation is electromagnetic, that is light from a laser or torch, and place the detector so that it responds only to reflected light and not to the source.
When the theory of plate tectonics was first proposed, some parts of the scientific community were reluctant to accept it. Discuss the theory of plate tectonics and the evidence leading to its acceptance.
A 'discuss' question worth 6 marks needs all three of: the theory, the evidence for it, and the reasons for the original resistance. Any one of these on its own caps the response well down the band.
For the evidence, the strongest items are the measurable ones: measured sea-floor spreading rates matching the age of the crust, the symmetrical age pattern either side of a mid-ocean ridge, and the actual distribution of shallow- and deep-focus earthquakes and of volcanoes along plate boundaries.
For the resistance, the original objections were methodological rather than observational: no known driving mechanism, a prevailing static-Earth assumption, and the palaeontological evidence being dismissed.
Discuss how information gathered from seismic observations has led to greater understanding of the structure of the Earth.
The question is about *inference*, so never describe an observation without also saying what structural conclusion it forces.
Three seismic facts pin down the interior: $S$ waves cannot travel through a liquid, $P$ waves bend as they cross boundaries between layers of different speed, and the difference in arrival time between $P$ and $S$ gives the distance to an earthquake, allowing an epicentre to be triangulated from several stations.
A labelled ray-path diagram showing the concentric layers, the shadow zones and the P and S arrivals is worth a great deal in an 8-mark answer. The examiner report notes that such diagrams were rare and usually unlabelled.

questions.current_path: Year 11 / Waves and Thermodynamics / Wave Properties / the role of the medium in the propagation of mechanical waves | Year 11 / Waves and Thermodynamics / Wave Properties / the transfer of energy involved in the propagation of mechanical waves (ACSPH067, ACSPH070)
questions.text:
Medical Physics. Attempt this question OR one other from Questions 27 to 31 in Section II (25 marks).
(i) asks for the *purpose* of a coherent bundle in an endoscope, so say what the surgeon ends up able to see, and why the word 'coherent' matters.
(ii) is a two-mark description built from two ingredients: which of the core and cladding has the higher refractive index, and the optical process that keeps the light inside the core. A well-labelled ray diagram is an acceptable alternative.
The table shows information relating to the transmission of sound through some types of body tissue.
(i) is a recall question about where ultrasound sits in the frequency spectrum, and the $20\,\mathrm{kHz}$ boundary is the number that matters.
(ii) is about reflection at a boundary, and the marks are won by relating the size of the *difference* in acoustic impedance to the strength of the echo returned to the transducer.
Calculate the reflection coefficient for both boundaries from the table and compare the two values, rather than only describing the phenomenon in words.
You have conducted a first-hand investigation to demonstrate the Doppler effect. Describe your investigation and conclusions.
Describe the method, the observations you actually made, and the conclusion. All three are needed for the top band, not just the apparatus.
Decide in advance what quantity your detector is measuring. Connect the microphone to a frequency meter or oscilloscope so that the Doppler shift appears as a change in *frequency*, not as a change in voltage or loudness.
In the conclusion use the words frequency and pitch, and do not describe the effect as a change in loudness. The examiner report for this question records that confusion between loudness, frequency and wavelength was a frequent error.
'CAT scans provide more information than X-rays, so they should be used whenever possible.' Discuss this statement.
The statement contains two claims joined by 'so': that CAT scans provide more information, and that they should therefore always be used. The second claim is the one that needs testing.
Weigh the extra information against the cost in dose of ionising radiation, money and time, and give concrete clinical situations, such as a chest film or a straightforward fracture, where a plain X-ray is the right choice.
Finish with a judgement on the statement. 'Discuss' requires you to commit, and the honest conclusion here is that the premise is right but the conclusion does not follow.
Explain why MRI can be used to detect cancerous tissues.
The examiner report for this question is unusually specific: the top band requires the words *magnetic field*, *precession* and *resonance* to be used and explained, and then applied to cancerous tissue. Use all three.
Be clear about what precesses, the hydrogen nuclei in the water of the body, not the electrons and not the field, and make sure the field is described as remaining on throughout, since several candidates wrongly said it was switched off.
The link to cancer is water content: cancerous cells hold more water, so more hydrogen nuclei respond and they relax at different rates. Say explicitly why a plain X-ray cannot distinguish the tissues.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Origins of the Elements / account for the production of emission and absorption spectra and compare these with a continuous black body spectrum (ACSPH137) | Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Origins of the Elements / investigate the key features of stellar spectra and describe how these are used to classify stars
questions.text:
Astrophysics. Attempt this question OR one other from Questions 27 to 31 in Section II (25 marks).
(i) is a definition, and a definition of binary stars has to say something about how the two stars move relative to each other, not merely that there are two of them.
(ii) asks for the *pattern* in the spectrum, so the word 'periodic' matters as much as the red and blue shifts themselves.
The table shows information about three stars in the Milky Way galaxy.
(i) is read straight off the table: surface temperature increases along the spectral sequence M, K, G, F, A, B, O.
(b)(ii) cannot be answered by comparing apparent magnitudes, because the two stars are at very different distances. Use the distance modulus $M = m - 5\log\left(\dfrac{d}{10\,\mathrm{pc}}\right)$ on both, then compare.
Remember that on the magnitude scale a *lower, more negative* number means a brighter star; the scale runs backwards.
A student carried out an experiment to examine the spectra of various light sources through spectroscopes as shown in the diagram. The student observed three different spectra. Account for the differences in the three observed spectra.
Take the three spectra one at a time and identify the *type* of each before you explain it: continuous emission, line emission, or continuous with dark absorption lines.
The explanation for all three is the same physics, the electron energy levels in the source and in the absorber, so once the two sodium levels involved are clear you can write all three.
For the spectrum with dark lines, remember the light reaching the spectroscope is continuous light that has already *passed through* the sodium vapour, so exactly those wavelengths have been removed by atoms being raised between the same two levels that emit in the second case.
A new generation of Earth-based optical telescopes is advancing optical astronomy. Describe the advances in design that have been incorporated in large telescopes over recent years.
The marks are for advances in *design* and for what each one bought you, being resolution, sensitivity or cost-effectiveness. An advance with no consequence named earns little.
Group them: materials that let much larger mirrors exist at all; active optics that keep a huge mirror within a fraction of a wavelength of shape; adaptive optics that cancel the atmosphere; and segmentation that makes an effective aperture larger than any single mirror.
Stay with Earth-based optical telescopes. Describing space telescopes or radio astronomy is outside the scope of the question, and examiners reported many such responses.
Explain how the data presented in Hertzsprung-Russell diagrams may be used to understand the evolution of stars.
Explain what the two axes of the diagram represent and name the groups stars fall into before you describe any evolution.
The marks are won by linking each stage of a star's life to a *movement* on the diagram, and by saying what determines the direction of that movement, which is the star's mass.
Draw the diagram with the evolutionary track on it. Examiners reported that most candidates left out the sketch, and that a common error is to place the protostar at the top right; it starts at the bottom right and moves up and left onto the main sequence.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Quantum Mechanical Nature of the Atom / relate qualitatively and quantitatively the quantised energy levels of the hydrogen atom and the law of conservation of energy to the line emission spectrum of hydrogen using: (ACSPH136)
questions.text:
From Quanta to Quarks. Attempt this question OR one other from Questions 27 to 31 in Section II (25 marks).
(i) is a definition of a term you use constantly in nuclear physics: say what the two particles are, not what they are made of.
(ii) needs one property and the correct difference in it. Charge is the easiest; mass and quark composition are also accepted, so choose whichever you are surest of and get the values right.
The table shows the quantum numbers of the four lowest states of the hydrogen atom, together with the energies of those states.
(i) is one subtraction: the photon carries the *difference* between the two level energies, not either energy on its own.
(ii) is a drawing. Plot energy vertically with $n = 1$ at the bottom, and check your spacing against the table, because the gaps between the levels shrink as $n$ increases and the levels crowd together.
You must also show where the levels for $n > 4$ lie. They converge on a limit, and a diagram with evenly spaced levels will not get the marks. Do not draw electron orbits.
Describe how you carried out a first-hand investigation to determine the penetrating power of alpha, beta and gamma radiation on a range of materials.
Markers award marks for four things: what you did, what you kept constant, how you detected and recorded the radiation, and how many times you repeated it.
The independent variable is the absorber, so change the material and the thickness and change nothing else, including the distance from source to detector and the exposure time.
Examiners reported that many responses read as though a computer simulation had been used, so describe apparatus you could physically set up in the laboratory and name the absorber for each type of radiation.
The Manhattan Project is the codename given to the development of atomic (nuclear fission) bombs during World War II. Discuss the significance of this project for society.
This is a 'discuss' question: you must weigh positive against negative consequences for society, and a one-sided answer caps your mark.
The positive case is the peaceful one, namely nuclear power, isotopes in medicine and industry, and the demonstration of fission itself. The negative case is Hiroshima and Nagasaki, the arms race, and the culture of secrecy the project fostered.
Finish with an overall judgement about the legacy, and be prepared to say something about the responsibility of the scientists involved.
Analyse how Chadwick's and Fermi's work resulted in a greater understanding of the atom.
Treat the two scientists separately first, giving apparatus, observation and inference for each, and only then combine them. Examiners reported that many candidates answered as though the two had worked together.
For Chadwick the decisive point is that the radiation could not be deflected in electric or magnetic fields and yet had a mass comparable with the proton, so it could not be gamma radiation, and that conservation of energy and momentum in collisions with nuclei of known mass fixed the particle mass.
For Fermi the decisive points are the slow-down of neutrons by wax, their capture by nuclei, and the production of new radioactive isotopes from uranium. Note also that the identification of barium as a fission product was his interpretation of the work of others, and that many candidates wrongly credited him with discovering the neutrino.

questions.current_path: Year 11 / Kinematics / Motion in a Straight Line / conduct practical investigations, selecting from a range of technologies, to record and analyse the motion of objects in a variety of situations in one dimension in order to measure or calculate: time; distance; displacement; speed; velocity; acceleration
questions.text:
Two students, Kim and Ali, performed an experiment to determine the acceleration due to gravity ($g$) using a simple pendulum consisting of a small mass hanging from a light string.
Their procedure was as follows:
1. Adjust the length of the string ($L$) to measure $0.08\,\mathrm{m}$.
2. Hold the mass to the side to give a small angular displacement, $\theta$.
3. Release the mass and measure the time for one period ($T$).
4. Record the result in a table.
5. Repeat using a string length ($L$) of $0.09\,\mathrm{m}$ and continue until the string length is $0.19\,\mathrm{m}$ (going up in $0.01\,\mathrm{m}$ increments, using the same initial angular displacement each time).
6. Calculate $g$ using the relationship $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}}$.
The results are shown in the table:
Kim used the data in the table to obtain a mean value for $g$. Kim's result was $g = 9.3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.
Ali used the results to produce the following graph. Ali's line of best fit was used to calculate $g$.
Outline TWO changes that could be made to the experimental procedure that would improve its accuracy.
(Note: the procedure as printed measures only one period for each length; maintaining a constant initial angular displacement does not by itself improve accuracy.)
Look at step 3 of the printed procedure. A single period at these lengths lasts about $0.6\,\mathrm{s}$, and a human reaction time is of order $0.2\,\mathrm{s}$, so most of what is being measured is reaction time. Decide what quantity you should actually be timing.
The second change should deal with the random scatter that survives at each length. Ask what you can do with several timings at the same length, and remember that a straight line drawn through all the results, as in part (c), is itself a way of averaging them.
Compare Kim's and Ali's methods of calculating $g$ and identify the better approach.
Kim computes a value of $g$ from each length separately and then averages, so every random error in every timing is carried straight into the answer. Ali's line of best fit is fitted to all twelve points at once. Ask which arrangement lets a single bad timing do the least damage.
It helps to be precise about what the gradient is. Since $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$ gives $T^{2} = \frac{4\pi^{2}}{g}L$, the gradient of that line is a single estimate of one number, so compare that with Kim's twelve separate estimates of the same number rather than judging the two methods in the abstract.
Calculate the value of $g$ from the line of best fit on Ali's graph.
For a pendulum $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$, so $T^{2} = \frac{4\pi^{2}}{g}L$: the line of best fit is a straight line through the origin whose gradient is $\frac{4\pi^{2}}{g}$. Rearrange for $g$ before substituting anything, and remember that $4\pi^{2} \approx 39.5$.
Read your two points off the line of best fit itself rather than off the data points, choosing the pair furthest apart on the graph, here roughly $L = 0.08\,\mathrm{m}$ and $L = 0.24\,\mathrm{m}$. Using raw data points is the commonest way to lose marks on a question of this kind.

In one of Einstein's famous thought experiments, a passenger travels on a train that passes through a station at $60\%$ of the speed of light. According to the passenger, the length of the train carriage is $22\,\mathrm{m}$ from front to rear.

This is Einstein's second postulate: the value of $c$ in a vacuum is the same for every inertial observer, whatever the motion of the source or of the observer. Nothing about the motion of the lamp changes the speed of the light it emits.
So write the ratio of the two measured velocities first, before substituting any numbers, and let the postulate decide what that ratio has to be.
Calculate the length of the carriage as observed by the rail worker on the station platform.
Use the length-contraction relationship $l_v = l_0\sqrt{1 - \frac{v^{2}}{c^{2}}}$, and decide which symbol each length belongs to before you substitute. The $22\,\mathrm{m}$ is the value measured by the passenger, who is at rest relative to the carriage.
Express the train's speed as a fraction of $c$ before substituting, and take the square root last rather than squaring the bracket. Check the sense of your answer at the end: the observer who sees the carriage moving must measure a shorter length than the passenger does.

questions.text:
Two types of generator are shown in the diagram.
What is the function of the brush in a generator?
The brushes are the only electrical path between the rotating coil and the stationary external circuit. Say what they have to stay in contact with, and what would happen to the circuit, and to the current, if they were removed.
Which of these generators is a DC generator? Justify your choice.
Compare the two ring assemblies carefully in the diagram: $P$ has two complete rings and $Q$ has a single ring cut into two halves. Work out what each one does to the current as the coil turns through a half rotation.
The current in the coil itself is the same alternating current in both machines, so the difference must lie entirely in what happens to the connection to the external circuit at the moment that current reverses. Ask what an external circuit would receive if the coil's connections were never swapped.
Outline why AC generators are used in large-scale electrical power production.
For a fixed amount of power, $P = VI$, so the current in a transmission line is inversely proportional to the voltage used to send it. Then look at how the energy lost heating those lines depends on that current: $P_{\text{loss}} = I^{2}R$.
The catch is that changing the voltage of a supply requires a transformer, and a transformer does nothing at all to a steady DC supply. Decide which of the two quantities a power station can conveniently change, and whether that choice is available to it if it generates DC.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / Electromagnetism / Electromagnetic Induction / the generation of an electromotive force (emf) and evidence for Lenz’s Law produced by the relative movement between a magnet, straight conductors, metal plates and solenoids
questions.text:
A metal rod lies between two magnets and is moved through the magnetic field, as shown in part (b).
State Lenz's law.
This is a statement about the direction of an induced current. Write it as 'the induced current flows in a direction such that it...', and make sure the thing it opposes is the CHANGE in magnetic flux, not the flux itself and not the motion of the circuit.
When the metal rod is moved upwards through the magnetic field as shown in the diagram, an emf is induced between the two ends.
For (b)(i): write down the direction of $\mathbf{v}$ and the direction of $\mathbf{B}$ - the field in the gap runs from the $N$ face of the left magnet to the $S$ face of the right magnet - and then use $\mathbf{F} = q\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B}$ with the sign of the charge carried by the current carriers in a metal in mind. Which end of the rod collects them?
For (b)(ii): an emf here is a separation of charge, not a flow of current. Say what force acts on the free charge carriers in the moving rod, in which direction along the rod it acts, and what that does to the distribution of positive and negative charge. The separation stops when the electric force from the separated charge just balances the magnetic force.
Explain how the principle of induction can be used to heat a conductor.
Two steps are needed and the question wants both. First ask what has to change for a current to be induced in a conductor at all; then ask what happens to that current in a conductor that has resistance.
There are two ways round the first step: put an alternating current in a fixed conductor, as in a transformer or an induction-coil supply, or keep the field fixed and move the conductor, as in an induction hob. Both change the flux through the conductor.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / Electromagnetism / Charged Particles, Conductors and Electric and Magnetic Fields / electric field between parallel charged plates | Year 11 / Electricity and Magnetism / Electrostatics / apply the electric field model to account for and quantitatively analyse interactions between charged objects using: (ACSPH103, ACSPH104); (ACSPH102)
questions.text:
A pair of parallel metal plates, placed in a vacuum, are separated by a distance of $5.00 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}$ and have a potential difference of $1000\,\mathrm{V}$ applied to them.
Calculate the magnitude of the electric field strength between the plates.
Between parallel plates the field is uniform, so its strength is the potential difference divided by the separation: $E = \frac{V}{d}$. Both numbers are in the stem of the question, so keep them in the right order and keep track of the power of ten when you divide by the $5.00\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}$.
Calculate the magnitude of the electrostatic force acting on an electron between the plates.
Use the field strength you calculated in part (a) with the force on a charge in an electric field, $F = qE$, taking $q$ as the magnitude of the electron's charge, $1.60\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$.
Check the size of your answer before moving on: the field is large, but this is the force on a single electron, so the result must be an extremely small number. If you have written something of order newtons, the electron's charge has not been included.
A beam of electrons is fired with a velocity of $3.00 \times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ between the plates as shown. A magnetic field is applied between the plates, sufficient to cancel the force on the electron beam due to the electric field.
Calculate the magnitude and direction of the magnetic field required between the plates to stop the deflection of the electron beam.
The beam goes straight when the magnetic force on it exactly cancels the electrostatic force, so write $qE = qvB$ and cancel $q$ before substituting. That the electron's charge disappears from the calculation is a useful check that the relationship is the right one, and it also means part (c) does not depend on part (b).
For the direction, track three separate things: the direction of $\mathbf{E}$, from the $+$ plate to the $-$ plate; the resulting force on the electrons; and the force the magnetic field must supply to cancel it. Only then decide which way $\mathbf{B}$ must point so that $\mathbf{F} = q\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B}$ gives that force, remembering that $q$ is negative and the electrons are travelling to the right.
A useful final check on the magnitude: the undeflected-beam condition is $v = \frac{E}{B}$, so the field you calculate must come out much smaller than the speed you started with. If it does not, a power of ten has gone astray.

For (iii) the evidence is the two curved branches labelled $P'$ and $P''$ that appear at large distances and arrive much later. Ask what path a P wave must follow to produce each of them, and what that implies about the layers it has crossed.
Assess the application and advantages of TWO geophysical methods in mineral exploration.

Finish with a judgement about how the two methods are used together in practice, rather than two unrelated descriptions.

questions.text:
Briefly describe how an endoscope works.
Part (i) is about how a bundle of optical fibres can carry both light and an image. Think about what happens to light at a glass-air boundary when the angle of incidence is large enough.
Part (ii) is about producing a two-dimensional image from one-dimensional measurements. Ask what a single X-ray photograph of the body can and cannot tell you, and what has to be varied to get around that.
Explain how a computed axial tomography (CAT) scan is produced.
Technetium 99m is an artificial isotope which is frequently used to obtain a scan of the human body.
The curve falls by half in a fixed time, so read the half-life by going from 100% across to the curve and then down to the time axis, and check it by seeing that the next halving takes the same time.
For (ii) the fraction remaining after a time $t$ is $(1/2)^{t/T_{1/2}}$, so substitute the half-life you read in (i) and keep the units of mass the same as the injected mass.
For (iii) the timing of a scan is a compromise between two opposing requirements: getting enough tracer into the organ being examined, and not letting the activity decay away or the patient be irradiated unnecessarily.
The diagrams shown are an MRI of the human upper arm, an X-ray of a human hand and a CAT scan of the human pelvis (hip bone) as seen in cross-section from above.
Procedure times: MRI 30–60 minutes; X-ray 5 minutes; CAT scan 40 minutes.
Before choosing a scan, list what each of the three techniques uses (X-rays, sound, a strong magnetic field) and what that implies about the risk to the patient.
For (i) you are comparing an MRI with a CAT scan, so compare them on the same criteria: radiation risk, contrast between soft tissues, procedure time and cost. For (ii) you are given a specific clinical question, whether there is a break in the bone, so ask which imaging method shows bone best and which is quickest and safest for that.
For (iii) the question has moved from bone to brain tissue, so choose the scan that images soft tissue best and justify the choice against the alternatives.
Assess the impact of medical applications based on ultrasound and the magnetic field of particles within the body on modern society.
An assessment needs more than a list of uses: for each application say what the physics allows it to do, what benefit that brings to patients, and what limits its use.

Finish with an overall judgement, including who gains most from these techniques and where they are still not available.

questions.text:
The star Algol is an eclipsing binary as viewed from Earth.
Describe the observations made by astronomers to identify a star as an eclipsing binary.
Part (i) asks what an astronomer actually sees, so describe the light curve rather than the physics: what happens to the brightness, how often it happens, and how the pattern differs from another regular variable.
Part (ii) turns an observation into a mass. Ask which measured quantities describe the orbit, and which law relates the period of an orbit to the size of that orbit and the mass it encloses.
Binary stars are important in determining stellar masses.
Explain how the total mass of a binary star system can be calculated.
The table gives information about various nearby stars.
The three sub-parts use three different columns of the table. Part (i) is about colour, which is set by temperature, and the table gives a column that orders the stars by colour.
Part (ii) needs the difference in apparent magnitude, and the useful relationship is that a difference of one magnitude is a fixed ratio in brightness, not a fixed difference in intensity.
Part (iii) is a drawing question. The parallax angle is the angle the star appears to move through as the Earth moves sideways in its orbit, so the diagram needs the Sun, the Earth's orbital radius as the baseline, and the angle at the star.
An H-R diagram can be used to show the evolutionary track of stars.
For (i) decide what two properties a white dwarf has, how small it is and how hot it is, and use $L = 4\pi R^{2}\sigma T^{4}$ to work out which corner of the diagram that puts it in. Read the axes of the printed diagram carefully, because the temperature scale runs backwards.
For (ii) ask what stops a normal star from collapsing: it is the pressure of the nuclear reactions. Then ask what could provide an outward pressure in a star that has no fuel left.
For (iii) name one specific fusion reaction and write down both its reactants and its products; 'hydrogen fuses' on its own will not earn the marks.
Discuss how the development of adaptive optics and at least one other development have improved resolution and sensitivity of ground based astronomy.
Start by being precise about the two things being improved: resolution is the ability to separate two nearby sources, and sensitivity is the ability to detect a faint source. They have different causes and different cures.
For resolution, work out what limits a ground-based telescope: the aperture sets one floor and the atmosphere sets a much worse one. Then ask how each development attacks that particular limit. For sensitivity, ask how much light is collected and how efficiently it is recorded.
A strong response weighs the developments against each other and against what still limits ground-based astronomy, rather than simply listing them.

questions.text:
Describe Davisson and Germer's experiment that confirmed the de Broglie hypothesis of wave-particle duality.
For (i), what has to be justified is not just that electrons were diffracted but that the diffraction pattern was consistent with the wavelength de Broglie predicted for the electrons actually used. State the crystal, the measured quantity and the comparison.
For (ii), start from de Broglie's relation and ask what has to be true about the circumference of the orbit if the electron is to be a stationary state. Then show that this condition is equivalent to Bohr's quantum condition on angular momentum.
Explain the stability of the electron orbits in the Bohr atom, using de Broglie's hypothesis.
The diagram shows the kinetic energy distribution of the electrons emitted in the $\alpha$-decay of ${}^{210}_{83}\mathrm{Bi}$ into ${}^{210}_{84}\mathrm{Po}$. The energy released during $\alpha$-decay depends on the mass defect in the transmutation, as it does in nuclear fission.
Identify the scientist who suggested that the existence of the neutrino relates to the need to account for the energy distribution of electrons.
The graph is the key. A line spectrum has a definite end-point and a continuous spectrum does not, so decide what the value of the end-point tells you about the energy available in the decay before you look at anything else.
For the mass defect, write the masses on each side of the decay and subtract them in that order, parent minus products. Convert to kilograms with $1\,\mathrm{u} = 1.661\times10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}$ before using $E = \Delta mc^{2}$.
The neutrino is introduced only to rescue a conservation law. Work out which of energy and momentum would be violated if the electron were the only particle emitted.
Use the data to calculate the mass defect.
Account for the energy distribution of electrons.
The diagram represents the four spectral lines in the visible region of the hydrogen spectrum known as the Balmer Series.
Look at which energy level every one of the four lines has in common. Once that is identified the series is fully defined and the wavelength of any line is fixed by the difference between that level and the upper level.
The four lines shown come from upper levels of 3, 4, 5 and 6, so the next line comes from the next whole number. Use $\frac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\frac{1}{n_f^{2}} - \frac{1}{n_i^{2}}\right)$ with $R = 1.097\times10^{7}\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}$.
Part (i) is an argument, not a description: state what Bohr's model predicts, state what is observed, and then say why no competing model could produce that result.
Discuss how neutron scattering and ONE other process have been used to increase our understanding of the structure of matter.
The marking scheme rewards a logical discussion, not two unrelated descriptions, so fix the plan first: for each process say what is sent in, what it interacts with, what is measured, and what can be concluded about structure from that measurement.
For each process also give one piece of evidence about the structure of matter that it produced and one modern use. The 'one other process' is your choice - X-ray diffraction, electron diffraction and alpha-particle scattering all qualify.

questions.text:
A student performed a first-hand investigation to examine projectile motion. A ball resting on a horizontal table was given an initial push at $X$, resulting in the ball following the path $XYZ$ as shown. A data logger used the motion sensor to measure the horizontal distance to the ball. When the ball was at position $Y$, a distance of $1.50\,\mathrm{m}$ from the motion sensor, it left the edge of the table. In the first trial, the range was $0.60\,\mathrm{m}$. The graph below was obtained from the data logger.
For this trial, determine the horizontal speed of the ball as it left the edge of the table.
While the ball is on the table it travels in a straight horizontal line, so the gradient of the motion sensor's distance-time line is its horizontal speed. The gradient is given in the box on the graph, so read it from there rather than measuring the slope yourself, and ignore the y-intercept, which only records where the ball was when logging began.
The experiment was repeated with the ball leaving the table at different speeds. Graph the relationship between the range and the horizontal speed at $Y$. Identify on your graph the results from the first trial.
Before drawing anything, work out how the range depends on the horizontal speed. The height of the table is the same in every trial, so the time the ball takes to reach the floor is the same in every trial, and the range is that fixed time multiplied by the horizontal speed. Ask what that implies about the shape of the graph and about where the line starts.
Plot range on the vertical axis and the horizontal speed at $Y$ on the horizontal axis, both with units, then use the first trial's data, $(1.85,\,0.60)$, to check that your line passes through the right place.
The apparatus described in this first-hand investigation was used to carry out an identical experiment on another planet where the acceleration due to gravity is less than that on Earth. The horizontal speed of the ball as it left the table on the planet was the same as in part (a). Compare the range of the ball on the planet to that on Earth. Explain your answer.
The horizontal speed at $Y$ is the same on the planet as on Earth, so the range can only differ if the time of flight differs. From $t = \sqrt{2h/g}$ decide which way the time of flight changes when $g$ is smaller, holding the table height fixed.
Then check the direction of your answer against the graph from part (b): the gradient of range against speed is the time of flight, so a larger gradient means a larger range for the same speed.

questions.text:
A satellite of mass $150\,\mathrm{kg}$ is launched from Earth's surface into a uniform circular orbit of radius $7.5\times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{m}$.
Calculate the magnitude of the gravitational potential energy $E_p$ of the satellite.
With zero gravitational potential energy assigned at infinite distance, a satellite in a radial field around a planet has negative potential energy: $E_p = -\frac{GMm}{r}$. Decide which of the two masses in the question is $M$ and which is $m$ before you substitute, and remember that $r$ is the distance from the centre of the Earth.
Keep the powers of ten straight when you divide by the $7.5\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{m}$ radius, and note that the question asks for the magnitude, so the value you report is $|E_p|$.
From this uniform circular orbit, the satellite can escape Earth's gravitational field when its kinetic energy is equal to the magnitude of the gravitational potential energy. Use this relationship to calculate the escape velocity of the satellite.
The stem states the escape condition for you: at escape the kinetic energy equals the magnitude of the potential energy. Write $\frac{1}{2}mv^{2} = |E_p|$ and rearrange for $v$, not for the energy, so that the quantity actually asked for comes out of the working.
The satellite's mass cancels, so you can substitute your part (a) answer directly even if you think it is wrong. As a check on the size of the result, an escape speed for a body in orbit close to the Earth should be of order $10^{4}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
Discuss the effect of Earth's rotational motion on the launch of this satellite.
The satellite is already moving before the rocket fires, because the launch site is carried round by the Earth's rotation. Which direction of launch gives the satellite the largest share of the speed it already has?
Then connect the direction to the practical consequence: what does the rocket no longer have to supply, and how does that translate into fuel?

Outline TWO features of the aether model for the transmission of light.

Avoid answering with physical properties of aether on their own. The 2003 guidelines record that candidates who listed properties such as rigidity or low density instead of features of the model did not attract the second mark.

The predicted result has to follow from the model. If the aether exists, the time taken by light to travel out and back along the arm that lies along Earth's direction of motion should differ from the time along the arm at right angles to it, and rotating the apparatus swaps which arm is which.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / Electromagnetism / Electromagnetic Induction / analyse applications of step-up and step-down transformers, including but not limited to: the distribution of energy using high-voltage transmission lines
questions.text:
The original paper gives this question no shared stem: parts (a) and (b) are standalone prompts about transformers. Answer both parts below; each part carries its own full answer, worked solution and marking criteria.
Explain the relationship between the current in the primary coil and the current in the secondary coil of an ideal step-down transformer in relation to the conservation of energy.
For an ideal transformer nothing is lost, so the power into the primary must equal the power out of the secondary: $V_pI_p = V_sI_s$.
Then bring in the turns relation $V_p/V_s = N_p/N_s$. Decide which voltage is the larger for a step-down transformer, and let conservation of energy fix which current is the larger.
Explain why a transformer will work in an AC circuit but not in a DC circuit.
Begin from $|\varepsilon| = N|\Delta\Phi/\Delta t|$. A secondary emf needs a changing flux, so ask separately what an AC primary current does to the core flux and what a DC primary current does.
Adding the switching case shows the difference cleanly: a DC supply produces a brief pulse of induced emf only at the instant it is switched on or off, and nothing at all once it is steady.

This question concerns superconductivity and the magnetic fields they produce. Part (a) explains why a magnet is able to hover above a superconducting disk. Part (b) compares the model for the conduction of electricity in metals at room temperature with the model for conduction of electricity in superconductors below the critical temperature.
The following image shows a magnet hovering above a superconducting disk. Explain why the magnet is able to hover above the superconductor.
The key is the superconducting state: zero resistance and expulsion of magnetic flux (the Meissner effect), which is produced by persistent screening currents in the surface of the disk.
Use the direction rule for induced currents to fix the sense of those screening currents, and hence the direction of the force on the magnet. Then say explicitly that the magnet is stationary, so the upward magnetic force must equal the weight.
Compare the model for the conduction of electricity in metals at room temperature with the model for conduction of electricity in superconductors below the critical temperature.
Set the two models out in the same order before comparing them: what carries the charge, what happens to those charge carriers in the lattice, and what happens to the energy that is supplied.
Three marks come from one similarity plus two differences, or from three clean differences. Write each point as an explicit comparison, for example 'in a metal ... whereas in a superconductor ...'.

questions.text:
A physics student was conducting an investigation on the photoelectric effect. The student used an infrared laser with a wavelength of $1.55\times 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m}$ for this investigation.
Calculate the energy of a photon from this laser.
Eliminate the frequency: from $E = hf$ and $c = f\lambda$ you get $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$, so the wavelength given in the stem is all you need.
Substitute the data-sheet values $h = 6.626\times10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\,s}$ and $c = 3.00\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, keeping the wavelength in metres. The result is of order $10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$, which is a useful check on the powers of ten.
When the laser light was shone onto a photo-cell, no current was detected. The student increased the intensity of the light but still detected no current. Explain this observation.
Emission of a photoelectron requires a minimum energy in a single photon, because the electron has to escape the metal's surface. Compare the energy of one photon from this laser, from part (a), with that threshold.
Then separate the two quantities that can be adjusted: the number of photons arriving each second, and the energy carried by each photon. Only one of them decides whether electrons are emitted at all, and the other only decides how many.

questions.text:
Geophysics
Identify THREE principal methods used by geophysicists to investigate the structure of Earth and the properties of Earth materials. (1 mark)
The methods are named after the physical property each one measures, so list properties rather than instruments.
For the treaty part, ask what has to be compared against what in order to tell an explosion apart from an earthquake, and where that comparison is carried out.
Describe the role that geophysicists play in the monitoring of nuclear test-ban treaties. (2 marks)
Summarise the geophysical evidence that supports the theory of plate tectonics.
Give each item as an observation plus the plate-tectonic process it supports, rather than as a bare fact.
The magnetic stripes in the ocean floor and the distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes are the two that are unambiguously geophysical - use those first if you are short of time.
Three distinct pieces of evidence reach the top band; two discussed in depth also reach it.
Describe how absorption and reflection of radiation can provide information about a reflecting surface. (2 marks)
Part (i) is about what the radiation returning from a surface tells you - intensity, wavelength, or both.
For part (ii) you need two separate things: how the fire spreads now, and how the vegetation recovers afterwards.
Compare the images mentally: what in a single image tells you where the fire is, and what a change between two images tells you about the past.
The picture below shows a satellite image of a bushfire burning in a forested area. Images such as the one below can be used as a part of the process of monitoring changes in vegetation.
Explain how remote-sensing techniques can be used to monitor the spread of a bushfire, and the regrowth of vegetation in regions affected by a bushfire. (3 marks)
Outline the structure and function of a geophone. (2 marks)
For the geophone, identify what is stationary and what moves relative to it, and what electrical quantity that relative motion produces.
On the travel-time graph the two lines cross because one wave has the faster speed but the greater initial delay - ask which of them has further to travel at short distances.
For the speed, remember the graph plots time against distance, so the gradient is the reciprocal of the speed and has to be inverted.
The method of seismic refraction is depicted in the diagram below. A series of eight geophones, G1 to G8, are arranged in a straight line along level ground. They are each separated by a distance of $10\,\mathrm{m}$. At a distance of $20\,\mathrm{m}$ from the first geophone, a hammer is used to strike the ground to produce seismic waves. The geophones are attached to a seismograph that records the time of arrival of the waves after the hammer strikes the ground.
The data from the geophones are analysed and the arrival times of the direct and refracted waves that reach each geophone are recorded. These data are shown in the graph on page 33. On the graph, a circle represents the arrival of the first wave to reach a geophone, and a square represents the arrival time of the second wave to reach a geophone. The points on the graph associated with the direct seismic wave and the refracted seismic wave are shown.
(1) Explain why the line for the refracted wave crosses the line for the direct wave on the graph. (2 marks)
(2) From the graph, calculate the speed of the direct wave in the soft rock layer. (2 marks)
Outline the application of Newton's theory of universal gravitation to the field of geophysics, and discuss how information obtained from gravity surveys has led to a greater understanding of the structure of Earth.
This part has two halves joined by one link: state Newton's law, say how $g$ is measured locally, and then say what that measurement reveals.
The link is density: because $g$ depends on the mass and therefore the density of the material beneath a point, a departure from the expected value means the structure is not what was assumed.
For the top band, name the concrete things gravity surveys have mapped - not just 'hidden structure'.

Identify the property of the hydrogen nucleus that makes it useful in magnetic resonance imaging.
For MRI, ask what the hydrogen nucleus must be able to do in a strong external field for the technique to work at all.
For the X-ray tube, account for the energy: an electron is given kinetic energy by the accelerating voltage, so where does that energy go when the electron reaches the anode?
There are two contributions to the X-ray beam. One produces a continuous range of photon energies and the other produces only a few discrete lines.
Describe how X-rays are produced when electrons strike the anode in an X-ray tube.
Outline the production of gamma rays and their use in the diagnostic procedure of positron emission tomography (PET).
Track the sequence: what the radiopharmaceutical emits, what that particle then does in the tissue, and what the detectors register as a result.
The arrangement of the detectors is the clue - why must two detectors on opposite sides of the body fire at the same time?
Think about how much of the radiation reaches a detector depending on how much tissue lies in its path.
This question refers to the bone scan of a person with cancer, and a chest X-ray of a healthy person. (The printed stimulus images are copyright placeholders in the source PDF and are not reproduced here.)

For the second half, ask what an X-ray image of bone shows and what a bone scan image of the same bone shows - anatomy or activity.
The strongest answers state explicitly that the source is external in one case and internal in the other, and that the contrast has a different origin in each.
This question refers to the bone scan of a person with cancer, and a chest X-ray of a healthy person. (The printed stimulus images are copyright placeholders in the source PDF and are not reproduced here.)

Define the term resolution of a telescope.
For the definition, say what the instrument must be able to do to two objects, and express that as a minimum angular separation.

Your description should mention what is measured and what is then adjusted.
Describe ONE method by which the resolution of a ground-based system can be improved.
An H-R diagram for the globular cluster M3 is shown below. The stars in the Lyrae gap have an absolute magnitude of 0.6. Use this information and their position on the H-R diagram to determine the distance of M3 from Earth.
The apparent magnitude is not given - read it off the horizontal axis of the H-R diagram at the marked square.
The distance modulus is the difference between apparent and absolute magnitude, and it is logarithmic, so a small difference in magnitude corresponds to a large factor in distance.
Watch the units: the relation is written in terms of a distance in parsecs referred to a standard distance of $10\,\mathrm{pc}$.

Line the two spectra up and compare the positions of corresponding dark lines, not their brightnesses.
For the absorption spectrum, radiation has to be produced somewhere and then pass through something else on its way out - both stages matter.
For the temperature part, the species that can exist depend on temperature: ionised atoms, then neutral atoms, then molecules.
The H-R diagram for a cluster is shown below.
For the age of the cluster, look at where the main sequence stops and whether hot blue stars survive on it.

questions.text:
From Quanta to Quarks
Identify the structure of the Rutherford model of the atom.
Rutherford's model came from alpha-particle scattering through a thin foil, so ask what the rare large deflections and the rare pass-throughs forced him to propose.
Bohr's refinement answers a specific failure of that model: a charged particle accelerating in an orbit is supposed to radiate, which would make the electron spiral into the nucleus.
The refinement has two linked ideas - where the electron is allowed to be, and what happens when it changes state.
Describe how Bohr refined Rutherford's model of the hydrogen atom.
The table below shows the different types of quarks and their charge. The standard model of matter says that protons and neutrons are composed of up and down quarks. There are three quarks in each particle.
Compare protons and neutrons in terms of their quark composition.
Use the charge column to work backwards: three quarks must add up to the charge of the particle.
Try $uud$ and check the total, then $udd$ and check again.
Finish by stating what the comparison shows, not just listing the two compositions.
The equations shown below describe three different types of transmutation reactions involving uranium.
For (i), ask what each reaction needs before it can happen: does it require a neutron to arrive, or energy to be supplied, or does it occur on its own?
Check which of the nuclides involved are naturally occurring isotopes.
For (ii), pick the reaction used in reactors or weapons and follow the chain: what happens to the neutrons it releases?
The two graphs below show the gravitational and electrostatic forces acting between two protons in the nucleus of an atom.
Both forces have the same dependence on distance, so calculate each one at the stated separation using its own law and the values of $G$, $k$, $m_p$ and $e$.
Compare the two answers by orders of magnitude, because the ratio between them is the whole point of the next part.
For the strong force properties, think about what lets it hold a nucleus together yet stops every nucleus collapsing to a point.
Describe the requirements for a nuclear fission explosion, and describe how these are controlled in a nuclear reactor.
List the requirements for an uncontrolled chain reaction first, then ask what a reactor does about each of them.
The link between the two cases is neutron economy: what happens to the neutrons produced, and how many are needed to keep the reaction going?
Name the specific components that control the neutron population and the neutron energy in a reactor.

Identify ONE electronic system that is digital, and ONE electronic system that is analogue.
One word for each system: which quantity does it process as discrete steps, and which as a continuously varying quantity?
For the graphs, plot output voltage against time and ask whether the voltage can take any value between the limits or only a few fixed ones.

Use diagrams to describe the variation between digital and analogue voltage outputs with time.
Construct a truth table showing the outputs at P, Q and R for each of the possible input states of A and B in the following circuit.
Trace the circuit from the inputs: find the gate fed directly by $A$, and note carefully what each gate's two inputs actually are - one of them is the output of the previous gate, not the raw input.
Fill $P$ for all four rows first, then use those values to fill $Q$, then use $Q$ to fill $R$.
When the table is complete, check for a pattern: is $R$ ever 1, and under exactly what condition?
The graph below shows how the density of transistors on a silicon chip has increased over the last 30 years.

The circuit below uses a thermistor as a temperature sensor to control the operation of a relay. The relay will close when the voltage across the relay coil is greater than 6 volts. The resistance of the thermistor, $R_\text{THERM}$, is given in the graph.

questions.text:
In July 1969 the Apollo 11 Command Module with Michael Collins on board orbited the Moon waiting for the Ascent Module to return from the Moon's surface. The mass of the Command Module was $9.98\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{kg}$, its period was 119 minutes, and the radius of its orbit from the Moon's centre was $1.85\times10^{6}$ metres.
Assuming the Command Module was in circular orbit, calculate the mass of the Moon.
Both quantities come from the same pair of ideas: the gravitational force on the Command Module supplies the centripetal force for the circular orbit, and the law of periods relates $r^{3}$ to $T^{2}$ for a fixed central mass.
Convert the period from minutes to seconds before substituting, since the formulae are in SI units. Part (ii) can be done without part (i) at all, from the definition of orbital speed.
Calculate the magnitude of the orbital velocity of the Command Module.
The docking of the Ascent Module with the Command Module resulted in an increase in mass of the orbiting spacecraft. The spacecraft remained at the same altitude. This docking procedure made no difference to the orbital speed. Justify this statement.
Equate the gravitational and centripetal forces for the orbiting spacecraft, $GMm/r^{2} = \dfrac{mv^{2}}{r}$, and then cancel $m$ and look at what is left.
A useful cross-check is the law of periods, $\dfrac{r^{3}}{T^{2}} = \dfrac{GM}{4\pi^{2}}$, which contains no mass of the orbiting body at all. Say what actually changed in the docking and which of the remaining quantities it touched.

questions.text:
A car with a mass of $800\ \mathrm{kg}$ travels at a constant speed of $7.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ on a roundabout so that it follows a circular path with a radius of $16\ \mathrm{m}$.
A person observing this situation makes the following statement.
‘There is no net force acting on the car because the speed is constant and the friction between the tyres and the road balances the centripetal force acting on the car.’
Assess this statement. Support your answer with an analysis of the horizontal forces acting on the car, using the numerical data provided above.

questions.text:
On 11 June 2003 the Mars Rover called Spirit was launched on a satellite from Earth when the planets were in the positions shown in the diagram below. The satellite arrived at Mars on 3 December 2003.
Indicate on the diagram the approximate positions of Earth and Mars on 3 December 2003 and show the satellite's trajectory to Mars.
Work from orbital periods, not from the picture. Count the days from 11 June to 3 December, divide by 365.25 days for Earth and by 687 days for Mars, and turn each fraction into an angle round the orbit.
Both planets move anticlockwise as the diagram is drawn, since it is a view from above the north pole. Mark the arrival positions on the orbit circles at those angles from the launch positions.
The trajectory is not a straight line. It is part of an ellipse with the Sun at one focus, leaving Earth's orbit tangentially at the launch point and arriving tangentially at Mars's orbit at the arrival point; sketching it on the printed diagram is part of the answer.
Discuss the effect of Earth's motion on the launch and trajectory to Mars of this satellite.
Separate the satellite's velocity after launch into the part supplied by the rocket motors and the part it already had from the Earth's own motion, and say which way each contribution points.
The Earth contributes twice: once from its rotation about its axis, and once from its revolution about the Sun. Then add the geometric point about why the launch had to happen at this particular place in Earth's orbit.

questions.text:
Parts (a) and (b) of this question refer to a small two-pole direct current (DC) motor.
The diagram shows a two-pole DC motor as constructed by a student. Identify THREE mistakes in the construction of this DC motor as shown in the diagram.
Start with the field. A motor needs a field that runs across the coil, so check which way each magnet is labelled on the face that points at the coil.
Then trace the electrical path. Ask whether the brushes are insulated from the metal base plate, and whether the coil is wound on something that is part of the metal axle and therefore part of the circuit.
Three separate errors are needed for the full marks, so keep going round the drawing (magnets, brushes, coil core, axle, frame) rather than stopping at the first two.
An ammeter was used to measure the current through a small DC motor. While it was running freely, a current of $2.09\ \mathrm{A}$ was recorded. While the motor was running, the axle of the motor was held firmly, preventing it from rotating, and the current was then recorded as $2.54\ \mathrm{A}$. Explain this observation.
This is a back-emf question. While the coil turns in the magnetic field, the flux linking it changes, so an emf is induced in the coil itself and, by Lenz's law, it opposes the supply.
The back emf is a voltage, not a current, so write the running motor as a voltage balance $V = \varepsilon_{back} + IR$. Then ask what happens to that induced emf when the axle is held and the coil stops turning.

The equation is given as $T$ in terms of $l$ and $g$, so square it before substituting to isolate $g$.
Convert $40.0\,\mathrm{cm}$ to metres and keep $1.268\,\mathrm{s}$ to four figures - the answer depends on $T^{2}$, so the rounding propagates.

Explain the uses of satellites in providing information about Earth. Include in your answer a comparison of geostationary and low Earth orbits, proposing which would be preferred for remote sensing.

Sub-part (ii) asks how the image is built, so organise it as emission, reflection at boundaries, reception, time of flight, brightness - and finish by explaining why the skulls of the twins appear as bright outlines.

questions.text:
Section II — Astrophysics (25 marks). Attempt this question OR one other from Questions 28 to 32.
Identify the initial and final elements of the principal sequence of nuclear reactions for a star on the Main Sequence.
Both sub-parts are limited by the same word: Main Sequence. Name only what happens while the star is on the Main Sequence, or only the very next stage after it.
For (ii), 'initially' means the first stage after the Main Sequence, and the energy source in the core is nuclear fusion converting mass into energy.
Identify the type of star that the Sun will initially turn into after it completes its Main Sequence evolution. State the main source of energy in the core at this stage.
The apparent magnitudes of three stars are measured with a telescope equipped with a camera, first with a red filter placed in front of the detector, and then with a blue filter placed in front of it. The absolute magnitudes of the three stars can be determined from their spectra, and are listed in the fourth column of the table for the red filter. The results are shown in the table.
Use the data in the table to determine which is the bluest of these three stars.
Two colours means you are being asked for a difference of magnitudes, not a sum. Fix the sign convention first: a star that is relatively brighter in the blue has a smaller (more negative) blue magnitude than red magnitude.
For the distance, the fourth column is the absolute magnitude - the apparent magnitude the star would have at 10 pc - so the difference between the second and fourth columns is the distance modulus.
Be careful with the exponent: it must be $(m - M)/5 + 1$, not $(m - M)/5$.
Calculate the distance to Rigel in parsecs.
Describe how the spectrum of a star can be used to determine its temperature, chemical composition and aspects of its motion.
Begin by naming what is actually present in the spectrum: a continuous part and a set of dark lines. Everything the question asks for then follows from which of the two you use.
Each of the three quantities the question asks about is read from a different part of the spectrum - the continuum, the positions of the lines, and the shifts and widths of the lines.
For motion, distinguish the shift of the whole pattern, which gives motion along the line of sight, from the broadening and splitting of individual lines, which gives rotation.
Describe the features of this light curve that suggest that the astronomer is observing an eclipsing binary system.
Three numbers come straight off the light curve and nothing else does: the interval between dips, the intensity between dips, and the intensity at the bottom of a dip. Write them down first.
In (ii) equal masses means each star orbits the centre of mass at half the separation - do not use the full separation as the orbital radius.
In (iii) you are given $I \propto \pi r^{2}$, so the blocked fraction of the light gives a ratio of AREAS, and areas go as the square of radii.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / Advanced Mechanics / Circular Motion / solve problems, model and make quantitative predictions about objects executing uniform circular motion in a variety of situations, using the following relationships: | Year 12 / Advanced Mechanics / Motion in Gravitational Fields / predict quantitatively the orbital properties of planets and satellites in a variety of situations, including near the Earth and geostationary orbits, and relate these to their uses (ACSPH101)
questions.text:
From nearest to furthest, the four satellite moons of Jupiter first observed by Galileo in the year 1610 are called Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto. For the first three moons, the orbital period $T$ of each is exactly twice the period of the one orbiting immediately inside it. That is,
The mass of Jupiter is $1.90 \times 10^{27}\,\mathrm{kg}$, and the orbital radius of Io is 421 600 km.
Use Kepler's Law of Periods to calculate Ganymede's orbital radius.
Use the law of periods as a ratio: write $\dfrac{r^{3}}{T^{2}} = \dfrac{GM}{4\pi^{2}}$ for Io and for Ganymede, then divide the two equations so that $G$ and Jupiter's mass cancel and only the ratio of radii and the ratio of periods remain.
Take care with the period ratio: Ganymede's period is four times Io's, not two, because the doubling in the stem happens twice. Then convert Io's orbital radius to metres before using it.
Calculate Ganymede's orbital speed.
Equate the gravitational force on Ganymede to the centripetal force required for its orbit, $GMm/r^{2} = \dfrac{mv^{2}}{r}$, and cancel $m$ to obtain $v$.
Substitute the data-sheet value of $G$, the mass of Jupiter from the stem, and the orbital radius you obtained in part (a), making sure the radius is in metres rather than kilometres.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / The Nature of Light / Light and Special Relativity / analyse and evaluate the evidence confirming or denying Einstein’s two postulates: | Year 12 / The Nature of Light / Light and Special Relativity / investigate the evidence, from Einstein’s thought experiments and subsequent experimental validation, for time dilation and length contraction , and analyse quantitatively situations in which these are observed, for example: observations of cosmic-origin muons at the Earth’s surface; atomic clocks (Hafele–Keating experiment); evidence from particle accelerators; evidence from cosmological studies
questions.text:
Einstein's 1905 theory of special relativity made several predictions that could not be verified for many years.
State ONE such prediction.
The prediction has to be something that two observers, moving relative to one another, could in principle measure differently. State it as a comparison between what each observer measures, and make sure it concerns a time or a length rather than a vague statement about time 'passing'.
Describe an experiment to test this prediction.
A test of time dilation needs a clock that has travelled and a clock that has not, both readable afterwards so that they can be compared. Ask what precision timing equipment could be carried on a commercial aircraft, and what should happen to the travelling clocks in the two directions around the world.
Do not stop at a description of the apparatus: the two marks need the stationary reference clock and the comparison after the journey, as well as the travelling clocks themselves.
Explain how technological advances since 1905 have made it possible to carry out this experiment.
Two things were missing in 1905 and both had to be supplied: a measuring instrument whose accumulated error was smaller than the effect, and a vehicle whose speed was large enough for the effect to be appreciable. Treat them separately.
For each, make the link quantitative where you can: how accurate did the clock have to be compared with the best clock of 1905, and how much of the effect would an aircraft travelling at a 1905 speed have produced?
