questions.current_path: Year 12 / Electromagnetism / The Motor Effect / conduct a quantitative investigation to demonstrate the interaction between two parallel current-carrying wires
questions.text:
Two thin metal tubes one metre long were supported in a vertical wooden rack as shown in the diagram.
The two ends were connected together, then the other two ends were connected briefly to a car battery as shown in the diagram. It was observed that one of the tubes jumped upward as the connection was made.
Explain why only one tube jumped upward.
Trace the whole circuit, from one battery terminal through the link at the far end and back again. That tells you which way the current runs in each of the two tubes.
Once you have the two directions, use the rule for what parallel conductors carrying currents in the same direction do to each other, and then ask why only one of the two tubes can move.
Each tube has a mass of $1 \times 10^{-2}$ kg, and the tubes lie on the rack 10 cm apart. What minimum current flows when one tube jumps?
At the moment the tube jumps, the upward magnetic force between the tubes equals its weight. Write both: the force between two long parallel wires each carrying current $I$ is $\frac{\mu_0 I^{2}L}{2\pi r}$, and the weight is $mg$.
Solve for $I$ and substitute in SI units, using metres, kilograms and $\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{T\,m\,A^{-1}}$. As a check, the result should be of order hundreds of amperes, which is what makes connecting a car battery to a bare conductor violent.
What is the implication of this result for power distribution networks?
The current required in part (b) was enormous. Ask how the force between two neighbouring cables depends on the current they carry, and on how far apart they are.
Then turn that into something a network designer can actually do about it.

questions.current_path: Year 11 / Electricity and Magnetism / Electric Circuits / investigate quantitatively the application of the law of conservation of energy to the heating effects of electric currents, including the application of and variations of this involving Ohm’s Law (ACSPH043)
questions.text:
A schematic diagram of a system to supply electricity to a house is shown below.
The step-down transformer in the substation has a turns ratio of 30 : 1.
What is the voltage carried by the high voltage transmission line?
For a transformer, $\frac{V_p}{V_s} = \frac{N_p}{N_s}$. Work out which transformer in the schematic the 30:1 ratio belongs to, and which side of it the 11 000 V label sits on.
It is a step-down transformer, so the 30 has to be the primary-to-secondary ratio; the transmission line is the primary and therefore carries the higher of the two voltages.
Identify the causes of the two main energy losses in the transmission of electricity between the power plant and the house.
There are two places where energy is lost between the plant and the house, and each has its own mechanism. Ask first what happens in the transmission lines, using $P = I^{2}R$ and remembering how large the current in them is.
Then ask what the alternating flux in the iron of a transformer core does to the core itself. The core is a conductor, and the flux through it is changing.
Explain how the application of superconductivity could minimise energy loss in the system.
Begin with the definition: what happens to a material's resistance below its critical temperature? Then go back to the two losses you identified in part (b) and consider each in turn.
Do not stop at the definition. A mark is only earned when you say what happens to the resistive loss in the lines and to the eddy currents in the transformer cores, and remember that $I^{2}$ heating vanishes when $R$ is zero.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / The Nature of Light / Light: Quantum Model / analyse the photoelectric effect as it occurs in metallic elements by applying the law of conservation of energy and the photon model of light, (ACSPH119)
questions.text:
A student conducts an experiment using a photoelectric cell as shown in the diagram.
Light is shone through a grid onto a metal surface. The metal is at earth potential and the grid is at 100 V, so that any electrons emitted from the surface produce a current in the external circuit.
The student shines light sources of different photon energies onto the metal surface and records the current flowing for each. The light sources are adjusted so that their intensities are equal.
The results are recorded in the table and shown on the graph.
On the grid provided, draw the straight line of best fit in the region where the photo-current varies greatest with photon energy.
The current is essentially flat near zero below about $1.2\,\mathrm{eV}$ and flat again on the saturation plateau above about $2.2\,\mathrm{eV}$. “Varies greatest” means the steep section in between, so fit only those points.
Carry the fitted line back to the horizontal axis, because part (b) reads the intercept from it.
From the line drawn on your graph, estimate the minimum energy (work function) for photoelectric emission.
The minimum energy is the point at which the current falls to zero, so read off the photon energy at which the line from part (a) meets the horizontal axis.
Do not read the intercept off the lowest photon energy that happened to give a non-zero current. The small current at $1.20\,\mathrm{eV}$ is within the scatter of the experiment, and the extrapolated line is the better estimate of the threshold.
Remember what the quantity represents: this is the energy that has to be supplied to get an electron out of the metal at all, not the energy of a typical emitted electron.
The experiment is repeated, but the intensities of the light sources are doubled. Predict the results of this new experiment by drawing a second line on the graph.
Intensity controls how many photons arrive each second; it does not change the energy of any individual photon, so the threshold energy found in part (b) cannot move.
With more photons arriving per second at every photon energy, more electrons are released per second at every photon energy. Work out separately what that does to the gradient of the line and what it does to where the line meets the axis.
Justify the line you have drawn in part (c).
Make the justification in two separate steps: first the effect on the number of electrons leaving the surface each second, then the effect, or lack of effect, on the minimum photon energy.
Be precise in the first step. Doubling the intensity doubles the number of photons incident each second, not the energy of each photon, and the current measures electrons per second rather than energy per second.

questions.current_path: Year 11 / Electricity and Magnetism / Electrostatics / apply the electric field model to account for and quantitatively analyse interactions between charged objects using: (ACSPH103, ACSPH104); (ACSPH102)
questions.text:
The diagram shows two parallel horizontal metal plates connected to a DC source of electricity. Suspended between the plates is a charged particle of mass $9.6 \times 10^{-6}$ kg.
Using conventional symbols, draw the electric field between the metal plates on the diagram above.
Read the signs off the diagram first: one plate is marked positive and the other negative, and the particle hangs in the space between them.
Then recall the convention for field lines — they begin on positive charge and end on negative charge — together with the fact that between two large parallel plates they come out straight, parallel and evenly spaced.
Determine the magnitude of the electric field between the plates.
The field between two large parallel plates is uniform, so you do not need the field-line sketch from part (a) at all — the magnitude follows from the potential difference and the plate separation alone.
Use $E = V/d$ and check that the separation is in metres before you substitute; a number left in centimetres will not give an answer in the right range.
Determine the sign and magnitude of the charge on the particle if it is suspended motionless between the plates.
Suspended motionless means the net force is zero, so the upward electric force on the particle must be exactly equal to its downward weight. Write that balance down before substituting any numbers.
The sign is a separate step from the size. The field direction you drew in part (a) fixes which way the electric force can point for a given sign of charge, and only one sign will push the particle upwards against its weight.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / Electromagnetism / Charged Particles, Conductors and Electric and Magnetic Fields / acceleration, perpendicular to the field, of charged particles | Year 12 / The Nature of Light / Light and Special Relativity / describe the consequences and applications of relativistic momentum with reference to: | Year 12 / The Nature of Light / Light and Special Relativity / the limitation on the maximum velocity of a particle imposed by special relativity (ACSPH133)
questions.text:
Bubble chambers are used in conjunction with particle accelerators to photographically record the tracks of fast-moving charged particles. An intense magnetic field is applied at right angles to the path of the particles to deflect them according to their charge and momentum.
The diagram shows a beam of protons travelling horizontally at $6.0 \times 10^{7}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and entering a liquid hydrogen bubble chamber in a vertical magnetic field of 1.82 T.
Examination of the photograph taken by the camera, as sketched below, shows that the protons were deflected along a circular path of radius 0.350 metres.
Derive an expression for the momentum of a proton from the forces it experiences in this experiment.
A path that curves is a path with acceleration, and here the acceleration points at the centre of the circle. So the one force that is acting must be directed at the centre — write that force down in two different ways and let the common terms cancel.
Check the geometry before you start: the protons move horizontally, the field is vertical and the radius is vertical, so the velocity, the field and the radius are all at right angles to each other. That settles the angle in the motor-effect equation.
Calculate the mass of a proton in the bubble chamber.
Use the expression derived in part (a), with every quantity in SI units: the charge is a fundamental constant, the field in tesla and the radius in metres. Check that your momentum comes out in $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$ before going any further.
Be clear about which mass you are recovering. At $6.0 \times 10^{7}\,\mathrm{m/s}$ the protons are moving at a fifth of the speed of light, so the mass that comes out of $p = mv$ is the relativistic mass; part (c) asks for the other one.
Calculate the rest mass of a proton found from this experiment.
Relate the relativistic mass from part (b) back to the rest mass with the Lorentz factor. Work out $v/c$ as a single small number before substituting, so you can see roughly how much smaller the rest mass has to be.
Evaluate that factor rather than dropping it. It comes out close to one but not equal to one, which is exactly why it is so easy to drop and report the part (b) value unchanged — but the two masses are genuinely different quantities and the mark is for using the relationship correctly.

questions.current_path: Year 11 / Kinematics / Motion in a Straight Line / conduct practical investigations, selecting from a range of technologies, to record and analyse the motion of objects in a variety of situations in one dimension in order to measure or calculate: time; distance; displacement; speed; velocity; acceleration
questions.text:
Geophysics.
During your study of geophysics you investigated the radiation reflected from various surfaces.
(i) is a first-hand practical, so name the two detectors you would really have used: one that responds to ionising radiation and one that measures the strength and direction of Earth’s magnetic field.
(ii) is about remote sensing. For each method be explicit about the three stages: what is sent towards the surface, what comes back, and which property of the returned signal is measured. The time of flight and the strength of the return are different measurements and give different information, so do not use them interchangeably.
On 6 December 2004 a meteor exploded in the atmosphere above northern NSW. The blast was detected by sensitive microphones in Hobart at 5.25 am (AEST) and in Tennant Creek at 6.12 am (AEST).
AEST = Australian Eastern Standard Time
You do not need to know when the explosion happened. The explosion time is common to both paths, so subtract the two equations and the unknown disappears, leaving the extra distance equal to the extra travel time multiplied by the speed of sound.
Both times are quoted in AEST already, so the time difference is a pure difference in travel time. State the speed of sound you take from the Data Sheet before you substitute it.
(ii) is a design question, not a calculation. It needs three things: the structure of the instrument, what it measures, and how the measurements from several stations are combined into a position.
The development of technologies that increased our understanding of Earth's magnetic field led to the acceptance of the principle of plate tectonics.
Evaluate this statement.
An evaluation needs all three of these in order: the technologies, the physical evidence they produced, and an explicit judgement about how far that evidence supports the statement. A description without the final judgement cannot score in the top band.
Be concrete about the technology. “Magnets” is not enough; the instruments that made the difference were fluxgate and proton-precession magnetometers carried on land, on survey ships and on satellites, which map the present field and its rate of change.
The strongest evidence comes from the sea floor. List the two things that can be measured in the ocean crust, the pattern across the ridge and the age, and say what each one rules in or rules out.
When you judge, ask what the measurements can and cannot do. They are direct and quantitative about where the continents are now; are they equally direct about the force that moved them?
The diagram below shows the deflection of a plumb-bob near a large mountain range. The diagram exaggerates the amount of deflection.
(i) The bob is not being pushed sideways by anything; it is being pulled. Ask what extra mass the mountain adds to the Earth directly beneath the plumb line, and in which direction that extra mass attracts the bob.
(ii) Compare what was predicted with what was observed. If the observed deflection is smaller than the mountains alone can explain, the assumption about the density of the material underneath must be wrong in a particular direction, and the direction of the error is the clue.
(iii) The pendulum is the key: the same pendulum, taken to different places, gives the same period only if the field strength is the same everywhere. Use $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$ to connect the measured period to the shape of the Earth.

questions.current_path: Year 11 / Working scientifically / Planning Investigations / justify and evaluate the use of variables and experimental controls to ensure that a valid procedure is developed that allows for the reliable collection of data (ACSPH002)
questions.text:
Medical Physics.
The images show a person's heart before and after a medical procedure.
(i) Think about what a scan of the heart has to show. A region that is not being supplied with blood will take up less of the injected material and will therefore look different from healthy tissue.
(ii) Choose from the table using two criteria: the radiation has to be able to get out of the body so that it can be detected outside, and the half-life has to be long enough to complete the scan but short enough that the patient is clear of radiation quickly.
A third, weaker criterion is that the isotope should be available in a form that can be injected and that reaches the heart, so read the table for more than just the numbers.
The acoustic impedance of fat is $1.38 \times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$.
The acoustic impedance of bone is $7.80 \times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$.
(i) Two media with different acoustic impedances do not pass all the incident energy across the boundary. The proportion reflected depends only on the two impedances, so identify them, apply the impedance reflection expression, and only then convert to a percentage.
The reflection is large here because the mismatch in impedance is large. If your reflected fraction comes out close to one half, check that the ratio has been squared once and not twice.
(ii) This part is about physics, not about instruments. For each technique identify what is sent into the body, how the image is formed from the differences in what comes back, and whether the radiation is ionising.
The images demonstrate advances in the use of ultrasound as a tool in medical diagnosis.
Describe advances in technology that have enabled the improvements shown in these images, and discuss current issues that have arisen from these advances.
Keep the two halves of the answer separate and label them. First the technology that produced the improvement, then the issue, and for each issue say what specifically causes it.
For the technology, name the change at the level of the hardware or of the signal processing: the number and arrangement of elements in the transducer, the frequency used, or what is done to the returning echoes. “Better computers” is too vague to score.
The strongest issues arise from the fact that ultrasound is not ionising and so has no dose limit. Follow that through and ask what happens to the way the technology is used when the usual restraint on scanning is removed.
The following diagram shows the constituent parts of an MRI system.
(i) There are two components with quite different jobs. One creates and maintains a field; the other sends a signal at a very specific frequency and then listens. Say what each does to the hydrogen nuclei in the body.
(ii) A contrast agent improves a scan by changing the rate at which tissue recovers, not by adding contrast artificially. Work out which of the two tissues in the T1 curves is affected more, and what that does to the difference between them.
(iii) The comparison is with a technique that images the same organ by a different physical property. Ask what MRI measures in the body and what a CT scan measures, and then draw out the consequences for image quality, for patient risk and for the ability to image in any plane.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Origins of the Elements / account for the production of emission and absorption spectra and compare these with a continuous black body spectrum (ACSPH137) | Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Origins of the Elements / investigate the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram and how it can be used to determine the following about a star: characteristics and evolutionary stage; surface temperature; colour; luminosity
questions.text:
Astrophysics.
Part A of the figure shows the absorption spectrum of light, produced by an incandescent filament, after it has been shone through a quantity of hydrogen gas.
Also shown in the figure are the spectra obtained from two stars, Star Croesus in part B and Star Dromus in part C.
The dark lines are absorption bands in A, B and C.
Compare each star’s spectrum with spectrum A feature by feature: are the dark lines in the same places, are they in different places, or have they lost their sharpness?
A uniform displacement of every line and a loss of sharpness of the same lines are separate observations, so give a separate cause for each rather than one cause for both.
For (ii), ask what motion of the source produces each effect. A motion of the whole star along the line of sight shifts every line the same way; a rotation shifts the approaching limb one way and the receding limb the other way.
Photographs taken of a one arcsecond by one arcsecond sector of the night sky show a group of fixed stars. Scales have been added to the photographs. One star appears to change position, swinging backward and forward over a period of one year. Two photographic negatives taken when the star was at the furthest ends of its apparent travel are shown.
The star is marked X.
The star swings backwards and forwards over a year, which is exactly one orbital period, and the two negatives were taken at the two extremes of that swing. The angle you measure on the plate is therefore twice the parallax angle, so halve it before using the parallax formula.
Part (ii) gives absolute magnitudes and a distance, so the distance modulus is the route in. Once you have the two apparent magnitudes, the ratio of the brightnesses follows from the magnitude scale.
Be careful with the logarithm: $5\log_{10}(d/10)$ is negative for a distance of less than 10 pc, so in this case the apparent magnitude is numerically larger than the absolute magnitude.
The Hertsprung-Russell (or H-R) diagram relates the magnitude or brightness of stars to their spectral classes or temperatures.
Describe the technological advances that have made it possible to add astrophysical data to the H-R diagram, and explain how this data contributes to our understanding of stellar evolution.
This part has two halves that must be joined. First the technology, with enough detail to show what it measures that the older methods could not; then the effect the resulting data has on the picture of stellar evolution.
The technologies worth naming are the ones that changed the sensitivity or the range of wavelengths observed: photoelectric rather than photographic photometry, cooled detectors, spectrographs, and telescopes above the atmosphere.
The link to evolution is made by comparing populations, not individual stars. Once whole clusters and other galaxies can be measured, you can see the sequence of positions stars occupy as they age.
The graph shows the apparent magnitude of a supergiant star recorded over a period of time. The star is identified as a Type I Cepheid variable.
Read the period from the graph as the time between successive maxima, and remember that the light curve is of apparent magnitude, so moving up the axis means getting fainter, not brighter.
For (ii) the two dips in the second graph are not the same event. Ask which star is doing the blocking at each, and remember that the amount of light removed depends on which star is hidden.
For (iii), find the orbital period from the graph, convert it to seconds, and use the separation given. The orbital formula gives the sum of the two masses, so the mass ratio is what lets you get the smaller one.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Quantum Mechanical Nature of the Atom / relate qualitatively and quantitatively the quantised energy levels of the hydrogen atom and the law of conservation of energy to the line emission spectrum of hydrogen using: (ACSPH136) | Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Properties of the Nucleus / analyse the spontaneous decay of unstable nuclei, and the properties of the alpha, beta and gamma radiation emitted (ACSPH028, ACSPH030) | Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Properties of the Nucleus / model and explain the process of nuclear fission, including the concepts of controlled and uncontrolled chain reactions, and account for the release of energy in the process (ACSPH033, ACSPH034)
questions.text:
From Quanta to Quarks.
During your study of From Quanta to Quarks you either performed a first-hand investigation, or you gathered information to observe nuclear radiation using a Wilson cloud chamber, or similar detection device.
Below is a true-size photograph in this type of device showing the tracks made by $\alpha$-particles.
In a cloud chamber the visible track is the record of ionisation along the path of the particle, so the appearance of a track tells you how much ionisation the particle makes and how much it is deflected.
For (i) you need two separate properties: one that explains why the tracks are thick and short, and one that explains why they run straight.
For (ii), predict the tracks of the other two radiations before you write anything. One of them is neutral, which is a surprise for students who expect every particle to leave a mark.
Naturally occurring uranium-238 spontaneously disintegrates according to the equation
The thorium radionuclide undergoes further decay according to the equation
Both equations are printed unbalanced, and that is deliberate: the missing mass numbers and atomic numbers are what the questions ask for. Write the two conservation equations for each decay.
In (i) only the alpha particle and the gamma photon carry mass number away, and a photon has zero mass number, so the mass number of the thorium follows directly.
In (ii) remember that a beta particle carries one unit of negative charge and no mass number, so the daughter has the same mass number as the parent and an atomic number one greater.

questions.text:
A projectile leaves the ground at point A with velocity components as shown in the diagram. It follows the path given by the dotted line and lands at point B.
State the horizontal component of the projectile's velocity when it lands.
Consider what could accelerate the projectile horizontally. Once it has left the launch point the only force acting is gravity, and gravity acts vertically.
So ask what happens to a velocity component when there is no acceleration in that direction, and remember that the answer must include the direction as well as the value.
Find the magnitude of the initial velocity of the projectile.
The two components are perpendicular, so the launch velocity is the hypotenuse of the right triangle they form, and the components are the two shorter sides.
Use the Pythagorean relation on the components themselves. Do not add them, and do not take the larger one: the magnitude has to lie between the two components and closer to the larger.
Calculate the maximum height attained by the projectile.
The maximum height is reached when the vertical component of the velocity becomes zero, so begin by finding that time.
The horizontal motion is irrelevant to the height; do not let $u_{x}$ enter this part at all.
There are two equivalent routes: find the time to the top and substitute into $\Delta y = u_{y} t - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^{2}$, or use $v_{y}^{2} = u_{y}^{2} - 2g\Delta y$ directly with $v_{y} = 0$ at the top.
Calculate the range of the projectile, if it lands level with its starting position.
Because the projectile lands level with the point it was launched from, the upward part of the flight takes the same time as the downward part, so the total time of flight is twice the time to the top.
The range is then the constant horizontal velocity multiplied by that total time, not by the time to the top.
Check that no vertical distance is left to be accounted for at landing; the symmetric flight is exactly what makes this a single multiplication.

questions.text:
Gravimetric surveys collect raw gravity data which must be further processed by the application of a number of corrections. The following data table, map, and cross-section are the result of a small-scale gravimetric survey.
Reduction of the raw gravity data using latitude, free air and Bouguer corrections.
The data for station A, the datum station, has been processed as below: latitude correction $-(0 \times 0.8)$; free air correction $+(50 \times 0.3)$; Bouguer correction $-(0 \times 0.1)$; total correction $+15.0$; observed $g$ at station $979158.1$; corrected $g$ at station $979173.1$; corrected $g$ at datum station $979173.1$; gravity anomaly at station (corrected $g$ − corrected datum $g$) $0$.
Watch which height each correction uses: the latitude correction uses the distance south of the datum, the free-air correction uses height above sea level, and the Bouguer correction uses height above the datum station, which is at $50\,\mathrm{m}$ — not height above sea level.
Add the three corrections to the raw reading first, then compare each corrected reading with the corrected datum reading of $979173.1\,\mathrm{mgal}$. The datum station's own anomaly is zero by definition.
For the inference, ask what a Bouguer correction assumes: that the rock it has just removed has one particular density. A residual anomaly is therefore a statement about how the real density compares with that assumed value.
Seismic wave reflection and refraction, and the path of seismic waves through Earth.
For (i), think about what a marker looks for in a survey that times waves over a fixed line: the same source energy, the same geophone positions each time, more than one reading per station, and a graph rather than a single number.
For (ii), trace each ray in the diagram and ask why it is bent rather than straight. Then ask which of the two wave types could travel through the fluid outer core — the answer explains both the shape of the S-type path and the band of distances over which P-waves go missing.
Refraction, not insensitivity, causes the missing P-waves: at the core-mantle boundary the seismic velocity jumps, so rays are bent steeply downwards and miss the surface over a range of distances.
'Our understanding of Earth has changed as a result of developments in geophysics.' Discuss this statement with reference to the geophysical methods you have studied.

The link between the development and the knowledge is where the marks are, not the list of instruments.
Close by returning to the judgement and giving one genuine limitation of both methods together. A balanced conclusion scores above an unqualified one, and coherence and logical progression are marked separately from content.
Paleomagnetic patterns in the seabed and the calculation of sea-floor spreading rate.

For each technology, state which property of the electromagnetic spectrum makes it work (penetrating power, wavelength, ionising energy) and what clinical problem that property solves. The notes require the spectrum to be explicitly linked, not merely named.
Before restating the judgement, weigh the two costs: capital and maintenance cost, which limits access, and ionising dose, which is a small real risk for X-ray, CAT and PET but absent for MRI and endoscopy.
Bones can be viewed with a range of different medical imaging techniques. The images shown below were obtained using three different techniques.
Identify each image from what it records rather than from how it looks: one records the chemistry of the bone, one records its shape directly, and one is a computed reconstruction assembled from many projections.
For the comparison, choose criteria that apply to both techniques at once — cost, radiation dose, resolution, whether structures are superimposed, and what you can do with the result once you have it.
For the bone scan contrast, the decisive difference is that it images metabolic activity, so it can show disease while the bone still looks normal in shape. Say what that lets a clinician do earlier than with X-ray or CAT.

questions.text:
Binary star systems, stellar spectra, astronomical instruments and technologies, and stellar life cycles on the H-R diagram.
Binary star systems.
Read the graph for specific features rather than a general impression: say how many minima there are, how deep each is, and how far apart the minima are.
The spacing between minima is not necessarily the period. In an eclipsing binary the primary and secondary eclipses alternate, so they are separated by half the period.
For the distance, remember that an eclipsing binary's light curve alone gives no distance. The route to a distance is angular (parallax) or photometric (apparent versus absolute magnitude).
First-hand investigation into spectra, and the production of stellar absorption spectra.
For the practical, ask what a marker wants to see in a spectra investigation: the same viewing geometry for every source, a way of making the lines sharp, and more than one way of checking the result.
For the spectrum, remember Kirchhoff's three laws as three separate situations: a hot dense source, a hot thin gas, and a cool thin gas in front of a hot dense source.
The dark lines in an absorption spectrum come from the gas, not from the source. Work out which of the two is producing the continuous background and which is removing specific wavelengths from it.
Astronomers employ a range of instruments and techniques to observe celestial objects. Assess the impact of technological advances on our understanding of the cosmos.
Organise the response by spectral band (optical, radio, infrared, space-based) rather than by a random list, and for each instrument name one specific thing that became knowable only with that instrument.
An impact is a change in what we believe, not a better-looking picture. The marking notes require at least one advance other than optical or adaptive optics, and two or more distinct impacts on understanding.
Close with a value statement about at least one technology, and acknowledge the one real constraint on it, so that the final judgement is supported rather than asserted.
The Hertsprung-Russell (H-R) diagram depicts a possible life cycle path of a known star. The diagram appears in the published paper only as an 'Awaiting Copyright Clearance' placeholder.
Each labelled point on the path is a stage at which a particular fusion reaction stops or starts. Before reading any point off the diagram, work out what is fusing at each stage and what happens when that fuel runs out.
The class and mass of the star are fixed by where the path stops: a path ending in a white dwarf belongs to a low-mass star, a path continuing to the supergiants to a high-mass one.
For a very massive star, the reason the sequence ends abruptly is not that it runs out of fuel but that the fusion reactions become net energy-consuming. Check the binding energy per nucleon at the end of the sequence.

questions.text:
The Bohr model of the atom, the development of atomic theory, nuclear fission reactors, and particle accelerators and quarks.
The Bohr picture of the atom explains the energy of the photons emitted when an electron falls from an initial orbit $n_i$ to find an orbit of $n_f$. The various energies depend upon the quantity $n_f/n_i$ and the values for this term are given in the table.
Table of values of $n_f/n_i$ for values of $n_i$ and $n_f$ from 1 to 6.
The blanks are all in the region where $n_f$ is greater than or equal to $n_i$. Ask what would have to happen to the electron's energy for those entries to be filled in, and remember that energy must be conserved.
Check the identification of the table entries against the formula $\left(\dfrac{1}{n_f^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{n_{i}^{2}}\right)$ before using them: for $n_i = 2$, $n_f = 1$ the value should be $1 - \tfrac14 = 0.75$, which matches the printed 0.7500.
The tabulated numbers are dimensionless, so the energy comes from multiplying by the Rydberg energy $hcR = 2.18\times10^{-18}\,\mathrm{J} = 13.6\,\mathrm{eV}$. Convert to joules if the answer is required in joules, and give $E = hc/\lambda$ a final check.
You have gathered, processed and analysed information related to the development of atomic theory.
For the source part, treat reliability as a criterion, not a formality: say which sources you used, why they can be trusted, and how you checked them against each other.
For the scientists part, take each in turn and state what the model was before, what observation forced the change, and what the new model got right that the old one could not.
A model that survives because it explains the data is worth more in the argument than a model that is merely elegant. Use each scientist's own experimental result as the reason for the change.
Australia has a large supply of uranium which may be used in fission reactors to create energy. The equation describes the relevant transmutation reaction:
Analyse how the process described in this equation has been developed into a technology which produces a sustained and controlled amount of energy.
Read the equation for what makes it self-sustaining: count the free neutrons released per fission, then ask what would have to happen for the process to die out.
Distinguish the two components that act on the rate of the chain. One slows the neutrons so that they can be absorbed; the other absorbs neutrons to set the rate. Naming only one of them is the commonest way to lose a mark here.
Do not stop at 'energy is released'. Follow the energy from the mass defect through the fuel to the working fluid and then to the electrical output, and tie the first step back to $E = \Delta m c^{2}$.
The cyclotron, invented in 1932, accelerates charged particles to a very high speed. The diagram shows the basic design of a cyclotron. The Dees provide a strong magnetic field into the plane of the page.
Split the two Dees' jobs apart. Ask what force keeps the particle on a circular path and therefore what it cannot do to the particle's speed, then ask which part of the machine does change the speed.
The source sits at the centre, so the radius grows as the particle gains energy. Work out what happens to the time for one half-turn as that happens — that is what makes the machine work, or fail.
For part (ii), ask what a high-energy collision buys you that a stationary particle does not: whether the particle and its antiparticle can be created out of the collision energy.

questions.text:
Light emitting diodes in traffic lights, the reliability of sources on the development of electronics, logic circuits, the development of computers, and thermistor sensors with feedback amplifiers.
Lately, traffic control authorities in NSW have been replacing the incandescent bulbs in traffic lights with arrays of light emitting diodes (LEDs).
Structure first, then operation: name the two doped semiconductor regions, the junction between them, and the direction the voltage is applied. The operation question is then just asking what happens to the electrons at the junction.
The colour of an LED is not a choice made afterwards — it follows from the energy of the photon, which equals the band gap of the compound semiconductor used. That single fact explains why the arrays must be built from separate red, amber and green chips.
For the reasons, look for three distinct categories rather than three versions of the same point: energy and cost, time and maintenance, and the physical properties a signal needs (speed of switching, direction of emission, temperature).
During your study of the Age of Silicon you identified data sources, and gathered, processed and analysed information to outline the rapid development of electronics.
For the source part, treat reliability as a set of separate criteria and apply at least two of them explicitly to named sources. Merely saying the sources were reliable earns nothing.
For the logic part, work from the inputs inwards: work out the intermediate gate outputs first, then combine them, and build the truth table a row at a time in binary order so nothing is missed.
Check your final expression against your table by substituting a couple of rows back into it. A shortcut is to write the answer as a product of sums using the symbols $\overline{A}$ and $\overline{C}$.
Computer developments since World War II (1945) have been characterised by increasing performance at decreasing cost. This trend may or may not continue in the future. Assess this statement.
The statement has two halves joined by 'may or may not'. A response that only documents the first half scores in the middle band of the rubric, so give the second half equal space.
Build a dated chain of developments and link each one to performance per unit of cost rather than listing them. The rubric asks for three to four developments, each tied to the trend.
For the future, argue from device physics rather than from opinion: as a dimension shrinks, at what point does tunnelling through the gate oxide and electron leakage into the channel stop producing useful speed, and what does the extra power do to the heat problem?
The resistance of a thermistor as a function of temperature is as shown, and a potential divider sensor and feedback amplifier are then designed.
Write the output voltage as a fraction of the supply before substituting anything, and keep straight which resistor the output is measured across — here the fixed resistor, so the thermistor is in the top arm of the divider.
Sensitivity is a difference divided by a difference: read two points off the graph, find the change in output voltage and the change in temperature. Use a range wide enough that the graph reading is not the dominant uncertainty.
For the amplifier, decide whether the sensor output needs to be buffered or amplified, and choose the configuration that gives the sign and the direction of change you want in the final output.

questions.text:
A group of students conducted an investigation in which ball bearings were released from various points on a ramp. The ball bearings rolled down the ramp to the edge of a table at point $P$ as shown. Their ranges were measured.
The results are shown in the table.
Plot the data from the table and draw a curve of best fit.
Height of release is the quantity the students deliberately varied, so it goes on the horizontal axis; the range they measured goes on the vertical axis.
Look at the size of the successive increases in range before you draw: if they shrink as the height grows, the relationship is curved and the line of best fit must be a smooth curve, not a straight line, with roughly the same number of points above and below it.

For (ii), treat the motion after $P$ as a projectile launched horizontally from 30 cm above the floor. The vertical motion has zero initial vertical velocity and constant acceleration $g$, so it fixes the time of fall; the horizontal motion is at constant speed over that same time, so the speed is the range divided by the time.

questions.text:
Answer this part of the question.
How has our understanding of time been influenced by the discovery of the constancy of the speed of light?
The marking guide credits any one of three things, so pick the one you can argue properly instead of touching all three: the relativity of time, using $c$ to define length, or a concrete example of a moving clock running slow.
Whichever you choose, tie it explicitly to $c$ having the same value for every observer. That single statement is what forces time and length to be attached to a frame of reference.
A piece of radioactive material of mass 2.5 kilogram undergoes radioactive decay. How much energy is released if 10 grams of this mass are converted to energy during the decay process?
This is mass-energy equivalence. Only the mass that is actually converted contributes, so the 2.5 kg total is not the number you want.
Convert the converted mass to kilograms before substituting and keep $c$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, so the energy comes out in joules without a second conversion.
A mass is moving in an inertial frame of reference at a velocity $v$ relative to a stationary observer. The observer measures an apparent mass increase of 0.37%.
Calculate the value of $v$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
The percentage gives you a ratio, not a mass, so the mass itself never has to appear in the working. Turn the percentage into that ratio first.
Then substitute the ratio into the relativistic mass relationship and rearrange it until $v$ is on its own. Getting the algebra into this shape is where the third mark is earned.

A simple motor consists of a flat rectangular coil with $n$ turns in a magnetic field $B$ as shown.
The coil has an area of $0.01\,\mathrm{m^{2}}$ and carries a current of 1 A. The motor drives a pulley of diameter 20 cm, and weights can be hung from either side of the pulley at point $X$ or point $Y$.
In order to prevent rotation, should a weight be hung at point $X$ or at point $Y$? Justify your answer.
This is decided by direction, so start from the diagram: it shows the current direction in the near conductor and the direction of the field lines through the coil.
Use the right-hand rule to find which way the coil turns about the dashed axis, then carry that sense through the axle to the pulley and ask which side of the pulley is driven down.

Two steps: find the weight of the suspended mass, then multiply by the perpendicular distance from the pulley axis to the cord carrying it.
That distance is the radius of the pulley, not its diameter, and it is the same for a weight at either point — which is why the torque does not depend on which side the mass hangs.

Part (b) already gave the torque that just stops the motor, so start from that number rather than recalculating it.
Set the motor's own torque, which depends on the number of turns, equal to the counter-torque from the mass and solve for the number of turns. Keep the coil area in square metres and take the field from the diagram.

questions.text:
The table shows the critical temperature $T_c$ at which some materials become superconducting.
1941 | Niobium nitride | $T_c$ = 16 K = $-257$ °C
1987 | YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_7$ (YBCO) | $T_c$ = 92 K = $-185$ °C
1993 | HgBa$_2$Ca$_2$Cu$_3$O$_7$ | $T_c$ = 133 K = $-140$ °C
With reference to the table, identify what scientists working in the area of superconductivity are trying to achieve.
Read the critical temperature column down the years rather than across the rows. The question is about where the field is heading, not about any one material.
Then compare the best value in the table with the temperature of an ordinary room, and ask what would be gained commercially if a material did not have to be cooled below that temperature to work.
Describe what happens to one property of superconductors near the critical temperature.
Only one property is required, but it has to be paired with what happens to that property as the temperature approaches $T_c$ from above. A property named with no change attached earns nothing.
Electrical resistance is the most obvious choice, but the expulsion of magnetic flux below $T_c$ and the anomaly in heat capacity are also acceptable provided the change is described.
Explain why magnetic levitation occurs in superconducting materials.
Two ideas carry the whole explanation and they must appear in this order: a superconductor below its critical temperature expels magnetic field from its interior, and an induced current always opposes a change in magnetic flux.
Follow the sequence through — magnet approaches, flux through the superconductor would change, induced currents oppose that change, the currents produce a field that repels the magnet — and the levitation explains itself without any additional mechanism.

Calculate the electric field intensity at $Y$.
The particle's acceleration is given, so use $F_{\text{net}} = ma$ first to find the force acting on it.
Then relate that force to the field strength with $F = Eq$, remembering that $q$ is the charge of the particle, not a charge on the plate or the cylinder.

Analyse this claim with reference to the structure and function of a simple DC generator and an electric motor.
Include diagrams in your answer.

questions.current_path: Year 11 / Electricity and Magnetism / Electrostatics / analyse the effects of a moving charge in an electric field, in order to relate potential energy, work and equipotential lines, by applying: (ACSPH105)
questions.text:
An electricity substation delivers a current of 10 A at a voltage of 6 kV to an office complex. The office complex uses a transformer to provide a current of 230 A at a voltage of 240 V.
Explain why AC is preferable to DC as an input current for transformers.
The marking guide gives the full mark only if the explanation is in terms of a change in magnetic flux, so build the answer around flux rather than around currents or electrons.
Ask what a steady DC current does to the flux in the primary coil, then what follows for the secondary coil when that flux does not change.
Outline possible causes of energy loss in the transformer.
Two causes earn the full mark, so name two and say where the energy goes in each. Look at what the windings are made of, what the core is made of, and what a changing flux does to the core.
Keep the two ideas separate: energy lost because current flows through resistance, and energy lost because the changing flux does something to the iron core. If you can only find one, that is worth one mark, so dig for a second before you stop.
Calculate the energy lost by the transformer in eight hours.
Compute the power in and the power out separately, using $P = VI$ on each side of the transformer with the pair of numbers that belongs to that side. Do not reach for the efficiency or the turns ratio — they are not needed.
Take the difference for the power lost, then convert the eight hours into seconds before using $E = Pt$. If you also report the loss in kilowatt hours, remember that it is the power loss in kilowatts multiplied by eight hours, not the joule figure divided by ten.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / The Nature of Light / Light: Quantum Model / analyse the experimental evidence gathered about black body radiation, including Wien’s Law related to Planck's contribution to a changed model of light (ACSPH137) | Year 12 / The Nature of Light / Light: Quantum Model / investigate the evidence from photoelectric effect investigations that demonstrated inconsistency with the wave model for light (ACSPH087, ACSPH123, ACSPH137) | Year 12 / The Nature of Light / Light: Quantum Model / analyse the photoelectric effect as it occurs in metallic elements by applying the law of conservation of energy and the photon model of light, (ACSPH119)
questions.text:
Answer this part of the question.
Scientists tried to explain observations of black-body radiation using classical wave theory and then quantum theory.
How does quantum theory satisfactorily explain black-body radiation?
The full mark needs two halves joined together: describe the black body and the shape of its radiation curve, then link that shape to energy being emitted in packets. Answering only one half caps the mark at two.
Make the failure of the classical account explicit, because that is what quantum theory has to explain. Say what classical theory predicted at the short-wavelength end of the spectrum and what is actually observed there.
The mechanism worth stating is that at high frequency the energy quantum is large, so very few oscillators in the body can be excited and little energy is radiated at short wavelengths.
Describe Hertz's observation of the photoelectric effect.
Hertz did not have modern apparatus, so describe what he actually had: his spark-gap transmitter as the source, a receiving loop, and a vacuum.
Give the surface the light fell on and what was seen at the receiver. The spark at the receiver is the crucial observation, because it is the evidence that electrons were emitted from the metal and crossed the gap.
An experiment was conducted in which light of different frequencies was shone onto the surfaces of four different metals. Electrons were found to be emitted and their kinetic energies were measured. The graph shows the results.
A gradient needs two points well separated on the same straight line, so use the point where the sodium line crosses the frequency axis and a second point near the top of that line. Write down both pairs of values before you subtract.
Keep the axis units in the answer. The horizontal axis is in units of $10^{15}\,\mathrm{Hz}$, and a gradient quoted per $10^{15}\,\mathrm{Hz}$ converts directly into electron-volts per second, which is Planck's constant in the units the graph uses.
For the second part, ask what a gradient that is identical for four different metals cannot be. If it were a property of the metals it would have to differ between them, so where does that leave it?

questions.current_path: Year 11 / Waves and Thermodynamics / Wave Properties / the role of the medium in the propagation of mechanical waves | Year 11 / Waves and Thermodynamics / Wave Properties / conduct practical investigations to explain and analyse the differences between: transverse and longitudinal waves (ACSPH068); mechanical and electromagnetic waves (ACSPH070, ACSPH074) | Year 11 / Waves and Thermodynamics / Wave Properties / solve problems and/or make predictions by modelling and applying the following relationships to a variety of situations: | Year 11 / Electricity and Magnetism / Magnetism / use magnetic field lines to model qualitatively the direction and strength of magnetic fields produced by magnets, current-carrying wires and solenoids and relate these fields to their effect on magnetic materials that are placed within them (ACSPH083)
questions.text:
The graph shows the velocity of $P$ and $S$ waves at different depths in the Earth.
[Figure not available: the 2007 paper prints an empty placeholder rectangle marked 'Awaiting copyright' in place of this graph, and no copy of it is stored with this item. A graph of $P$- and $S$-wave velocity against depth must be supplied before publication.]
Describe the rigidity and density of rocks at different depths in the Earth and relate this to the velocity of both $P$ and $S$ waves. (3 marks)
Whatever survey is being described, its corrections exist to remove the known effects of position and height so that what is left over is a property of the ground itself.
Work each station separately and write the three corrections in the order latitude, free air, Bouguer, keeping track of which height each one uses.
Then ask what the size and the sign of the remaining anomaly implies about the density of the rock beneath each station, compared with the density the corrections assumed.
The velocity of $S$ waves through rock is given by the formula
where $\mu$ = rigidity and $\rho$ = density.
Two rocks, $A$ and $B$, are compared. Both have the same rigidity but rock $A$ has twice the density of rock $B$. If the velocity of $S$ waves in rock $B$ is $7\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$, calculate the velocity of $S$ waves in rock $A$. (2 marks)
In your study of Geophysics you performed an investigation that models the variation of the inclination of Earth's magnetic field with latitude.
Describe how you modelled the variation and the results obtained. (2 marks)
When locating an event from wave arrivals, the quantity that matters is the difference between the two arrival times, not either time on its own — because that difference removes the unknown travel time from the source.
Each station therefore defines a circle, not a point. Ask how many circles are needed before the epicentre is fixed, and how you would combine them.
For the second sub-part, ask what the two wave types do differently in a fluid, and what the distance range over which one of them is never recorded therefore tells you about Earth's interior.
The map below shows the positions of the south magnetic pole about 200 million years ago as measured from each of five present day land masses. The positions of the south magnetic pole are shown as $\star$ on the map.
[Figure not available: the polar projection map of the five apparent south magnetic pole positions is not attached to this part. It survives in imports/physics/2007-hsc-physics.qbx as assets/q28b_map.png and must be attached before publication.]
Explain how these south magnetic pole positions were determined and how they provide evidence for continental drift. (4 marks)
Remote sensing by satellites has added greatly to our ability to understand Earth.
Analyse how the introduction of satellites has contributed to TWO areas of knowledge of Earth that were previously inaccessible.
Choose two areas and give each its own paragraph. In each paragraph make three things explicit: what could not be done before, what the satellite measures, and how that measurement changed the area of knowledge.
The marking notes require the previously inaccessible feature to be named, not implied. Say precisely what no ground-based instrument could do — a single satellite in orbit can see a whole hemisphere at once.
Close by contrasting the satellite record with the old local, spot measurement. That contrast is what makes the relationship between the technology and the new knowledge evident.
Seismograms are shown for a nuclear test and an earthquake.
Compare the traces feature by feature: onset sharpness, peak amplitude, total duration of the wave train, and how quickly the amplitude decays.
Then ask what the source must have been doing to produce each trace. Duration of the train is set by how long the source radiates energy, not by how far the waves travel.
For locating and identifying the source, remember that two wave types are recorded, and that the interval between their arrivals depends on distance but not on when the event happened.

questions.current_path: Year 11 / Waves and Thermodynamics / Sound Waves / conduct investigations to analyse the reflection, diffraction, resonance and superposition of sound waves (ACSPH071)
questions.text:
Ultrasound imaging depends on the fact that different materials have different acoustic impedances. The density and acoustic impedance of fat and muscle are shown.
The speed is not given in the table: it is the impedance divided by the density, and doing this for both tissues also gives you the ratio of the speeds.
For the boundary between the two tissues, use the reflection coefficients. Work out the amplitude coefficient first, then remember that the fraction of intensity reflected is its square.
Then ask the imaging question: an ultrasound image is built from returning echoes, so any interface that reflects part of the pulse draws a line on the image. Fat and muscle are exactly such an interface.
In your study of Medical Physics you performed an investigation to identify the function of the components of MRI equipment. The following information is from the Australian Twin Registry Newsletter, 2006.
Unlike conventional radiography Computed Tomography (CT) scans, which make use of potentially harmful X-rays passing through a patient to generate images, MRI is based on the magnetic properties of atoms within the tissue. A powerful magnet generates a magnetic field roughly 10,000 times stronger than the Earth's. A very small percentage of hydrogen atoms within the body will line up with this field. Radio waves are passed through the person's body then "bounce back" depending on how many lined up atoms they meet. The subtle differences in how the radio waves bounce back provide the information needed to construct the image.
Australian Twin Registry
Assess the information provided in this article in terms of its scientific accuracy.
Part (i) is about mechanism at the level of atoms: start from what happens when a photon interacts with matter, and follow it through to the outcome for the cell.
Dose is measured in gray, and the biological effect also depends on the radiation type; make sure you distinguish energy absorbed per unit mass from the amount of energy in the beam.
For part (ii), think about how the tumour can be spared: shaping the beam, choosing a source whose energy is deposited over the right depth, and exploiting the fact that healthy cells can repair between doses but a tumour cannot keep up.
Why is ultrasound imaging NOT used for investigating the function and structure of the brain?
Assess the effects on the lives of individuals and the wider community of the production and use of X-rays, CAT scans and MRI.
Split the response into three clearly signposted sections: effects on the individual, effects on the wider community, then the judgement. The rubric assesses all three separately, so do not let one run into another.
Be specific about production as well as use. Saying how each image is made is worth a mark in its own right and shows the distinction between an X-ray photograph, a computed reconstruction and a magnetic resonance measurement.
Make the judgement explicit at the end and justify it against the two real negatives — cost and access, and ionising dose — rather than leaving it to be inferred.
Compare the advantages and disadvantages of CAT and PET scans in investigating the structure and function of the brain with reference to the images shown.
Image A: Dark areas show abnormal brain activity function.
Image B: White area shows the result of a stroke.
Osteoporosis is a degenerative disease in which there is a gradual loss of minerals in the bone. This leads to decreased bone strength and an increased chance of bone fractures.
Identify each image by what it is a record of: one shows where a substance has accumulated in the body, the other shows where the density of tissue differs from normal. The captions in the figures give the clue.
Then compare what each technique can see: one gives excellent anatomical detail but says nothing about function, the other shows function clearly but with poor anatomical detail.
For the second sub-part, use the same contrast idea as the rest of the question — matching the property of the radiation (or field) to the clinical question being asked — and make sure you say what each image actually tells the clinician to do next.
With reference to the images shown, compare TWO imaging techniques which can be used to diagnose osteoporosis.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Origins of the Elements / investigate the key features of stellar spectra and describe how these are used to classify stars | Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Origins of the Elements / investigate the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram and how it can be used to determine the following about a star: characteristics and evolutionary stage; surface temperature; colour; luminosity
questions.text:
Describe how the existence of a binary star may be deduced.
A distance is never obtained from a brightness alone. Decide first whether the route is angular (an angle on the sky) or photometric (a comparison between apparent and absolute brightness), and write the corresponding relation before substituting.
For the angular route, a star with a smaller parallax is further away, and the scale of parallax for nearby stars is a few hundredths of an arcsecond, so a decimal point error changes the answer by a factor of ten.
For the photometric route, remember that magnitude is logarithmic and that the constant 5 comes from the definition of the parsec, so check the answer against the range of distances that is physically reasonable.
The distance from the Sun to Earth is 1 astronomical unit (1 AU). The apparent magnitude of the Sun, when viewed from Earth, is $-26.5$. Calculate the apparent magnitude of the Sun when viewed from Saturn, a distance of 10 AU from the Sun.
In your study of Astrophysics you performed a first-hand investigation to demonstrate ONE characteristic of a star that can be deduced by observing the light received from it. Describe your investigation and the results obtained.
Every stage in a star's life is set by the question 'what is fusing in the core now?', so work out the fuel at each stage before you describe the path.
When a core runs out of fuel it contracts, and that is what causes the next stage. Follow the contraction from stage to stage rather than trying to remember the path as a list.
For the last sub-part, the key is a graph of binding energy per nucleon: fusion pays out energy only while that quantity is still rising with mass number.
Explain how TWO other characteristics or properties of a star can be deduced by observing the light received from the star.
Evaluate the ways that TWO technologies used in modern astrophysics have changed scientific understanding of celestial objects.
Give each technology its own paragraph and, in each, three things: what it is, how it works at the level of the physics, and the specific understanding it changed.
The rubric rewards a technology that overturned an accepted understanding. A technology that merely produced a better image does not score as highly, so choose two that changed what we believed.
End with an evaluation rather than a summary, and make the judgement about how scientific understanding changed, not about whether the technology is good.
The table shows some characteristics of selected stars.
Work out the distances first, using the difference between the two magnitudes. Every distance in the table can then be checked, because a distance of a few parsecs should go with a nearby star such as Sirius.
Then rank the stars twice: once on apparent magnitude, which mixes intrinsic brightness with distance, and once on absolute magnitude, which depends only on the star. Comparing the two rankings is where the explanation lies.
The spectral class is an ordering of surface temperature, so it also orders the colour. Use the letters themselves (M, K, G, A) as a mnemonic and remember that the letter index runs backwards relative to temperature.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Quantum Mechanical Nature of the Atom / investigate de Broglie’s matter waves, and the experimental evidence that developed the following formula: (ACSPH140) | Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Quantum Mechanical Nature of the Atom / assess the limitations of the Rutherford and Bohr atomic models | Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Quantum Mechanical Nature of the Atom / relate qualitatively and quantitatively the quantised energy levels of the hydrogen atom and the law of conservation of energy to the line emission spectrum of hydrogen using: (ACSPH136) | Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Properties of the Nucleus / analyse the spontaneous decay of unstable nuclei, and the properties of the alpha, beta and gamma radiation emitted (ACSPH028, ACSPH030) | Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Properties of the Nucleus / binding energy
questions.text:
The Bohr model of the atom describes a nucleus with electron shells surrounding it.
Part (a)(i) is a calculation and part (a)(ii) is an outline, so keep them apart. For (i), removing the electron means taking it from $n = 2$ all the way to $n = \infty$, so the energy needed is the binding energy of the second shell, $13.6/2^{2}$ eV, not the 13.6 eV of the ground state.
Turn that energy into a wavelength with $E = hf$ and $c = f\lambda$ together, so that $\lambda = hc/E$.
For (ii), the model gets the frequencies right, so ask the opposite question: which things seen in a real spectrum does it not reproduce at all? Intensity of the lines, splitting of the lines in a magnetic or electric field, and the finite width of each line are all candidates; features the model does explain earn nothing here.
In your study of Quanta to Quarks you have performed an investigation to observe radiation emitted from a nucleus using a Wilson Cloud Chamber or a similar detection device.
Part (b)(i) is marked on method, so name the set-up, where the source sat, what the vapour was and why it was cooled, what the electric field did, and what you actually saw. A method with no observation earns only the lower mark.
Part (b)(ii) is worth 4 marks and is the harder half. Choose two of the three areas and a different isotope for each, then for each isotope write down its emission type, its penetration and its half-life before you say anything about the application.
Check each link with a test question: could this isotope's property be any other value and the application would still work? If the answer is no, the property is the reason the isotope was chosen. A medical tracer, for example, must emit what the scanner detects and its half-life must be long enough to complete the scan but short enough not to harm the patient.
Analyse how de Broglie's proposal and supporting experimental evidence led to the move from classical physics to quantum physics.
This part is worth 7 marks and the mark scheme wants four things joined together: a limitation of classical physics, de Broglie's idea, the experimental evidence, and the explicit link from the evidence to the change of model. Four separate paragraphs earn fewer marks than three linked ones.
Have these three facts ready before writing. Classical mechanics lets an electron possess a continuous range of energies, so it cannot explain why only particular wavelengths are absorbed and emitted. de Broglie's proposal is that a particle of momentum $p$ has an associated wavelength $\lambda = h/p$, which applied to a Bohr orbit requires the circumference to hold a whole number of wavelengths and so quantises the energy. The evidence is the electron diffraction of Davisson and Germer and the diffraction rings of G.P. Thomson, found at the angles $\lambda = h/mv$ predicts.
End with the consequence, not with more history: because the electron is a standing wave, the idea of a definite path becomes meaningless and matter itself has to be described quantum mechanically. That is the 'move' the question asks you to analyse.
The graph shows the force between nucleons as a function of the distance between them.
[Figure not available: the graph of force between nucleons against distance, with the point $Z$ marked on the distance axis, is not attached to this part. It survives in imports/physics/2007-hsc-physics.qbx as assets/q31di_force.png and must be attached before publication.]
Explain what would happen if two nucleons were separated by the distance indicated as $Z$ on the graph. (2 marks)
Part (d)(i) is a graph reading. Go to the point marked $Z$ on the distance axis, up to the curve, and read the force. Then ask what a nucleon does when the only force acting on it is negligible.
Part (d)(ii) is about the reactor diagram. Fission is sustained by free neutrons, so the component that regulates the rate must be the one that changes the number of free neutrons, and the justification has to say how it does that rather than just naming it.
Part (d)(iii) is worth 3 marks, so give three separate properties of the neutron and link each to a different thing it lets you probe: it is uncharged, so it penetrates deep into matter; nuclei absorb neutrons with very different probabilities, so a scan maps nuclear density; and it has a de Broglie wavelength, so it diffracts from a crystal lattice and gives inter-nuclear spacings.
The figure shows the basic features of a nuclear fission reactor.
[Figure not available: the labelled diagram of a nuclear fission reactor (reactor core/moderator, reactor pressure vessel, control rods, hot and cool water, pumps, steam, steam condenser, turbine, generator, electric power) is not attached to this part. It survives in imports/physics/2007-hsc-physics.qbx as assets/q31dii_reactor.png and must be attached before publication.]
Which part of a nuclear reactor regulates the rate of fission reaction taking place? Justify your answer. (2 marks)
Neutron beams can be extracted from nuclear reactors.
Describe how the neutrons can be used as a probe for investigating the properties of matter. (3 marks)

questions.current_path: Year 11 / Electricity and Magnetism / Electric Circuits / investigate quantitatively the current–voltage relationships in ohmic and non-ohmic resistors to explore the usefulness and limitations of Ohm’s Law using: (ACSPH003, ACSPH041, ACSPH043)
questions.text:
Consider the logic expression $C = (\overline{A} + \overline{B})(A + B)$.
Simplify the expression before you draw anything, because the diagram has to correspond to the expression and not to a guess. Apply De Morgan's theorem to each bracket first, then use the distributive law.
Count the gates the expression needs: one NOT gate for each complemented input, one OR gate to combine the two complemented inputs, and one more OR gate to combine that result with the undelayed inputs. Labelling the intermediate output is what the 2 marks are paying for.
For the truth table, the mark scheme wants the intermediate columns as well as the inputs and the final output, and it checks the columns in order. Fill in the NOT-gate outputs, then each OR gate, then $C$, for all four input combinations before you decide the output column is right.
In your study of the Age of Silicon you have investigated operational amplifiers. The two operational amplifier circuits shown below have the indicated waveforms applied at their inputs.
In each case, copy the input waveforms into your writing booklet, and on the same axes sketch the output produced by the circuit. Show all relevant calculations.
Start each circuit the same way: find the non-inverting $(+)$ input and check whether it is grounded. Once the inverting node is at a virtual ground, Kirchhoff's current law at that node gives the whole answer, and the sign is fixed by the fact that a current flowing into the node through an input resistor must return through the feedback resistor.
Circuit (i) has two input resistors and one feedback resistor, so it is a summing amplifier and the gains add; work out the gain of each input path separately, then add the two contributions rather than averaging them. Circuit (ii) has one input resistor, so it is a plain inverting amplifier and the output is the input multiplied by a single negative gain.
Do not read both circuits off the same habit. In (i) the input waveforms are d.c. levels, so the output is a constant level and the sign tells you whether the sketch sits above or below the time axis. In (ii) the input is a sinusoid that is not symmetric about zero, so apply the gain to the positive peak and to the negative peak separately and the output will not be symmetric either.
Analyse how developments in the semiconductor industry could help to reduce energy consumption.
Part (c) is worth 7 marks and the mark scheme repeatedly penalises answers that describe semiconductor developments without linking them to an energy saving. Make a two-column list before writing: development on the left, the specific energy it saves on the right, and only write about items that can fill both cells.
The three developments that carry the argument are the replacement of thermionic valves by solid-state devices, the falling cost and size of integrated circuits, and the arrival of efficient specific devices. For each, ask what energy term it removes: a heater power, an unwanted conversion to heat, or a waste of energy because a device was running when it did not need to.
Your last paragraph should make the relationship explicit rather than adding a new example. The point is that a development reduces energy consumption for the same task and that the control made possible by cheap integrated circuits lets existing equipment avoid waste, so the savings appear in lighting, transport, industry and buildings rather than only inside the chip.
Electronic circuits may use both input and output transducers. Explain the difference between these types of transducer, using an example of each.
Part (d)(i) turns on the direction of the energy conversion: ask whether the device is feeding information into the circuit or taking energy out of it. An example from the electronics on your course for each direction is required as well as the definition.
Part (d)(ii) and (d)(iii) are both potential-divider questions, and in both the unknown is the lower branch. Find the voltage across that branch from the divider relation, then invert the relation to get the resistance, and only then use any extra information the question gives you.
In (d)(ii) the switch-on threshold of 0.7 V is the base voltage at the instant the transistor turns on, and the current through the LED plays no part in the calculation, so do not try to use it. In (d)(iii) the trap is the thermistor: look at the circuit and decide whether it is in series or in parallel with the 2 k$\Omega$ resistor before you substitute anything, then work out the parallel value before going to the graph.
The circuit below is used to illuminate an alarm clock display.
Figure: circuit diagram. A $+15\,\mathrm{V}$ supply rail feeds a $220\,\Omega$ resistor connected to the base terminal $b$ of transistor $Q$, and an LDR labelled $R_1$ connects $b$ to the $0\,\mathrm{V}$ (ground) rail. The emitter terminal $e$ of $Q$ is connected to the ground rail. The collector terminal $c$ of $Q$ connects through a $1000\,\Omega$ resistor to the LED, and the LED completes the path back to the $+15\,\mathrm{V}$ rail.
$R_1$ is a light-dependent resistor (LDR) and $Q$ is a transistor with $b$, $c$ and $e$ as its base, collector and emitter terminals, respectively.
It is found that when the voltage at the base (ie across $R_1$) is below $0.7\,\mathrm{V}$, the transistor is OFF, preventing current from flowing in the LED. If the base voltage is $0.7\,\mathrm{V}$ or more, the transistor is ON, causing $10\,\mathrm{mA}$ to flow through the LED.
Calculate the value of $R_1$ at the instant when the transistor switches on.
A thermistor is used to construct a thermometer circuit as shown.
Figure: circuit diagram. A $9\,\mathrm{V}$ supply feeds a $10\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ resistor connected to the output node $V_{\text{out}}$. A $2\,\mathrm{k}\Omega$ resistor and the thermistor are connected in parallel between $V_{\text{out}}$ and the $0\,\mathrm{V}$ (ground) rail.
The thermistor's resistance as a function of temperature is plotted below.
Figure: graph of thermistor resistance (vertical axis, from $0$ to $10000\,\Omega$) against temperature (horizontal axis, from $0$ to $50\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$). A single smooth curve rises with increasing temperature.
At a certain temperature the output voltage $V_{\text{out}}$ is found to be $1.2\,\mathrm{V}$.
What is the temperature of the environment in which the thermometer circuit is located?

questions.text:
A satellite is propelled from Orbit 1 to Orbit 2.
Explain the changes in momentum when a satellite fires its propulsion system.
Draw the momentum arrows for the satellite and for the exhaust gases, in opposite directions, both before and after the motor fires.

State the effect on the satellite and on the gases, and then say what that pair of effects does to the total momentum of the satellite-plus-gas system.
A satellite is propelled from Orbit 1 to Orbit 2 as shown in the diagram.
Orbit 2 has a radius of $27\,000\,\mathrm{km}$. What is the satellite’s speed in this orbit?
For a circular orbit the gravitational force supplies the centripetal force, so set $\frac{GMm}{r^{2}}$ equal to $\frac{mv^{2}}{r}$ and cancel the satellite's mass.
Convert the orbital radius to metres before substituting. The printed value is in kilometres and $G$ is only usable in SI units, so the arithmetic only works if the conversion is done first.
Check your answer against the low-orbit case: a satellite just a few hundred kilometres up travels at about $7.9\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and a satellite further out must travel more slowly.
The radius of Orbit 2 is four times that of Orbit 1. What is the ratio of the new orbital period to the original period?
You do not need $G$, the mass of the planet, or the value of either orbital radius. The stem gives you the ratio of the radii, and that is all this part uses.
Kepler's third law in the form $T^{2} \propto r^{3}$ links the period to the orbital radius. Substitute the radius ratio into that relation before you take any square root.
The quantity asked for is the ratio $T_{2}/T_{1}$, so the cubes you get from the relation must be followed by a square root before you quote a value.
