questions.text:
Two parallel metal plates in a magnetic field are separated by a distance $d$, as shown. An electron enters the space between the plates.
On the diagram indicate with an arrow the direction of the force on the electron due to the magnetic field.
Use $\vec{F} = q\vec{v}\times\vec{B}$, and do the right-hand rule in two stages: point your fingers along the velocity, curl them into the field, and the thumb gives the force on a positive charge. Because an electron is negative, the force on it is the reverse of that, which is the step most answers miss.
Check your answer against the page rather than against memory: draw the arrow you chose and ask whether it points into the gap between the plates or out of it, and whether it is parallel or perpendicular to the field lines.
The strength of the magnetic field is $B = 0.001\,\mathrm{T}$ and the electron’s velocity is $v = 2\times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Calculate the magnitude of the magnetic force on the electron.
Decide the geometry before you write anything. The electron enters between the plates travelling across the field, so $\theta = 90^{\circ}$ and the general expression $F = qvB\sin\theta$ becomes simply $qvB$; there is no component of the velocity to resolve.
Use three quantities: the magnitude of the electron's charge $1.602\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$ from the data sheet, the given velocity, and the given field. Convert the field to scientific notation first so the powers of ten are easy to track, and keep the units $\mathrm{C\,m\,s^{-1}\,T} = \mathrm{N}$ in mind as a check.
If $d = 10\,\mathrm{mm}$, calculate the voltage required for the electron to continue on a straight path parallel to the plates.
For the electron to keep going straight, the net force on it must be zero, so write $qE = qvB$ and cancel the charge. Notice that the charge cancels completely, which is a useful check that you have set the physics up correctly.
You already have the magnetic force from the previous part, so you could get $E$ either from $qvB$ or by dividing that force by $q$; both give the same field. Then use $E = V/d$ and remember that $V = Ed$ multiplies, it does not divide.
Do the unit conversion for $d$ first: it is given in millimetres and the formulae require metres, and this conversion is worth a mark on its own. Also decide the sign of the voltage you are quoting, from which plate has to be positive for the electric force to oppose the magnetic force.
How was this experimental set-up used by Thomson to determine the charge/mass ratio of an electron?
Thomson used this arrangement in two stages, and each stage bought him one measured quantity. Ask what the undeflected condition $qE = qvB$ lets him calculate, then ask what happens when he keeps the magnetic field but removes the electric one.
In the second stage the beam traces a circle, so set the magnetic force equal to the centripetal force, $qvB = mv^{2}/r$, and cancel $v$ rather than evaluating anything. The quantity the question asks for then falls straight out.
The mark scheme wants both halves: recognising that the same method as the earlier parts is being used, and describing the sequence of measurements. A single sentence naming one feature of Thomson's experiment earns only the lower mark.

questions.text:
An induction coil is a type of transformer that allows a small voltage to be stepped up to a higher voltage. An induction coil consists of a primary coil wound around an iron core and a secondary coil. The secondary coil can be moved sideways so that different lengths of the iron core are within the secondary coil.
The photographs show an induction coil with the secondary coil in two different arrangements with the power supply turned off. At sufficiently high voltages a spark can be produced between the secondary coil electrodes.
Which arrangement would produce a spark when the power supply is turned on? Justify your choice.
Compare how much of the iron core, and how much of the primary coil, lies inside the secondary coil in each arrangement.

Explain how different voltages are induced when the secondary coil is moved to different positions.

questions.current_path: Year 11 / Electricity and Magnetism / Electric Circuits / investigate the flow of electric current in metals and apply models to represent current, including: (ACSPH038)
questions.text:
A student was given a sample of wire $X$ and a sample of wire $Y$. The wires looked identical. However, one was pure chromium and the other was nichrome, an alloy containing chromium and nickel.
To differentiate between the two wires, the student set up the circuit below and obtained the results shown in the table.
The data for wire $X$ has been plotted on the graph below. Plot the data, including a trend line, for wire $Y$ on the same graph.
You do not need to calculate anything for this part. The axes are already drawn with current on the vertical axis and potential difference on the horizontal one, so plot the wire $Y$ current values against the voltage values from the table, using the existing scale, and keep the plot points small and the trend line thin.
Before you draw the line, look at whether the ratio of current to voltage is the same for every wire $Y$ reading. If it is, the correct trend line is straight, and drawing a curve would lose the mark.
Then compare the two lines without stating your conclusion yet: at any given potential difference, is the wire $Y$ current above or below the wire $X$ line, and does the new line pass through the origin? Those two judgements are the whole of what the graph has to show.
Calculate the resistance of wire $Y$.
You want the resistance of the wire $Y$ itself, and the voltmeter is connected across the wire sample, so the tabulated potential difference is already the voltage across the wire. The 2 $\Omega$ series resistor is only there to protect the sample and needs no correction.
Use $R = V/I$ and take both values from the same row of the wire $Y$ columns. Using the row with the largest voltage gives the smallest percentage uncertainty, since the meter readings are most significant there.
Quote the answer to two significant figures and add the unit, and check that it is of the same order as the reciprocal of the gradient of the line you drew in part (a).
Which sample of wire was pure chromium? Justify your response with reference to your graph.
Turn the question into a resistance comparison first. On a graph of current against potential difference the gradient is $1/R$, so the line that is steeper is the wire with the smaller resistance. Decide that from the graph, since the guideline requires the choice to be justified by reference to the graph.
Only then give the physical reason, and make it about scattering rather than about the wires looking different. Think about what happens to the regular arrangement of lattice ions when a second metal is dissolved into chromium to make nichrome, and what that does to the motion of the conduction electrons.
A two-mark answer needs both halves: the resistance comparison, and the pure-metal-versus-alloy argument that turns it into an identification of which sample was pure chromium.
When the data for wire $X$ was plotted, one data point was considered inconsistent and was disregarded when drawing the trend line for calculating its resistance.
Suggest a physical reason why this data point is inconsistent with the trend line.
Read the outlier against the trend line before you explain anything. The point at $7.5\,\mathrm{V}$ falls below the wire $X$ line, so at that voltage the current is smaller than the line predicts. Translate that into a statement about the resistance of the sample at that moment.
Now ask why the resistance of a metal would be larger for one reading than for the others. Look at what is different about this reading: it has the largest voltage and therefore the largest power dissipated in the sample. Where does that power go, and what does a hotter lattice do to the conduction electrons?
The mark scheme awards the single mark for any physical reason, but a restatement of the data scores nothing, so the explanation has to name a physical effect rather than a discrepancy.

questions.current_path: Year 11 / Waves and Thermodynamics / Wave Properties / construct and/or interpret graphs of displacement as a function of time and as a function of position of transverse and longitudinal waves, and relate the features of those graphs to the following wave characteristics: velocity; frequency; period; wavelength; displacement and amplitude (ACSPH069)
questions.text:
Geophysics
The table lists some of the principal methods used in geophysics, a property on which each method is based and an application of each method.
Part (a)(i) is three single-word answers, one for each blank, so read the two columns that are given and ask what a method based on that property is actually used to find. The property column tells you what the method responds to, and the application column tells you what has to be found in the ground.
Be careful with the third row: the property given is the elasticity of the medium, so the application is the one that uses the arrival of the waves from a distant event rather than a survey of a local one.
Part (a)(ii) is worth 3 marks and the mark scheme wants three separate things, so structure the answer as a list: the information the method produces, the picture of the Earth it supports, and the link between them. Choosing one method and doing it thoroughly scores more than naming all four.
An $S$ wave can be modelled by a transverse pulse sent along a string as indicated below.
A $P$ wave can be modelled by a compression wave sent along a slinky spring as indicated below.
Both diagrams use the same scale, 1 cm = 1 km, and both show the wave at $t = 0$, $1$ and $2$ s, so each speed is a distance read off the scale divided by 1 s. Read the position of the crest for the string and the position of the region of closest coils for the slinky, and subtract the $t = 0$ position from the $t = 1$ s position rather than reading an absolute position.
For the second half, remember that a seismic wave is a mechanical wave, so every statement about the string and the slinky transfers to rock. The words to define carefully are reflection, where part of the wave is sent back into the medium it came from, and refraction, where the wave changes direction because its speed has changed at the boundary.
Then attach the physics to the two wave types. The $S$ wave is transverse and needs a medium with rigidity, so it is the slower of the pair; the $P$ wave is longitudinal and compressional, and is faster. Because the two speeds differ so much they are refracted by very different amounts at the same boundary, which is the reason earthquakes can be located from the gap between their arrivals.
The CSIRO Remote Sensing Project used images from the NOAA satellites to produce the following scenes of the NSW bushfires in December 1997. The two images were taken simultaneously using different techniques.
The two images were taken at the same instant by the same satellite, so time and viewpoint are ruled out and the difference has to be a difference in the physics. For each image, identify the part of the electromagnetic spectrum the sensor used, and then ask what quantity of the surface that band actually measures.
For the visible image the measured quantity is reflected sunlight, so the shading is about how much each surface reflects. For the thermal image the measured quantity is the infrared radiation the surface emits, so the brightness is about temperature. Once you have that, the dark patches and the bright hot spots in each image explain themselves.
Part (c)(ii) has three separate marks, so write three separate points: a feature of the monitoring, what the technique lets authorities do, and the benefit that follows. Repeated wide-area coverage without needing to reach the site is the feature to lead with, because everything else depends on it.
Both geophones and seismometers detect seismic activity.
Compare the structure and function of these devices and the information they provide about the large-scale structure of the Earth.
This is a comparison, so build the answer from the same three headings for each device: how it is put together, what it does, and what the data it produces reveal about the Earth's interior. Using parallel headings for the two instruments is what turns a list into a comparison and picks up the coherence mark.
For structure, think about what is actually moving in each instrument. In one case a coil is forced to move relative to a fixed magnet by the ground, which generates a current; in the other case a heavy mass stays still by inertia while the ground moves under it, and that relative motion is written to a rotating surface. That difference in mechanism is the whole of the structure contrast.
For the third heading, do not stop at 'they detect earthquakes'. The question asks what the information tells you about the large-scale structure of the Earth, and the key facts are that the two wave types travel at different speeds and that one of them cannot pass through a liquid. Work out what those two facts alone prove about the core.

questions.current_path: Year 11 / Waves and Thermodynamics / Sound Waves / conduct investigations to analyse the reflection, diffraction, resonance and superposition of sound waves (ACSPH071)
questions.text:
Medical Physics
The transducer of an ultrasound machine.
Part (a) is one crystal doing two opposite jobs, and the mark scheme wants both jobs. Ask what a piezoelectric crystal does when a potential difference is applied across it, and then ask what it does when pressure is applied to it. The answer to the second is the reverse of the answer to the first, and that reversal is the detection mechanism.
Be specific about the kind of potential difference. A steady d.c. voltage distorts the crystal once and produces nothing sustained, so the source has to alternate, and the frequency of that alternation is the frequency of the emitted ultrasound.
For part (a)(ii) the key word is impedance, not intensity or density on its own. Define acoustic impedance as the product of density and the speed of sound in the tissue, then use the difference in that product between two tissues to explain both why a reflection occurs and why some boundaries echo much more strongly than others.
Endoscopy.
Part (b)(i) is only 2 marks but each use must be sketched in general terms, so give a purpose and a consequence for each, not just a name. One use is about seeing and one is about obtaining material, and choosing two uses from different categories is safer than two versions of the same idea.
Part (b)(ii) is worth 3 marks and the guideline is explicit that diagrams are part of the answer. Draw each bundle in cross-section, shade in a single fibre and trace a ray from one end to the other. The test is where the ray emerges: in one case it must emerge from the same end position it entered, and in the other it must not. That single difference is the physics and the roles follow from it.
Part (b)(iii) is a single mark for one advantage over alternative surgical procedures. Think about the size of the incision and the consequences of a large one, and about what the patient has to undergo. One clear advantage stated well is all that is needed.
Medical imaging of bone.
Part (c)(i) is a contrast, so the mark scheme will not give credit for two descriptions of the same technique. State the advantage of each in one sentence and then state explicitly how the advantages differ, because the guideline asks for that link.
For part (c)(ii) remember the whole chain: electrons must first be given very high speeds, then made to strike a target. Ask what happens to an electron when it is stopped abruptly, and ask separately what happens when it knocks an inner-shell electron out of a target atom.
Part (c)(iii) is about the substance, not the scan. For any candidate isotope ask three questions: does it emit the radiation the scanner detects, will it end up in the bone, and will it decay fast enough that the patient is not still carrying the dose after the scan is finished?
Explain how different medical imaging techniques use tomography to improve our diagnostic abilities.
Build this answer in two halves: the idea of tomography itself, and then the same idea applied to at least two named scans. The mark scheme awards the top band only when the concept, two applications and the effect on diagnosis are all present, so do not spend the whole answer on only one technique.
Define tomography in terms of slices and voxels: the body is cut into thin cross-sections, each section is divided into very small boxes called voxels, and one measurement is made on each voxel. Ask why that matters for diagnosis, and the answer involves detail and the ability to view the same data from many angles.
For the applications, the question is always 'what is actually measured in each voxel?'. For CT think absorption of X-rays; for MRI think the radio signal from hydrogen nuclei after nuclear magnetic resonance; for PET think the gamma rays from positron-electron annihilation. Two fully developed scans carry the top band.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Origins of the Elements / account for the production of emission and absorption spectra and compare these with a continuous black body spectrum (ACSPH137) | Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Origins of the Elements / investigate the key features of stellar spectra and describe how these are used to classify stars | Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Origins of the Elements / investigate the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram and how it can be used to determine the following about a star: characteristics and evolutionary stage; surface temperature; colour; luminosity
questions.text:
Astrophysics
The analysis of electromagnetic radiation is widely used by astronomers.
Part (a)(i) is about the two processes, not about the appearance of the two spectra, and the mark scheme wants the appearance as the outcome rather than the cause. For each, identify what is happening to the electrons: in one case they are falling and radiating, in the other they are being raised and then re-radiating at the same frequencies.
Once the processes are described, the comparison falls out: the emission spectrum has bright lines on a dark background and the absorption spectrum has dark lines on a continuous background, at exactly the same set of frequencies for the same element, because both are fixed by the same differences between energy levels.
Part (a)(ii) is worth 3 marks, so give two or more characteristics of stars and their motion and say what each reveals. Three areas cover the marks: what the star is made of, how hot its surface is, and how fast it is moving through space.
The table shows some photometric measurements of certain stars.
Before calculating anything, state the property of the magnitude scale you need: it is logarithmic and inverted, so a star of lower apparent magnitude is brighter, and a difference of one magnitude is a factor of about 2.51 in intensity. Writing that down first prevents a sign error in part (i).
Part (b)(i) compares two stars as seen from Earth, so only apparent magnitudes are involved and the distance of each star cancels out. Form the difference in the right order, brightest minus faintest, so the exponent comes out positive.
Part (b)(ii) is a different relation altogether. Use the distance modulus $m - M = 5\log_{10}(d/10)$ with $d$ in parsecs, take $m$ and $M$ from the same row of the table, and check your answer by asking whether the star is intrinsically brighter or fainter than it appears; a star that is much more luminous than it looks must be far away.
Part (b)(iii) is about the filters, not about the star. $B$ and $V$ are magnitudes measured through a blue and a yellow-green filter, and because the scale is inverted a star that is relatively brighter in one filter has the lower magnitude there. Work out which filter each kind of star favours and the sign of the difference follows.
The HR diagram below shows positions X and Y.
Part (c)(i) is about the two competing processes in a forming star, one that compresses and one that expands, and the mark scheme wants each with the reason it occurs. Do not leave it at 'gravity pulls in and pressure pushes out'; say what the pressure is and where its energy comes from.
Part (c)(ii) is a reading of the H-R diagram, so begin by locating $X$ and $Y$. Ask in each case where the star is in its life: a star on the main sequence is still fusing hydrogen, and a star sitting above and to the cool side of the main sequence has already run out of hydrogen in its core. The reaction in each position then follows from that, and you must name the pathway, not just the fuel.
Part (c)(iii) asks for a flowchart, so draw boxes and arrows. A red giant has more than one possible end, so the chart has a branch, and each branch needs a condition stated beside it, otherwise the second mark is not earned. The three headings the guideline looks for are a sequence, the possible outcomes, and the pathways followed.
Explain how observations of binary and variable stars can be used to infer physical properties of these stars.
This is a 6-mark explanation, so start by saying why inference is necessary at all: direct measurement in astronomy is very limited, so nearly everything known about stars is inferred from relationships between quantities that can be measured from the ground. That opening sentence is what the coherence mark is built on.
For binary stars work through the measurable quantities and what each yields. For a visual binary the period and the separation can both be measured, so ask what Newton's law of gravitation gives from those two. For an eclipsing binary ask what the drops in brightness tell you. For a spectroscopic binary ask what the Doppler shift of the lines reveals, and note that it works even when the two stars cannot be seen separately.
For variable stars, the essential fact is that a Cepheid's period of variation is directly related to its true luminosity. Follow the chain: period, then luminosity, then absolute magnitude, then the distance modulus with the measured apparent magnitude, and you have a distance to a star that cannot be measured any other way.

Intensity is the energy delivered each second. Ask what that changes in a photon model: the number of photons arriving per second, or the energy carried by each photon.
Each photoelectron absorbs one photon, and the energy of that photon is set by the frequency alone. So decide whether anything in $K_{max} = hf - \phi$ contains the intensity.
Say what does change when the intensity is raised, as well as what does not: the number of electrons released per second, and hence the size of the photoelectric current.
With reference to the photoelectric effect, and the semiconductors shown in the diagram, explain the operation of a solar cell.
Start with the photoelectric effect in its simplest form: light delivers energy in quanta, and a quantum with enough energy frees an electron from a material.
Now use the structure in the diagram. An n-type layer is in contact with a p-type layer, so there is a junction between them, and there is a built-in electric field across that junction.
Finish with the external circuit. Say which layer collects the free electrons and which collects the holes, which layer therefore becomes negative, and how that drives current through the load.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / Advanced Mechanics / Motion in Gravitational Fields / predict the gravitational field strength at any point in a gravitational field, including at the surface of a planet (ACSPH094, ACSPH095, ACSPH097)
questions.text:
Radiation is used to obtain information about a surface from a distance.
Part (a)(i) is worth 2 marks and the guideline asks for a labelled diagram and text, so draw the arrangement first: a radiation source above a surface, a detector to collect the reflected radiation, and at least two different surfaces to compare. Label all three components and show the path of the radiation, then write the method underneath.
Control the variables you are not testing. Keep the distance from the source to the surface, the distance and angle from the surface to the detector, and the orientation of the surfaces the same for every reading, so that any change in the detected intensity has to come from the surface itself. Repeat the readings to make the comparison reliable.
Part (a)(ii) is about interpreting what you measured, and part (a)(iii) is about transferring the idea to satellite work. For (ii) the key is that radiation incident on a surface is shared between absorption, reflection and transmission, and the sharing depends on what the surface is made of. For (iii) the mark scheme wants a specific case, so pick one concrete scenario and say what changes in the signal.
A pendulum was used to determine the acceleration due to gravity, $g$, at the base of a mountain. The period, $T$, was $2.00\,\mathrm{s}$, and the length of the string, $l$, was $1.00\,\mathrm{m}$.
Part (b)(i) is a single-step rearrangement. Start from $T = 2\pi\sqrt{l/g}$, square both sides so that $T^{2} = 4\pi^{2}l/g$, and solve for $g$ before substituting anything. The pendulum's bob mass never appears, so leave it out.
Part (b)(ii) uses the same measured $g$ but a different relationship. For a planet, $g$ is the gravitational field strength at distance $r$ from the centre, and it depends on the planet's mass, so rearrange that relationship to solve for $r$. Use the Earth's mass and $G$ from the data sheet, and keep the units consistent throughout.
Part (b)(iii) is worth 3 marks and is the conceptual heart of the part. Before you explain it, work out the implication of the value of $r$ you obtained in (ii): how does it compare with the mean radius of the Earth? Then ask what that tells you about where the extra mass acting on the pendulum must be, and whether a mountain is the only possibility.
Seismograms from three different geophysical stations showing the records of a small earthquake somewhere in California are shown. Time is marked on each seismogram by offsets in the records. The interval between the offsets is 1 minute.
Each record shows two groups of motion, not one, and identifying which is which is the first job. The faster seismic wave arrives first and is the smaller of the two; the slower one arrives later and is much more violent. Write down which is which before reading any times.
Then use the 1 minute calibration to compare the stations. The interval between the two arrivals is the same physical quantity at every station, and it grows with distance from the source, so the station with the widest gap between its two arrivals is the closest to the epicentre. The time marks let you turn the gaps into actual times if you need them.
Part (c)(ii) is about applying the same physics in a controlled way. Ask what would be different if the source were a deliberate, repeatable signal of known origin rather than an unpredictable earthquake, and what the travel times to a whole array of detectors would then let you work out about the ground in between.
Name THREE geophysical techniques, and explain how each of these provides evidence to support the claim that Earth is dynamic.
This is a 6-mark research question and the mark scheme only gives the top band for THREE techniques with the evidence for each, so choose the three for which you can state both what is measured and what a change in that measurement would prove. Naming a technique and describing its measurement earns the middle band; naming it and linking it to a theory of a changing Earth earns the top one.
Good candidates are the three that record change over time: seismic surveying and earthquake location, radiometric dating of rocks and sediments, and magnetic surveying of igneous rock. Each of these leaves a record that can be read long after the event, and that is exactly why each supports the claim that Earth is dynamic rather than merely describing its present state.
For each technique, structure the entry the same way: what is measured, what the record shows, and which theory of a changing Earth that supports. If you can do that three times, the marks are there; if you can only do it once, the 4 to 5 band is the realistic target.

questions.current_path: Year 11 / Electricity and Magnetism / Magnetism / use magnetic field lines to model qualitatively the direction and strength of magnetic fields produced by magnets, current-carrying wires and solenoids and relate these fields to their effect on magnetic materials that are placed within them (ACSPH083)
questions.text:
In X-ray images, the small intestine is not normally visible.
Contrast in an X-ray image comes from differences in absorption, so ask which material in the body would absorb a larger fraction of the beam than the soft tissue around it.
For X-ray production, treat the tube as a two-stage energy conversion: electrical energy becomes electron kinetic energy, and then electron kinetic energy becomes photon energy. Name what supplies the energy, what accelerates the electrons, and what happens where they stop.
The diagram carries marks of its own, so sketch the tube and label the filament, the anode/target, the accelerating voltage, the electron beam, and the X-ray beam leaving the target.
Ultrasound is used in medical diagnosis.
For the impedance calculation the quantity is just the product of the medium's density and the speed of sound in it, so substitute both given values and keep the units.
A boundary between two media of different impedance always both reflects and transmits. Consider the limiting case where the second medium is far 'harder' than the first.
For the crystal, remember that 'piezoelectric' means pressure produces a voltage, which also means a voltage can produce pressure. Describe both directions of operation.
Imaging techniques can be used to investigate the body.
A claim of the form 'have a scan and live longer' mixes two separate questions: what the scan is able to show, and what harm the scan itself may do. Answer both, and only then say whether the claim is justified.
For the PET image, follow the chain: a tracer is taken up by the target cells, the tracer is radioactive, its nucleus decays and emits a positron, the positron meets an electron, and the machine detects what comes out of that meeting rather than the original emitted particle.
Describe the sequence of events and associated processes of physics by which an image is produced using magnetic resonance imaging.
An MRI image is not formed from rays that arrive; it is reconstructed from a signal. Work in this order: align the nuclei, disturb them, detect their response, and then work out where in the body the response came from.
For the disturbance and the response, remember that a magnetic field splits the available energy levels of a nucleus, and that the radiation involved is at a frequency fixed by that splitting.
For the position information, note that the magnet is not uniform: the field strength, and therefore the frequency of the signal, varies with position, and that is exactly what lets the signal be located and then computed into an image.

questions.text:

Both words describe a telescope but they are not the same thing: one asks how faint a source can be seen, the other asks how close together two sources can be and still be told apart.
For the second part, decide which technique is limited by the wavelength of the radiation being collected. Anything that depends on the reflecting surface being optically perfect is irrelevant if the wavelength is very long.
Binary stars can be detected by several techniques.
For the light-curve simulation be explicit about what is modelled and what the software computes from it: the orbit is the model, the light curve is the output.
For the mass calculation the two stars are far apart compared with their sizes, so treat them as two bodies orbiting a common centre of mass and use the period and the separation in the one equation that connects them.
For the spectra remember that each spectrum contains lines from BOTH stars, and that the orbital motion reverses direction for each star during a cycle.
The colour of a star gives information about its temperature.
Work out $B - V$ first and think about what a positive value means, remembering that magnitude is logarithmic so a LARGER magnitude is a FAINTER flux.

questions.text:
Marsden and Geiger conducted an experiment in which they fired alpha particles at a thin gold foil. Most of the particles passed straight through.
Two outcomes of the gold foil experiment need explaining - the large number of undeflected particles and the small number of large-angle deflections. Each constrains the model in a different way.
For the second part, name the two specific failures of Rutherford's classical orbits before you describe how Bohr's postulates removed them.
Electrons can be shown to have wave-like properties.
de Broglie's argument rests on treating light's energy and its momentum with the wave and the particle formula at the same time and asking what the two have in common.
Davisson and Germer's result came from an accident with their vacuum tube. Ask what had to happen to the nickel surface before a diffraction pattern could appear at all.
For the calculation the de Broglie relation connects wavelength to momentum, so isolate the velocity - and check your powers of ten, because the result is far below $c$.
Nuclear stability can be related to binding energy.
Mass defect is a difference between two masses - be careful which is larger, and say why.
For the graph, the quantity on the vertical axis is already an average PER NUCLEON. Read it at both mass numbers and then ask which nucleus needs more energy per nucleon to break up.
In 1920, Rutherford suggested the existence of an undiscovered nuclear particle.

Chadwick had two things to establish: that the extra radiation really was a particle, and what its mass and charge were.
Both follow from the same experiment if you assume the collisions were elastic and then apply conservation of momentum and conservation of kinetic energy to them.
Theories and experiments not only help increase our understanding but also generate new questions.
Use the standard model of matter to support this statement.
Use the standard model's own content - the matter particles, the force-carrying bosons and how the forces are mediated - rather than a list of particles.
The second half of the question asks for questions the model still raises. Choosing two or three genuine open problems and saying why each is a problem shows the model generating new questions.

questions.text:

Analyse how the development of the integrated circuit has affected energy consumption.
Separate the two effects: what happened to the energy used by an individual device, and what happened to the number of devices in the world.
An analysis needs an implication drawn out at the end, not just the two trends stated.
The advancement of silicon-based integrated circuit technology has resulted in progressive miniaturisation and a doubling of circuit performance roughly every 18 months. It is expected that physics limitations will soon halt this progress, requiring a reconceptualisation of the way integrated circuits are constructed.
If this reconceptualisation cannot be realised, what would be the likely impact on society?
First state the physical reason progress must stop - it is the size of atoms and quantum effects, not economics or a lack of demand.

questions.text:
Geophysics
(i) List THREE properties of earth materials studied in geophysics.
(ii) Observations of the period of a pendulum on a ship show variations with location. Explain how these observations could be used to deduce information about the shape of Earth. Your answer must include a description of the shape of Earth.
(iii) The period of a pendulum is $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g}}$. The period of a particular pendulum is measured at one location as 2.00 seconds. When measured at a second location the period is 2.05 seconds.
(iii) Determine the ratio of the strength of the gravitational field at the first location to that at the second location.
For the first sub-part this is a list question: name the measurable properties of earth materials that geophysicists actually use, and do not include things such as chemical composition that cannot be measured directly on a rock sample in the field.
For the second, write the pendulum period formula and the field formula, eliminate the length of the pendulum, and remember the answer must include a description of the shape of Earth as well as the reasoning that leads to it.
For the ratio, notice that it is the same pendulum at both locations, so the length cancels and you can go straight from the two periods to the ratio of the two field strengths.
How are gravity measurements used to obtain information about the structure of Earth?
Set out the chain in order: how the local value of $g$ is measured, what has to be corrected for before the readings mean anything, what the corrected value is then compared against, and what a difference between the two reveals about the rock below.
Keep two ideas apart as you write: $g$ depends on mass and on distance, so denser rock and a smaller radius both raise it; and because the interpretation of any anomaly is not unique, gravity data always have to be combined with seismic and geological data.
Seismic waves provide information about the larger scale structure of Earth.
For the first sub-part, classify each wave by the direction of the particle motion relative to the direction of travel, then use the fact that shear waves need rigidity to decide which media each can cross.
For the second, do not argue qualitatively: take each formula, note the effect of increasing each quantity, and write down the conclusions that follow about how the two speeds change with depth and about which is larger.
For the third, examine each drawn path in turn and ask two questions: can the wave actually exist in the material it is drawn crossing, and is it shown changing direction at a boundary where its speed changes?
There is current acceptance of the idea that the continents have moved relative to each other.
Why was there initial reluctance to accept this idea, and what evidence led to its acceptance?
Separate the two demands of the question: the reasons for the initial reluctance, and the evidence that finally settled it. Do not mix them, and note that the marking guide requires you to link the evidence back to the specific objections it overcame.
The reluctance was methodological rather than observational, so look for the missing mechanism and the assumed age of the Earth. The decisive evidence came decades later, and the two key items are the symmetrical magnetic striping either side of the mid-ocean ridges and the measured youth of the ocean floor.

Medical Physics
Describe how an X-ray image of the bones in the hand is produced.
The image is a shadow image. Ask what reaches the detector where there is bone and what reaches it where there is only soft tissue.
Absorption depends on density and atomic number, so compare the calcium in bone with the water and soft tissue around it.
The half-life of Tc-99m is 6 hours.
A half-life is a trade-off: think about what is gained by the activity decaying quickly and what is lost because the isotope cannot be stored.
For the graph, remember that halving continues indefinitely - the mass approaches zero but never reaches it, so the curve is exponential and flattening, not a straight line down to the axis.
Why is hydrogen the most commonly targeted element in the magnetic resonance imaging process?
Part (i) is about why one nucleus is chosen above all others for imaging - consider both how abundant it is in the body and what its nucleus is like.
Part (ii) asks what happens in three stages: what the static field does to the nuclei, what the radio frequency pulse does to them, and what they do when the oscillator is switched off.
Describe how energy from the radio frequency oscillator of a magnetic resonance imaging machine interacts with hydrogen to obtain information about the inside of the body.
The acoustic impedance of air is $400\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$.
Calculate the intensity of the reflected ultrasound at the interface between chest muscle and air as a proportion of the incident intensity.
Reflection at a boundary depends on the change in acoustic impedance across it, and the impedance of a tissue is the product of its density and the speed of sound in it. Both numbers are in the table.
The intensity reflection coefficient involves the impedances squared, as the square of their difference divided by the square of their sum - check the order of the terms before substituting.
For the second part, remember that a moving scatterer becomes a moving source, and that the SIZE of the frequency shift is what carries the diagnostic information.
A cancer specialist has access to ultrasound, CAT and PET scanners.
Which of these technologies is the most appropriate to detect a 3 mm brain tumour? Justify your choice.
The three techniques do not measure the same thing: one shows anatomy, one shows function, and one depends on whether sound can reach the organ at all. Decide which of those properties the question actually needs before you compare resolutions.
Justifying a choice means naming it and then explicitly ruling the other two out with valid reasons.

questions.text:
Astrophysics
The Japanese radio telescope HALCA was placed in an elliptical orbit which took it as far as $21\,000\,\mathrm{km}$ from Earth. It took measurements simultaneously with ground-based radio telescopes.
Explain the benefit that the HALCA telescope gives radio astronomers.
For the first sub-part the key word is that both instruments observed simultaneously. Ask what a pair of widely separated receivers observing the same source at the same instant amounts to, and how the angular resolution of that arrangement depends on their separation rather than on the size of either dish.
For the second sub-part there are two separate improvements available from flying at altitude, and the marking guide wants two: one concerns how much of the incoming signal reaches the detector at all, the other concerns how much irrelevant background reaches it along with the signal.
SOFIA is an infrared telescope. It is operated from high-altitude aircraft.
Give TWO reasons for the greater validity of data from this telescope, compared with ground-based observations.
Properties of stars, including their surface temperature and chemical composition, can be measured by using their spectra.
For the first sub-part, list what a spectrum reveals besides composition and temperature: the line positions, widths, strengths and any overall shift each carry different information, and each points to a different stellar property.
For the second sub-part, separate the two jobs. Composition comes from the narrow dark lines, because each element absorbs at its own discrete set of frequencies. Temperature comes both from the continuous part of the spectrum and from how strongly and how deeply the lines are formed.
Trace the light outwards from the interior as you write: the continuous spectrum is generated deep inside the star, while the line spectrum is produced in the cooler, thinner outer layers. That split is what allows the composition question and the temperature question to be answered independently.
Hertzsprung-Russell diagrams can be used to deduce the properties of stars.
Read the two circled positions off the diagram before explaining anything. The vertical axis is luminosity and the horizontal axis is temperature (spectral type), so describe each region in those two terms first and name the class of star second.
For the energy question, ask in each case what is actually supplying the radiated power: a nuclear reaction, or the release of gravitational potential energy as the star contracts.
For the sketch, use the fact that all the stars in the cluster formed at the same time, so whatever is missing from the diagram must be the group that has already died. The survivors lie along the lower main sequence and in a branch bending away from it.
Identify THREE advances in measurement technologies, and describe how they have improved our understanding of celestial objects.
Choose three technologies that each improved a different thing: sensitivity, resolution, or the range of wavelengths available. For each one, state a specific thing astronomers can now do that they could not do before.
The marking guide awards its top band for identifying THREE advances and showing the relationship between each advance and the specific improvement in understanding, so avoid writing a bare list of names.

questions.text:
From Quanta to Quarks
Outline the relationship between Bohr's atomic model and Planck's equation $E = hf$.
Start with what the model says: how many orbits are there, and what is special about the energy of the electron in each of them?
Now think about what has to happen if the electron moves from one orbit to another, and by what route that energy leaves or enters the atom.
Planck's equation relates the energy of a photon to its frequency, so the link between the two ideas is a statement about exactly when a photon is emitted or absorbed.
Calculate the wavelength of a photon which is emitted when an electron in a hydrogen atom moves from energy level $n = 4$ to $n = 2$.
Write the Rydberg formula for hydrogen as $\frac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\frac{1}{n_f^{2}} - \frac{1}{n_i^{2}}\right)$, and decide which of the two levels given in the question is $n_i$ and which is $n_f$.
Keep the calculation in $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$ for the reciprocal wavelength, then invert at the end rather than inverting at the start.
Convert the final wavelength to nanometres and check that it falls in the visible region of the spectrum, which is a useful confirmation that the levels were substituted the right way round.
How did Louis de Broglie explain the stability of electron orbits in hydrogen atoms?
de Broglie's starting point was that matter, not only light, has a wave character. Write down the wavelength he gave for a particle of mass $m$ moving at speed $v$.
Apply that wavelength to an electron travelling round a nucleus and ask what must be true for the wave to be physically allowed - a travelling wave would interfere with itself unless the pattern closes.
Then make the final link: what is it about a standing wave that stops the electron radiating, and therefore stops the atom collapsing?
How did Pauli account for the distribution of energies in the $\beta$-decay curve?
Read the shape of the curve first. It is continuous, running from nearly zero energy up to a marked maximum $E_{max}$, rather than being a set of separate lines.
Then ask what conservation of energy alone predicts for a decay that emits only one particle. If only the electron were emitted, what would its energy have to be, and why?
The resolution is a third product that carries away an unknown share of the released energy and momentum, and that is invisible both to the apparatus and, for a very long time, to experiment.
James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932. How did Chadwick apply conservation laws?
For (i), Chadwick was not given the particle, he inferred its properties. Begin with what he actually did: he bombarded beryllium with alpha particles and then let whatever came out strike a block of paraffin containing hydrogen.
Ask what the collisions with the hydrogen nuclei would reveal if the unknown particle had a mass comparable with a proton, and which two conservation laws are needed to extract that mass from the recoil energies.
For (ii), two properties carry the marks. Think first about charge: what would a neutral particle be able to do that a charged one cannot, as it enters matter? Then think about wavelength, using $\lambda = h/mv$ and the size of the spacing between atoms in a material.
Outline how the properties of neutrons make them useful in scattering experiments.
Account for the existence of stable isotopes, referring to the forces which act within the atomic nucleus.
Name the forces that act inside a nucleus and, for each, say whether it attracts or repels and over what distance it acts.
The short-range attractive force is what holds the nucleus together. The repulsive force acts between every pair of protons, not merely between neighbours, so its total grows quickly as the number of protons rises.
A neutron adds strong-force attraction but no electrostatic repulsion, so work out what range of neutron numbers can be stable, and what a nucleus does when it falls above or below that range.
'Important fundamental discoveries in physics often lead to applications which have a significant effect on society.'
Evaluate this statement, with reference to the contributions of Rutherford, Einstein and Fermi to the development of the atomic bomb.
Treat this as three separate contributions and keep them in order, attaching a piece of evidence or a date to each so that they cannot be blurred together.
For each scientist ask what became possible that was not possible before: a target for later experiments, a quantity that could be calculated, or a demonstration that a process could be sustained.
The statement has two clauses - that fundamental discoveries lead to applications, and that those applications have a significant effect on society - so both must be addressed before you judge it. End with the judgement itself.

A circuit and a graph of a thermistor characteristic curve are shown.
Section A converts temperature into a voltage and section B converts that voltage into a switching output. Establish the divider formula first, then the reference voltage the comparator compares against.
For the value at $60^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, read the thermistor's resistance off the LOG graph - the vertical axis is logarithmic, so read the decade and minor marks carefully.
For the transfer graph the output can only be $0\\,\mathrm{V}$ or $5\\,\mathrm{V}$, so the curve is a step. Find the switching temperature from the condition $V_t$ equals the reference, and remember that the feedback resistor alters the threshold.
Outline the construction and operation of a relay. Include diagrams in your answer.
A relay is two circuits that never touch electrically. Draw them side by side before you describe anything.
For the marks, name the components - electromagnet and coil, soft iron core, pivot, spring, contacts - and then trace what happens when, and when not, the control current flows.
In your writing booklet, draw a truth table for the following logic circuit.
There are three inputs, so work through $2^{3} = 8$ rows, evaluating the AND gate and the NOT gate before the OR gate in every row.
A useful check: find the rows in which the two inputs of the OR gate are both 0 - the output must be 0 in exactly those rows.
What is the function of an input transducer?
The test for an input transducer is whether energy flows FROM the measured quantity INTO the circuit.
Apply that test to each of the two devices in turn, remembering that a component's classification depends on the job it is doing, not on the component itself.

questions.current_path: Year 11 / Electricity and Magnetism / Electric Circuits / investigate the flow of electric current in metals and apply models to represent current, including: (ACSPH038)
questions.text:
The electrical resistance, $R$, of a piece of wire was measured at different temperatures, $T$. Near room temperature, the resistance of the wire can be modelled by the equation $R = mT + b$.
Plot the TWO remaining data points on the graph provided. Draw a line of best fit on the graph and use it to estimate the electrical resistance of the wire at 24 degrees C.
The two points still to be plotted come straight from the table, one at $32\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and one at $36\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.
Draw a single straight best-fit line through all four points rather than joining them in order, then check that about two points lie above it and two below.
Read the estimate by going up from $24\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ on the horizontal axis to the line and then across to the resistance axis. A sensible line has a gradient of a few $10^{-4}\,\Omega$ per degree.
Assess the validity of using the data from this experiment to estimate the electrical resistance at $-100\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.
A straight-line model is only guaranteed over the range that was actually tested, so identify that range from the table first.
$-100\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ lies far below every measured point, so ask what the model is being asked to predict with no data at all, and whether a property such as resistance really keeps a straight-line dependence over a change of that size.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / The Nature of Light / Light and Special Relativity / analyse and evaluate the evidence confirming or denying Einstein’s two postulates: | Year 12 / The Nature of Light / Light and Special Relativity / the speed of light in a vacuum is an absolute constant
questions.text:
Michelson and Morley, 1887.
What was the purpose of the experiment that Michelson and Morley conducted in 1887?
This was a null experiment, so think about the luminiferous aether hypothesis and what difference it predicts for light travelling along two directions at right angles to the Earth's motion.
The instrument was an interferometer: it compares two beams that have travelled by different routes and then interfere. Work out what would be observed if the prediction were correct, since an instrument is chosen for the size of the effect it can resolve.
Draw a labelled diagram that outlines how the experiment was performed.
Draw the path of the light with arrows first, then add the components: the source, the half-silvered plate that splits the beam, the two arms, the mirrors and the viewing telescope.
The two arms must be at right angles and of equal length, and the element most often left off the diagram is the mounting that lets the whole apparatus be rotated about a vertical axis. Label that too.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / Advanced Mechanics / Motion in Gravitational Fields / predict quantitatively the orbital properties of planets and satellites in a variety of situations, including near the Earth and geostationary orbits, and relate these to their uses (ACSPH101)
questions.text:
A rocket launches a satellite into an orbit 350 km above Earth's surface. The weight of the satellite is 14.0 kN at launch, and is 12.6 kN when in orbit.
(Radius of Earth = 6380 km, mass of Earth = $5.97 \times 10^{24}\,\mathrm{kg}$)
Why does the weight of the satellite change?
Weighting forces use $W = mg$, so the question is really about the gravitational field strength, not about the satellite itself.
Compare the distance of the satellite from Earth's centre in the two situations, and recall that $g = GM/r^{2}$ falls as that distance increases.
Calculate the orbital velocity of this satellite.
For a satellite in a circular orbit, gravity supplies the centripetal force: set $\frac{GMm}{r^{2}}$ equal to $\frac{mv^{2}}{r}$ and cancel the mass of the satellite.
Use the orbital radius, not the altitude: add the $350\,\mathrm{km}$ to the $6380\,\mathrm{km}$ radius of the Earth before converting to metres.
Check the quantity inside the square root has units of $\mathrm{m^{2}s^{-2}}$, and that the result is in the range expected of a low Earth orbit.
Explain TWO effects that a reduction in altitude would have on the motion of this satellite.
Reducing the altitude means a smaller orbital radius. Every relationship you need here has $r$ in it, so write those relationships down first.
For each effect, quote the relationship, for example $v_{orb} = \sqrt{GM/r}$ and $T = 2\pi\sqrt{r^{3}/GM}$, and then say whether a decrease in $r$ makes the quantity increase or decrease.
Two effects are required and each must be linked to its cause; two unexplained statements earn fewer marks. Both causes trace back to the satellite being closer to Earth.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / The Nature of Light / Light and Special Relativity / investigate the evidence, from Einstein’s thought experiments and subsequent experimental validation, for time dilation and length contraction , and analyse quantitatively situations in which these are observed, for example: observations of cosmic-origin muons at the Earth’s surface; atomic clocks (Hafele–Keating experiment); evidence from particle accelerators; evidence from cosmological studies
questions.text:

A scientist on board a spaceship wishes to synchronise two clocks. To achieve this, beams of light from a source placed midway between the clocks activate photocells, turning on both clocks.
