questions.current_path: Year 11 / Kinematics / Motion in a Straight Line / conduct practical investigations, selecting from a range of technologies, to record and analyse the motion of objects in a variety of situations in one dimension in order to measure or calculate: time; distance; displacement; speed; velocity; acceleration
questions.text:
Electrical energy transfer from a power station to its point of use.
Use a flowchart to show how electrical energy is transferred from a power station to its point of use.
Write one labelled box for each stage and join them with arrows, starting with the generator and ending with the consumer; the two transformer stages are the boxes candidates forget.
Annotate each line of the chart with the voltage it carries, high on the transmission run and low at the point of use, because that is the justification for having transformers at all.
Discuss the effects on the environment of the development of AC generators.
This is a discussion, so take one effect at a time and give the cause for each rather than listing nouns.
For the positive effects use the transmission efficiency of AC: what does raising the voltage do to the current in the lines, and what does that do to the power wasted in them?
For the negative effects think about what a large thermal or hydro station physically requires, such as cooling water, fuel or a dam, and about what transmission lines and substations do to the land and to wildlife.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / Electromagnetism / The Motor Effect / investigate qualitatively and quantitatively the interaction between a current-carrying conductor and a uniform magnetic field to establish: (ACSPH080, ACSPH081)
questions.text:
A single turn coil is positioned in a region of uniform magnetic field with a strength of 0.2 T. The plane of the coil is at $45^{\circ}$ to the magnetic field. The coil is a square with 5 cm sides, and carries a current of 10.0 A.
Calculate the magnitude of the force on side AB.
Use $F = BIL\sin\theta$ with $L$ equal to the length of side AB, and convert the side length to metres before substituting.
Identify $\theta$ from the diagram: it is the angle between the current in AB and the field lines, which is not the same as the angle between the plane of the coil and the field.
Explain why the net force produced by the magnetic field on the coil is zero.
All four sides carry the same current in the same uniform field, so begin by comparing the magnitudes of the four forces from $F = BIL\sin\theta$.
The currents in opposite sides of the coil run in opposite directions, and the direction of the force reverses with the current, so compare the direction of the force on each side rather than its size.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / Electromagnetism / Charged Particles, Conductors and Electric and Magnetic Fields / acceleration of charged particles by the electric field
questions.text:
Cathode rays and the electron gun.
How could a student test the hypothesis that cathode rays are streams of particles? In your answer refer to the results that would be observed.
Choose an observation that could only be explained by particles. A small mechanical obstruction placed in the path is the classic choice.
Then add a second observation that tests for charge: place electric or magnetic fields across the beam and say how the deflection reveals the sign of the charge.
How is an electron beam produced in an electron gun?
An electron gun does three jobs in order: it produces electrons, it accelerates them, and it makes them into a narrow beam. Name the component responsible for each.
Think about what happens to a metal when it is heated, and about how you would stop electrons spreading out in every direction once they are emitted.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / The Nature of Light / Light: Quantum Model / analyse the photoelectric effect as it occurs in metallic elements by applying the law of conservation of energy and the photon model of light, (ACSPH119)
questions.text:
Photons and the particle model of light.
Calculate the number of photons, $\lambda = 450\,\mathrm{nm}$, which are required to transfer $1.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{J}$ of energy.
Find the energy carried by one photon before using the total energy; the number of photons is just the total divided by the energy per photon.
Write $E_{\text{photon}} = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$ and convert $450\,\mathrm{nm}$ to metres before substituting, since the power of ten dominates the answer.
A 1 W beam of light transfers 1 J per second from one point to another. With reference to the particle model of light, contrast a 1 W beam of red light and a 1 W beam of blue light.
Both beams are $1\,\mathrm{W}$, so the energy transferred each second is the same; the difference has to lie in the energy of each photon.
Use $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$ to compare the photon energies, then divide the power by the energy per photon to compare how many photons each beam contains.

questions.current_path: Year 11 / Electricity and Magnetism / Electric Circuits / investigate the flow of electric current in metals and apply models to represent current, including: (ACSPH038)
questions.text:
The graph shows the relationship between the resistance of a metal alloy sample and its temperature.
Why is the resistance of the sample higher at 60 K than at 30 K?
Read the two temperatures off the horizontal axis and remember they are absolute temperatures, so $60\,\mathrm{K}$ is twice as hot as $30\,\mathrm{K}$ in terms of the thermal motion of the lattice.
Resistance in a metal comes from the scattering of the conduction electrons by the vibrating ion lattice, so link the greater lattice vibration at the higher temperature to the shorter time between collisions.
Use BCS theory to explain why the resistance of the sample is zero at temperatures below 18 K.
BCS stands for Bardeen, Cooper and Schrieffer, and its key idea is that electrons do not travel through the lattice alone.
Work through it in this order: the interaction that binds two electrons, the name and size of the resulting pair, the critical temperature, and why a pair is not scattered.
The zero on the graph is not because the lattice has stopped vibrating, since below $18\,\mathrm{K}$ it is still vibrating. Ask what the charge carriers are instead.

questions.current_path: Year 11 / Waves and Thermodynamics / Wave Properties / the role of the medium in the propagation of mechanical waves | Year 11 / Waves and Thermodynamics / Wave Properties / conduct practical investigations to explain and analyse the differences between: transverse and longitudinal waves (ACSPH068); mechanical and electromagnetic waves (ACSPH070, ACSPH074)
questions.text:
Describe how geophysicists have reduced the risks from a natural hazard. In your answer, refer to a specific natural hazard and the instruments used to monitor it.
Choose a hazard for which a single, well understood instrument gives early warning, and think about what that instrument actually detects.
The marks need all three links: the hazard and its risk, the instrument, and what the monitoring data is used to do.
Magnetic anomalies and sea-floor spreading.
The striping of the ocean floor is a record written into the rock at the time it formed. Ask what the rock records about Earth's field, and how the ages of the stripes can be found independently.
For the graph, convert the stripe WIDTHS into TIME INTERVALS using the stated rate before you plot anything, and remember what shape a record of polarity against time has.
Radiation, remote sensing and vegetation regrowth.
For a first-hand investigation the marks are for control of variables and for a clear record of what was measured - decide which variables must be held constant and which are changed deliberately.
For remote sensing, use the fact that different surfaces have different ratios of reflected red to near-infrared radiation, and that the same ground can be measured repeatedly from orbit.
Gravity surveys.
Start from $g = GM/r^{2}$ and ask whether the distance from Earth's centre is the same everywhere on its surface.
For the exploration application, distinguish the smooth regional change in $g$ produced by the shape of the ground from the local change produced by something buried under it.
Explain how seismic methods and a knowledge of wave properties have increased our understanding of the structure of Earth.
Build the answer around the two seismic wave types and the single property that separates them: one travels through liquids, the other does not.
Then use the way wave speed varies with density to deduce how the Earth's layers are arranged, and use the shadow zone to locate the core.
Every deduction about the Earth's structure must be tied to a specific wave observation, not merely asserted.

questions.current_path: Year 11 / Waves and Thermodynamics / Sound Waves / conduct investigations to analyse the reflection, diffraction, resonance and superposition of sound waves (ACSPH071)
questions.text:
An ultrasound probe fires a pulse of ultrasound into the abdomen as shown in the diagram.
Analysis of the reflected sound produced the following scan.
Ultrasound scanning of the abdomen.
Each peak on the scan comes from one boundary between two tissues. Convert the time at which a peak appears into a depth using $d = \frac{vt}{2}$ - remember the pulse makes a round trip.
To compare the peaks at $X$ and $Y$, compare the tissues either side of each boundary rather than the distances involved: the deciding quantity is the acoustic impedance $Z = \rho v$, and the fraction reflected rises steeply as the jump in $Z$ grows.
For the numerical part, the useful result is the intensity reflection coefficient $R = \left(\frac{Z_2 - Z_1}{Z_2 + Z_1}\right)^{2}$. Build $Z$ for the two media first, then substitute; you want a fraction, so remember to convert it to a percentage at the end.
X-rays.
Explain how X-rays are produced in an X-ray tube
An X-ray tube converts the kinetic energy of fast electrons into radiation, and there are two distinct ways this happens. A complete answer needs both mechanisms, not just the tube description.
For the comparison, ask what each picture is a view of: a shadow of the whole body, or a thin slice through it? Overlapping structures are superimposed in one and separated in the other, which is exactly why one of them shows soft tissue and the other does not.
X-rays.
The photographs A and B show scans of the same part of the body. Compare the information provided by the two scans
Explain why MRI is an effective tool for diagnosing brain tumours.
Start from what the MRI image is actually a map of. It is not a density of tissue in the x-ray sense; it is a density of hydrogen nuclei, and hydrogen nuclei are found almost entirely in water.
So the question becomes a comparison: how does the water content of a tumour differ from that of the healthy brain tissue around it, and how does that difference show up in the image?
With reference to coherent and incoherent bundles of fibres, explain how an endoscope is used to observe internal organs.
Both bundles are doing the same physics: each fibre guides light by repeated total internal reflection at the glass-air boundary between its core and its cladding. The only difference between them is how the fibres are arranged.
Ask of each bundle what its arrangement has to guarantee. Does the light need to arrive at the right end only, or does it also have to arrive at the right place?
An increased understanding of the properties of radioactive isotopes has been important in the development of medical technologies used to analyse bodily processes.
Justify this statement.
You need at least two scanning techniques that use a radioisotope, and for each one you must name the specific property of the isotope that makes it work - the type of radiation, the energy, or the half-life.
For each technique also state what the tracer is taken up by or attached to, and how the detected radiation becomes an image. That uptake mechanism is what turns the position of the isotope into a record of a bodily process rather than just a picture of an organ.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Origins of the Elements / account for the production of emission and absorption spectra and compare these with a continuous black body spectrum (ACSPH137) | Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Origins of the Elements / investigate the key features of stellar spectra and describe how these are used to classify stars | Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Origins of the Elements / investigate the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram and how it can be used to determine the following about a star: characteristics and evolutionary stage; surface temperature; colour; luminosity
questions.text:
Parsecs, and the resolution and sensitivity of telescopes.
For the definition, remember that a parsec is built from the geometry of Earth's orbit: a right triangle with a baseline of 1 AU and a very small angle at the star. Draw it and label the sides and the angle.
For Galileo, do not just define resolution and sensitivity. The question asks which one was limiting for the objects he actually looked at, so bring the small size of his objective lens and the brightness of those objects into the argument.
For the technology, the question wants a description of how it works and why that improves resolution, not just a name.
The Pleiades cluster and its H-R diagram.
The first sub-part compares two stars on the same diagram, so for each say which stage of its life it has reached and therefore where its fusion is occurring, then state the one thing they have in common and the physical reason for the difference.
For the apparent magnitude, the absolute magnitude is the one read off the diagram, so the distance modulus is the only calculation needed. Give your answer to a sensible precision, since an absolute magnitude can only be read to about the nearest half magnitude.
For the relative brightness, remember that the magnitude scale is logarithmic, so convert the magnitude difference into a ratio using a power of ten, and check the sign so that the ratio you end up with is greater than one.
Using a Cepheid and one other named example, explain the difference between intrinsic and extrinsic variable stars.
The distinction is where the cause of the variation lies: inside the star, or outside it. Test each example against that question. Does the total energy emitted by the system change, or only the amount that reaches us?
For the examples themselves, a Cepheid pulses, while an eclipsing binary has one star pass in front of the other along our line of sight. Name both, and say in each case which quantity actually changes.
Spectroscopy is an important tool in obtaining information about stars, but it is a much more powerful tool when combined with photometry.
Justify this statement.
A justification needs a limitation, not just two descriptions. The test question is: what can spectroscopy NOT tell you about a star, and what does photometry not tell you?
Then give at least one worked example where putting the two together yields something neither gives alone, for instance motion plus distance, or a light curve plus a spectral type.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / The Nature of Light / Light and Special Relativity / Use Einstein’s mass–energy equivalence relationship to calculate the energy released by processes in which mass is converted to energy, for example: (ACSPH134)
questions.text:
Name a radioisotope used in agriculture and describe its use.
Agricultural radioisotopes are used in two quite different ways: as tracers that follow where something goes, and as sources that irradiate the plant or the produce. Either will do for full marks.
For a tracer, the essential feature is that the isotope behaves chemically like the ordinary element, so it can take part in the same processes, while still being detectable because it is radioactive.
Say how the radiation is detected, and what that detection then reveals about the plant.
Explain how the reaction rate in a nuclear reactor can be increased or decreased.
Three separate quantities control the rate, and the marks need all three related to the rate of fission: the energies of the neutrons, the moderator that sets those energies, and the control rods that remove neutrons.
Ask first what has to be true of a neutron before a uranium-235 nucleus will capture it, then what the moderator is for, then which direction the control rods must move to slow the reaction down.
For (ii), check the equation first by adding the mass numbers and then the atomic numbers on each side, and then compare the *actual* masses, not the mass numbers, of reactants and products.
$\,{}^{235}_{92}\mathrm{U} + {}^{1}_{0}\mathrm{n} \rightarrow {}^{140}_{56}\mathrm{Ba} + {}^{92}_{36}\mathrm{Kr} + 4\,{}^{1}_{0}\mathrm{n}$
Explain why energy is released in this reaction.
Copy and complete in your booklet the following table comparing forces in the atomic nucleus.
Do the table one force at a time. For the electrostatic force ask two separate questions: does it push or pull, and how far does it reach?
Compare that range with the strong nuclear force's. The strong force acts only across a distance comparable with a nucleus, which is exactly why it cannot hold a proton at one end of a large nucleus to a proton at the other end.
The gravitational column is supplied as a reference. Use it to order the three forces by strength, and remember that only one of the three has a range limited to nuclear dimensions.
A cricket ball has a mass of 156 g and a velocity of $20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Calculate its de Broglie wavelength.
The de Broglie wavelength of a macroscopic object comes from the same relation as for an electron, $\lambda = h/mv$, but the mass term behaves in a completely different way.
Convert the mass to kilograms before substituting. A factor of a thousand in the mass changes the answer by a factor of a thousand, and this question is really about what that does to the size of the wavelength.
When you have the wavelength, compare it with the size of the ball itself. That comparison, not the arithmetic, is the point of the question.
Identify the types and number of quarks and leptons in a tritium (${}^{3}_{1}\mathrm{H}$) atom.
A tritium atom has one proton and two neutrons in its nucleus, and one electron outside it. Start by building each nucleon out of quarks.
Recall the quark composition of a proton and of a neutron, and then add them up for the whole nucleus rather than for a single nucleon.
Count the leptons separately at the end: the electron is the only lepton, and neither a proton nor a neutron contains one.
Outline the main contributions of Heisenberg and Pauli to the development of atomic theory.
Two physicists and two contributions each. Decide for each scientist what the single most important thing was that he produced.
For Heisenberg, ask what the uncertainty principle says about knowing the position and the momentum of a particle at the same time, and what that does to the classical picture of an electron in a definite orbit.
For Pauli, ask what would happen if two electrons in an atom were allowed to have the same set of quantum numbers, and connect your answer to the shape of the periodic table.
Mathematical models, validated by experimental evidence, have improved our understanding of the atom.
Justify this statement, focusing on the models developed by Bohr and de Broglie.
A model is validated when a measurement agrees with something the model predicted, so for each of your two models write the prediction down first and the experimental test down second, and do not reverse the order.
For Bohr, the predictions to quote are the pattern of the hydrogen spectrum and the value of the ionisation energy; for de Broglie, the prediction is that the electron should behave as a wave, with a wavelength set by its momentum.
Finish by saying what the two models together replaced, and how the modern picture differs from Bohr's idea of a definite orbit.

questions.current_path: Year 11 / Electricity and Magnetism / Electric Circuits / investigate quantitatively the current–voltage relationships in ohmic and non-ohmic resistors to explore the usefulness and limitations of Ohm’s Law using: (ACSPH003, ACSPH041, ACSPH043) | Year 11 / Electricity and Magnetism / Electric Circuits / investigate qualitatively and quantitatively series and parallel circuits to relate the flow of current through the individual components, the potential differences across those components and the rate of energy conversion by the components to the laws of conservation of charge and energy, by deriving the following relationships: (ACSPH038, ACSPH039, ACSPH044)
questions.text:
A circuit for a solar battery charger is shown.
Construct a truth table for the logic circuit contained in Section D.
Section D contains only two elements: a NOT gate on one of the comparator outputs and an AND gate. Write the output as a single Boolean expression in $I_0$ and $I_1$ before you fill in any table entries.
Then evaluate that expression for all four input combinations. The row in which the inverter's input is 0 and the AND gate's other input is 1 is the one that catches people out, so check it separately.
Explain whether the operational amplifiers in Section C of the circuit are used in an open loop or closed loop configuration.
Trace the wires from each amplifier's output and ask whether any of them returns to one of that amplifier's own inputs. That single question settles the configuration.
Once you know there is no return path, think about what an amplifier does with an enormous voltage gain: even a millivolt between the inputs is enough to drive the output hard against one of the supply rails, so the device acts as a switch rather than as an analogue amplifier.
Determine the formula relating $V_{\text{batt}}$ to $V_{\text{in}}$.
Section A is a two-resistor potential divider. Write the divider rule as $V_{\text{out}} = V_{\text{in}} \times \dfrac{R_{\text{below}}}{R_{\text{above}} + R_{\text{below}}}$ and decide which of the $23\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ and $10\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistors lies above the $V_{\text{in}}$ tap.
Then rearrange your expression so that $V_{\text{batt}}$ is the subject. The result should be a single constant multiplying $V_{\text{in}}$, and you will need that constant again in part (d).
Calculate the range of voltages for $V_{\text{batt}}$ for which the LED indicator lights up.
Decide first which logic state of $O_0$ lights the LED. Trace the current path from the $+5\ \mathrm{V}$ rail through the $1\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor, through the LED, into the $O_0$ node.
Next find both reference voltages. All three resistors of Section B lie in one series chain across $+5\ \mathrm{V}$, so a single current value gives the voltage at each tap, and each of those taps feeds one op-amp input.
Combine the two comparator outputs using the truth table from part (a) to find when $O_0$ is in that state, then use the relationship between $V_{\text{batt}}$ and $V_{\text{in}}$ from part (c) to convert your limits into $V_{\text{batt}}$.
Light-emitting diodes and optical fibres.
This part has two halves about two different devices. Answer each half separately rather than writing one continuous paragraph, because the marks are split between them.
For the LED, the ideas you need are the p-type and n-type layers, what forward bias does to the junction, and what happens when an electron meets a hole there. For the optical fibre, the ideas are the core and the cladding and the condition on the angle at which light strikes their boundary.
The detailed material properties of silica that make the fibre work are the subject of part (f), so keep that material for part (f) and concentrate here on how each device works.
What properties of silica make it a suitable material for use in optical fibres?
Sort the required properties into optical ones and mechanical or chemical ones. The optical properties decide whether the light stays in the fibre and whether it survives the journey; the others decide whether the fibre can be drawn into long, thin, strong strands that survive being laid.
For the guiding property you need two refractive indices, the core and the cladding, and a condition on the angle of incidence at the boundary between them. For the transparency property think about which part of the spectrum has to be used for telecommunications and how far ordinary glass would attenuate it.
Three distinct, clearly stated properties earn the full marks. General statements such as 'it is a good material' do not, so name the property and say what it does for the fibre.
The semiconductor integrated circuit industry is rapidly approaching fundamental physics limitations for the design of integrated circuits for computers.
Explain what these limitations are and why this will require a reconceptualisation of the way computers are designed.
Organise the answer as separate physical limits rather than one long list. Good headings are the size of the transistor, the heat produced, the speed at which signals can move along the wires, and the quantum limit.
For each limit write the sentence 'this stops being improvable when ...' and then say what it prevents the chip from doing. The mark is for the physics together with its consequence, not for naming a phenomenon.
The question ends with a judgement, so your list of limits has to lead somewhere: it must explain why simply making today's architecture smaller and faster can no longer be the answer, and what will have to change instead.

The graph shows how the gravitational potential energy ($E_p$) of a satellite changes with its altitude. What is the change in gravitational potential energy of the satellite when its altitude is reduced from 14 000 km to 4000 km?
$+8.8 \times 10^{9}\,\mathrm{J}$
$-2.8 \times 10^{9}\,\mathrm{J}$

questions.text:
Answer the questions in the spaces provided. These spaces provide guidance for the expected length of response.
Outline a first-hand investigation that could be performed to measure a value for acceleration due to gravity.
Whatever method you choose, the outline must state the quantities you will measure and the equation that connects them to $g$, and it must be a first-hand method. A pendulum works if you can measure length and period; free fall works if you can measure distance and time. This part is worth 1 mark, so a bare method is enough.
How would you assess the accuracy of the result of the investigation?
Accuracy is about closeness to the true value, not about scatter, so the answer needs a source for the accepted value and a number for the size of the difference, such as a percentage difference. Say which part of your method would cause a systematic error.
How would you increase the reliability of the data collected?
Reliability is about scatter between repeats, so the technique is to collect more data: repeat each measurement, and time many oscillations per trial rather than one, then average. Taking readings across a range of values of the independent variable is also what makes the analysis possible.
How would you assess the reliability of the data collected?
You need a numerical measure of the scatter: the range, the standard deviation, or half the difference between the highest and lowest repeat, calculated at a fixed value of the independent variable. Then state a judgement about whether it is small enough, and say how you would improve the results if it were not.

questions.current_path: Year 11 / Electricity and Magnetism / Magnetism / use magnetic field lines to model qualitatively the direction and strength of magnetic fields produced by magnets, current-carrying wires and solenoids and relate these fields to their effect on magnetic materials that are placed within them (ACSPH083)
questions.text:
A bar magnet is placed on a sensitive electronic balance as shown in the diagram. A hollow solenoid is held stationary, such that the magnet is partly within the solenoid. The solenoid is then lifted straight up without touching the magnet. The reading on the balance is observed to change briefly.
Why does a current flow in the solenoid?
The magnet stays still while the solenoid moves, so ask what is happening to the magnetic field linking the coil as it moves relative to the magnet.
A current needs two things: an emf across the coil and a complete circuit. The diagram shows whether the circuit through the copper wire is open or closed.
Explain the reason for changes in the reading on the electronic balance as the solenoid is removed.
Use Lenz's law: the induced current sets up a field that opposes the change in flux which produced it.
The flux is decreasing as the solenoid is lifted off the magnet, so work out whether the solenoid is trying to pull the magnet back or push it away, and on which side of the magnet the solenoid is.
The reading is a force measurement, so ask what extra force the pan has to support. Then remember the reading returns to the true mass once the motion stops, since the effect exists only while the flux is changing.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / The Nature of Light / Light and Special Relativity / analyse and evaluate the evidence confirming or denying Einstein’s two postulates: | Year 12 / The Nature of Light / Light and Special Relativity / investigate the evidence, from Einstein’s thought experiments and subsequent experimental validation, for time dilation and length contraction , and analyse quantitatively situations in which these are observed, for example: observations of cosmic-origin muons at the Earth’s surface; atomic clocks (Hafele–Keating experiment); evidence from particle accelerators; evidence from cosmological studies
questions.text:
Show all relevant working in questions involving calculations.
Outline ONE piece of evidence supporting Einstein's theory of relativity.
Choose an observation that has actually been measured: something involving muons, the speed of light, clocks flown on aircraft, or the fringes from Michelson-Morley.
The two marks are one for naming the evidence and one for linking it to what the theory predicts, so write both halves of that link in your answer.
What criteria are used to test and validate a theory?
Start with the strongest test: does the theory make quantitative predictions, and do controlled, repeated experiments agree with them to within experimental uncertainty?
Then consider the other criteria examiners accept, such as internal and mathematical consistency, and whether the theory explains and predicts phenomena that were not known when it was proposed.
Three distinct criteria earn the three marks, so avoid restating a single idea in different words. Agreement from several independent experiments is the strongest evidence of all.
The distance between the cathode and screen in a cathode ray tube is 40 cm. If an electron travels through the tube at $3.0 \times 10^{7}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, what is the apparent distance from the cathode to the screen in the electron's frame of reference?
The separation is measured along the direction of the electron's motion, so the relevant effect is length contraction: $l = l_{0}\sqrt{1 - v^{2}/c^{2}}$.
Substitute the speed as a fraction of $c$ first. The answer then follows from a square root that is close to 1, so expect only a small change from $40\,\mathrm{cm}$.
Check the direction of the effect: length contraction can only shorten the distance, never lengthen it.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / Electromagnetism / Charged Particles, Conductors and Electric and Magnetic Fields / acceleration, perpendicular to the field, of charged particles
questions.text:
The diagram shows the paths taken by two moving charged particles when they enter a region of uniform magnetic field.
Why do the paths curve in different directions?
The field, the speed and the point of entry are all the same for the two particles, so the only quantity in $F = qvB$ that can differ between them is the sign of the charge.
Ask which quantity in that equation can be negative, and how a change in its sign reverses the direction of the force.
Why are the paths circular?
Ask what the magnetic force does to the speed. It is always at right angles to the velocity, so it does no work and the speed cannot change.
Then ask what a constant, non-zero force of fixed magnitude, always perpendicular to the velocity, does to the direction of travel. That is the definition of uniform circular motion, which is why the paths are circular arcs rather than spirals.
Use the fact that the field is uniform: that is what makes the size of the force, and so the radius, constant.
How do the properties of a particle affect the radius of curvature of its path in a uniform magnetic field?
Two forces must be equated: the magnetic force $qvB$ and the centripetal force $\frac{mv^{2}}{r}$.
Set them equal and cancel one factor of $v$ before you read off how the radius depends on the mass, the speed, the charge and the field strength.
Check the sense of each dependence: a heavier or faster particle bends less sharply through the same field, so it must trace a wider circle.

questions.text:
Geophysics
Answer parts (a)-(c) in Section II Answer Booklet 1. Answer parts (d)-(e) in Section II Answer Booklet 2.
Show all relevant working in questions involving calculations.
Jean Richer observed that a pendulum clock, which was accurately calibrated in Paris, lost about 150 seconds per day when it was used on the equatorial island of Cayenne.
Outline the effects of TWO variables that changed the behaviour of the clock.
Write down $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$ and decide which of $L$ and $g$ changed between Paris and Cayenne. Remember that Cayenne is almost on the equator, that Earth is flattened at the poles so $g$ is lower there, and that the equatorial climate is much warmer than Paris.
For each variable you choose, finish the chain: value of the variable at Cayenne -> value of $L$ or $g$ -> value of $T$ -> whether the clock gains or loses time.
Why does Earth's magnetic field change over time?
(i) The field is not produced by a permanently magnetised body. Identify what is actually moving, and carrying current, inside the Earth, then note that this motion is not the same at all times or in all places.
(ii) Judge the bar-magnet drawing as a model of a field, not as a statement of fact. Check the direction convention on the field lines it shows, check how the real field is tilted relative to the axis of rotation, and check whether a permanently magnetised bar of iron could exist at the temperatures inside the Earth.
Data obtained from a shot-geophone analysis is shown on the following graph.
Read the axes first: time for signal arrival against distance from the shot, plotted to both sides of the shot. On a graph like this the gradient of each line is the reciprocal of the velocity of the path the signal actually took.
One line passes through the origin and the other does not. A non-zero intercept time on the time axis tells you the signal has had to travel down to a boundary between layers and back up to the surface before its travel through the top layer can begin.
For each line, say which path the signal followed and what its gradient therefore means - do not stop at describing the shape of the line.
Other than the geometric fit of continents or magnetic evidence, what evidence supports the theory of plate tectonics?
Leave out continental fit and the magnetic stripes, as the question says. List the ways the Earth itself can be tested: where on the planet the activity happens, how old the rock at a given place is, whether the same rock and fossils match across ocean basins, and whether anyone has measured movement directly.
For each item you list, add the sentence that turns it into evidence - say what you would expect to observe if plate tectonics were true, and what would be observed if it were not.
How is remote sensing used to obtain information about Earth?
Sort the instruments into two families: those that simply record radiation arriving from the Earth, and those that send out a pulse of their own and time the echo. Passive and active is the usual terminology.
For each family name one instrument and the physics it relies on - emission and reflection for passive, the speed of the wave and the inverse square law for active.
Then give the trade-off that decides where a satellite goes: how much ground it can cover against how much detail it can resolve. This is the kind of limitation the question is looking for.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Properties of the Nucleus / analyse the spontaneous decay of unstable nuclei, and the properties of the alpha, beta and gamma radiation emitted (ACSPH028, ACSPH030) | Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Properties of the Nucleus / analyse relationships that represent conservation of mass-energy in spontaneous and artificial nuclear transmutations, including alpha decay, beta decay, nuclear fission and nuclear fusion (ACSPH032)
questions.text:
Medical Physics
Answer parts (a)-(c) in Section II Answer Booklet 1. Answer parts (d)-(e) in Section II Answer Booklet 2.
Show all relevant working in questions involving calculations.
The first X-ray image of a human was made in 1895 but it was not until 1972 that CAT scan imaging was developed.
The 77-year gap is a gap in technology, not in physics. Identify the step a plain radiograph does not need but a CAT scan does, and then ask what had to be invented before that step was practical.
For the PET and CAT contrasts keep two questions apart: what information the image carries, and where the radiation is produced. Answering both for each modality avoids the usual confusion.
When you write about the 20th century developments, be specific about what each one contributed - processing speed, memory, storage, display, detector quality - rather than simply saying 'computers were invented'.
What effects do the pulses of radio waves have on hydrogen nuclei in the body of a person having a magnetic resonance image scan?
In the strong static field the hydrogen nuclei line up with the field, producing a small net magnetisation. Ask what a radio wave at exactly the right frequency does to that arrangement, and what the nuclei do immediately afterwards.
The image is built from signals the nuclei themselves give out on the way back to equilibrium, so describe the whole cycle in order: align, disturb, precess, relax, emit.
For the second half, name the 20th century physics behind each ingredient separately - the source of the strong field, and the machinery that turns a large volume of measured data into an image.
Describe the properties that make a radioactive isotope useful for medical imaging. Include a specific example of a radioactive isotope in your answer.
There are three separate requirements, and you need all three: the radiation must be able to get out of the body and be detected outside it, the half-life must suit the time the scan takes, and the element must be chemically able to be put where you want it to go.
Then give a named isotope with its half-life and its use, and say why that half-life is the right one for that particular job - too short and the tracer decays before the scan, too long and the patient is irradiated for no reason.
Explain how endoscopes obtain images of internal organs.
One piece of physics does all the work here: light is trapped inside a fibre by repeated total internal reflection at the boundary between the glass core and the cladding, so it can follow a bundle round corners inside the body.
Then work out why one bundle of fibres is enough to light the organ while the other has to preserve the image, and what the arrangement of the fibres in each bundle must guarantee for that to work.
Discuss the range of information obtained from, and the limitations of, ultrasound medical imaging technology.
Take the range of information first and the limitations second, and do not let them run together - a limitation only has meaning once the reader knows what the scan can do.
For the limitations, remember that ultrasound is a mechanical wave: the resolution is set by its wavelength, and it needs a medium to travel in, which is why a gas-filled cavity and bone defeat it.
Include the advantages as well - no ionising radiation and a real-time image - because a 'limitations' mark usually expects the comparison with the alternatives.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Origins of the Elements / investigate the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram and how it can be used to determine the following about a star: characteristics and evolutionary stage; surface temperature; colour; luminosity
questions.text:
Astrophysics
Answer parts (a)-(c) in Section II Answer Booklet 1. Answer parts (d)-(e) in Section II Answer Booklet 2.
Show all relevant working in questions involving calculations.
Why do astronomers use both apparent and absolute measurements in photometry?
Apparent brightness is what actually arrives at the telescope; absolute brightness is what would arrive if the star were placed at a standard distance. Ask what extra variable apparent brightness folds in that absolute brightness removes.
For the second half, do not confuse the two techniques: one measures the total light arriving from the star, the other sorts that light by wavelength before measuring it. Then say what each can tell you that the other cannot.
Describe the problems associated with ground-based optical astronomy in terms of resolution.
There are two independent limits on the resolution of a telescope, and only one of them responds to building a bigger instrument. Identify both before deciding which one governs in practice.
Compare them numerically in order of magnitude - one improves as the aperture grows and the other does not, and that comparison is the heart of the answer.
Then treat loss of contrast as a separate problem from loss of resolution: the sky's own light, from airglow, light pollution and the daytime sky, raises the background and hides faint objects even when the resolution is good.
Draw a flow diagram for stellar evolution using the following celestial objects: Black hole; Main sequence star; Neutron star/pulsar; Planetary nebula; Red giant; Supernova; White dwarf. Your flow diagram must include all of the objects listed above.
Every star starts the same way; what differs is the mass, and mass decides what happens after the core has run out of fuel.
Sketch the common trunk first, then add the branches. Two branches are needed because the objects on the list include alternatives to each other - a neutron star and a black hole cannot both lie on a single path.
Decide what the core becomes once it can no longer release energy by fusion; that single step is what splits your diagram in two, and where the masses of the branches differ is what decides the final remnant.
Explain how trigonometric parallax is used to determine the distances to stars.
Parallax needs a baseline that is large compared with the distance being measured, so ask where on Earth you could put the telescope to make that baseline as long as possible, and how long you would have to wait.
Then relate the small angle you measure to the distance with $p = b/d$, and take care with the factor of two between the total apparent shift and the parallax angle itself.
The convenient result is $d(\mathrm{pc}) = 1/p(\mathrm{arcsec})$. Check your units are consistent before substituting, and think about why this method stops working for distant stars.
Astronomers have obtained the following data about stars in a binary system.
Analyse the above data to write a detailed description of this binary system.
Take the table first: divide the two luminosities to get how unequal the stars are, and subtract the apparent magnitudes to see how much brighter the brighter star looks from Earth.
Then place each star on the H-R diagram. A spectral class fixes the surface temperature, but a star is only on the main sequence if its luminosity is the one expected for that class - work out which of these two does.
For the period, measure the spacing of the repeating dips on the light curve, and remember that two different depths mean the two stars are eclipsing each other in turn. Finally, put the average separation and that period into $M = 4\pi^{2}a^{3}/GT^{2}$ for the total mass of the system.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Quantum Mechanical Nature of the Atom / investigate the line emission spectra to examine the Balmer series in hydrogen (ACSPH138) | Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Quantum Mechanical Nature of the Atom / relate qualitatively and quantitatively the quantised energy levels of the hydrogen atom and the law of conservation of energy to the line emission spectrum of hydrogen using: (ACSPH136)
questions.text:
From Quanta to Quarks
Answer parts (a)-(c) in Section II Answer Booklet 1. Answer parts (d)-(e) in Section II Answer Booklet 2.
Show all relevant working in questions involving calculations.
Using diagrams and text, outline Bohr's explanation of the Balmer series.
Begin from Bohr's two postulates: the electron may occupy only certain allowed orbits, each with a fixed energy, and it neither radiates while in an orbit nor changes energy without absorbing or emitting a photon.
Conservation of energy then fixes the photon: $hf = E_i - E_f$. Work out which initial and final states produce the visible lines, and say why the series is called the Balmer series.
The diagram is part of the answer: draw the nucleus with a few labelled orbits and arrows for every transition that ends in $n = 2$, then combine $E = hf$ with $c = f\lambda$ to show that the wavelengths are discrete and crowd together towards the short-wavelength limit.
What are the requirements for an uncontrolled nuclear chain reaction, and how does the equivalence between mass and energy relate to what occurs during the natural radioactivity process?
Work through the chain-reaction conditions one at a time: the fuel must be able to absorb a neutron and split, and each split must release enough free neutrons to keep the neutron population growing rather than shrinking.
Ask what would happen if neutrons leaked out of the fuel or were absorbed by impurities - that is what sets the quantity and purity conditions, and it is why a moderator is not required in the fast chain reaction.
For the radioactivity half, compare the mass of the parent nucleus with the total mass of the daughter nucleus and the emitted particles. A difference in mass is not a violation of anything: by $E = \Delta m c^{2}$ it is energy.
How can neutrons be used to probe the positions of nuclei within the structure of a metal crystal? Make reference to the work of Louis de Broglie in your answer.
Neutrons carry no charge, so they are not deflected by the electron cloud. A neutron beam is therefore scattered almost entirely by the nuclei - which is what makes it a probe of nuclear positions rather than of electron structure.
Now use de Broglie: choose the neutron's speed so that its wavelength is comparable with the spacing of the atomic planes, and regularly spaced nuclei will diffract the beam just as a diffraction grating does.
The measurement to make is the angle at which the diffracted beams appear, and the quantity it gives you is the separation of the planes. Say explicitly how you get from the angle to the spacing.
Explain how the internal structures of the proton and neutron determine their properties.

Think about what attachments would have to be built into that tube so that a small piece of tissue can be cut and then brought back out again.
How is the orientation of the magnetic axis of a hydrogen nucleus affected by the application of a strong magnetic field during an MRI scan?
Explain the difference in the relaxation time of hydrogen in water and the relaxation time of hydrogen in other molecules.
For the first sub-question, start from what the strong field does to the orientation of each hydrogen nucleus's magnetic moment, given that before the field was applied those moments were pointing in all directions at random.
For the second sub-question, remember that relaxation requires energy to be transferred to the surroundings. It is the rate at which the surrounding molecules tumble, not the nucleus itself, that sets the relaxation time, so ask why water behaves differently from other molecules.
How is the Doppler effect used in ultrasonics to investigate blood flow characteristics?
Outline TWO technologies that are required for an ultrasound scan.
For the Doppler sub-question, remember that the shift depends on whether the blood cells are moving towards or away from the transducer, and that only the component of their velocity along the beam is measured.
For the technologies sub-question, name TWO things the scan needs: the device that generates and receives the sound, and the device or method that turns echo timing into a picture.
The data set gives information about a variety of radioactive isotopes, some of which can be used in diagnostic tools for medicine.
Using the information in the table, justify which radioactive isotopes are suitable for use in diagnostic imaging techniques.
Start from the radiation column: whatever imaging technique you choose, the radiation that is detected must be able to leave the body and be detected outside it.
Then test each isotope's half-life against the practical demands of an imaging scan: long enough to be manufactured, transported, administered and imaged, but short enough to decay away so the patient is not exposed for long.
Be alert to entries whose half-life is far too long, and to any isotope that emits the right radiation but has a half-life that makes it impractical.

questions.text:
- Astrophysics.
Describe an investigation that can be used to show why it is desirable in terms of sensitivity for a telescope to have a larger diameter lens.
The quantity that decides how faint a source can be detected is how much light the instrument gathers, so begin by asking what changes when only the diameter of the lens is changed.
A photometer is the instrument that gives a numerical reading proportional to the light arriving at it. Set out the investigation as: what is held constant, what is varied, what is measured, and what result is expected.
Finish by making the last step explicit rather than implied: relate the extra light collected to the faintest object that can then be detected, and say what that is called.
Matar is a star in the same spectral class as the Sun, yet it has four times the mass of the Sun.
Draw a labelled Hertzsprung-Russell (H-R) diagram, and mark the position of Matar on the diagram with an X.
On an H-R diagram the horizontal axis is surface temperature and the vertical axis is luminosity. Spectral class tells you which way to move horizontally, so the word *same spectral class* fixes one coordinate for you.
For the other coordinate, remember that on the main sequence mass fixes luminosity. Ask what would happen to the surface temperature of a main-sequence star four times the mass of the Sun, and whether that is compatible with the spectral class given.
For (ii), write down $L = 4\pi R^{2}\sigma T^{4}$. Since the temperature is the same for both stars, every difference in luminosity must come from the radius - and then work out what a bigger radius does to the density for the same mass.
Matar is a star in the same spectral class as the Sun, yet it has four times the mass of the Sun.
Contrast the physical properties, other than mass, of Matar and the Sun.
Describe the dominant nuclear reaction in an A2 main sequence star.
Which fusion cycle dominates depends on the temperature of the core, so start by deciding which cycle belongs to the hottest main-sequence stars rather than to the coolest like the Sun.
Write the overall reaction as a balance: how many hydrogen nuclei are consumed, what nucleus they are converted into, and what else appears among the products that has to be accounted for.
Name the heavy nuclei that take part but are not used up. Those catalytic nuclei are the reason this cycle runs faster than the proton-proton chain at the same temperature.
Describe the transition process of a G2 main sequence star, such as the Sun, evolving into a red giant.
Follow the star forward in time. The first thing that happens is that a fuel is used up, and the question is where and how.
Fusion does not stop everywhere at once. Once the core hydrogen is gone, ask where the fusion moves to, what that does to the layer surrounding the core, and what the increased radiation pressure from that layer does to the envelope above it.
The envelope expanding and cooling changes the star's colour. Name the process that eventually begins abruptly in the core once the envelope has peeled away, and give the name of that event.
The graphs give information that could be used to calculate the distance from Earth to a Type 1 Cepheid Variable.
The star is claimed to be approximately 1260 parsecs from Earth. Show how this claim is supported or refuted by the information in the graphs.
State an advantage and a disadvantage of using the graphs above to calculate the distance to a star.
The period of the light variation of a Cepheid is linked to its true luminosity, so one of the graphs converts a measured period into an absolute magnitude, and the other gives the apparent magnitude as seen from Earth. You then have two magnitudes for the same star, so write down the relation that links apparent magnitude, absolute magnitude and distance before substituting, and note that the distance comes out of it in a form that still has to be evaluated.
Compare the distance you obtain with the claimed 1260 pc and state whether the claim is supported or refuted. Check the size of your answer against the size of the magnitude difference - if the two differ by a factor of ten, look for a misplaced $+5$.
For (ii), keep the two halves separate: an advantage of using these graphs, and a disadvantage of using these graphs. Both are about the method, not about this particular star.
How is light analysed, using physics principles, in order to determine the standard properties for the main sequence stars of Spectral Class A shown in this table?
Acknowledgement: CSIRO.
Each column of the table needs a different instrument or a different physics principle, so sort the four standard properties into groups before you write anything.
Spectroscopy and photometry are the two workhorses. One of them gives a temperature and a composition by splitting the light into lines; the other gives brightness. Decide which is which, and then think about what extra piece of information is needed to turn brightness into luminosity.
Mass is the difficult one, because a single isolated star cannot be weighed. Recall how the masses of the two stars in a binary system are obtained from the period and separation of their orbit, and which conservation law that relies on.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Quantum Mechanical Nature of the Atom / assess the limitations of the Rutherford and Bohr atomic models
questions.text:
- From Quanta to Quarks.
Outline the key features of the Rutherford model of the atom.
Explain how the Bohr model of the atom overcomes an identified limitation of the Rutherford model of the atom.
List what Rutherford kept and what he threw away. The small dense nucleus survived the change of model; the large extended positive charge did not, and the atom is mostly empty space with the electrons far out.
For the second half, name the specific observation the Rutherford model could not reproduce - the observed line spectrum of hydrogen - and then state the single Bohr assumption that removes the difficulty.
Keep the quantisation precise: it is the discrete set of allowed energy levels, and hence the discrete set of emitted photon energies, that does the work. Electrons do not radiate merely because they are accelerating.
This equation describes a nuclear reaction.
Use the data above to calculate the energy released in this reaction.
Apply Einstein's idea of the equivalence of mass and energy to explain the production of energy in the reaction above.
Write down the total mass of the reactants, remembering the incident neutron, and the total mass of the products, remembering all three released neutrons, then take the difference. Do not cancel the neutrons before you have counted them.
Convert that mass difference to energy with $E = \Delta m c^{2}$. Using $1\,\mathrm{amu}\,c^{2} = 931.5\,\mathrm{MeV}$ gives the answer directly in MeV, which is the natural unit here.
As a check: the mass difference should be a few tenths of an atomic mass unit, so the energy should be of order $10^{2}\,\mathrm{MeV}$. If you get something near zero, your masses still contain electrons - use nuclear masses or atomic masses consistently on both sides.
Pauli is said to have 'suggested' the existence of the neutrino. Explain why the neutrino was 'suggested' but not discovered by Pauli.
Start from the observation that motivated the particle: in beta decay the spectrum of electron energies was continuous and its maximum was lower than the energy difference between the parent and daughter nuclei, and momentum did not balance either.
The proposed particle had to carry the missing energy and momentum so that both were conserved. That is the sense in which it was 'suggested' - the conservation laws demanded it.
For 'not discovered', think about what detecting a particle requires: it must interact with something. Compare how readily a neutral, almost massless particle interacts with matter compared with a charged particle or an alpha particle.
Identify the fundamental forces proposed by the standard model of the atom.
Explain how the stability of atomic nuclei is maintained.
The standard model names four interactions. Remember that gravity is included in the list even though the model does not actually describe it - that is a fair point to make about its limits.
For nuclear stability, set out the competing contributions inside a nucleus: one is enormously strong but acts only over a very short range, the other acts between every pair of protons and grows with their number. Which is which?
Then write the two as an inequality and ask how it changes as the proton number increases. Remember that the protons would not need any help if they were not electrically charged.
How did de Broglie use existing concepts and ideas to come up with new interpretations that have increased our understanding of the structure of matter?
Identify the two things that were already known before de Broglie: the particle-like behaviour of light, and the existence of quantised electron energy levels in the atom that nobody could explain.
His move was to transfer the first idea from light to matter, giving every particle a wavelength $\lambda = h/p$, and then to relate that wavelength to the allowed orbits of the electron so the energy levels could be accounted for.
Keep the two halves of the answer strictly separate - what de Broglie contributed, and which existing concepts he used to get there. That separation is exactly what this question rewards.

- The Age of Silicon.
This circuit shows how a light-dependent resistor (LDR) can be used to control a voltage output.
The response curve of the LDR in the circuit is shown.
What would the voltage $V_{out}$ be when the light intensity at the LDR is 20 lux?
The circuit is a potential divider. Identify the two components in series and, more importantly, which one the output voltage is measured across.
Both axes of the response curve are logarithmic, so locate the decade on the resistance axis and interpolate within it before you write the value down.
Write the divider as the supply voltage split in the ratio of the two resistances, then substitute the value read from the graph in place of the LDR. Keep the units consistent.
Describe the role of a LDR in a camera.
The LDR does not report a light level directly; it produces an electrical quantity that changes with the light falling on it. Name that quantity.
Follow that quantity into the camera: which part of the camera receives it, and which two adjustable settings does it act on?
The whole arrangement has a common name, used in every camera including a phone. Ending with that name is a clean way to close the answer.
Explain how input and output transducers can be used to control the temperature in a room.
A control system needs at least two transducers. Identify which device is the input and what it converts, and which device is the output and what it converts.
Ask what would happen if the output transducer were driven directly by the small signal from the sensing circuit, and use that to justify the component that is actually used.
A complete answer describes the whole loop: measure, compare with a set value, act, and then note that the change produced feeds back into the original measurement.
For the logic circuit, construct a truth table showing the output, $O$, for all possible combinations of inputs $A$, $B$ and $C$.
Rewrite the circuit as a Boolean expression, working from the inputs towards the output and writing down what each gate does as you go.
One of the inputs passes through an inverting gate, so a 0 at that input arrives at the next gate as a 1. That single fact changes several rows of the table, so be careful which rows.
Fill the table in a fixed order, starting from all inputs zero, and check one row by substituting its values into your expression before you trust the rest.
Describe an ideal operational amplifier.
Start with the ideal properties themselves. There are four of them that matter, and one of them - the resistance looking into the inputs - is the reason the rest of the circuit becomes simple.
For (ii), decide first where the signal must go and where the feedback must go. An inverting amplifier sends the input to one particular input terminal and returns a fraction of the output to that same terminal, so draw the feedback path and work backwards to the resistance needed.
For (iii), the gain of an inverting amplifier is negative. Treat the magnitude and the sign as two separate pieces of information: one of them fixes the height of your sketch, the other decides whether crests stay crests or become troughs.
The diagram shows an operational amplifier with $R_{in} = 4.7\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ connected between $V_{in}$ and the inverting input, and $V_{out}$ taken from the output. Reproduce this diagram in your writing booklet and modify it to perform as an inverting amplifier with a gain of 2.
The diagram shows an input waveform $V_{in}$ for an inverting amplifier with a gain of 2. Sketch the output waveform $V_{out}$ in your writing booklet.
Assess how the development of electronics since the invention of the transistor has met the increasing computing needs of society.
An assessment question needs both sides: state what the development of electronics has achieved, and then state what it has not been able to achieve. Use specific stages rather than a general trend - discrete transistors, then integrated circuits, then multiple cores - and for each say what it changed about speed, size and power consumption.
The physical limit to watch is the size of an atom itself. Once a transistor is only a few atoms across, quantum effects such as tunnelling between neighbouring channels become significant and the device stops behaving classically.
Finish with an explicit judgement about the extent to which these developments have met the needs of society, and do not leave out the drawbacks that remain.

The diagram illustrates the path of a space probe launched from Earth and sent to Neptune.
Explain, using physics principles, why the space probe takes this path instead of travelling directly to Neptune.
Answer in two stages: first why the probe is placed in orbit around the Earth at all, and then what happens when it passes Jupiter. A one-sentence answer will not earn all three marks.
For the launch stage, compare the two options: what does a probe placed in Earth orbit not have to carry or supply that a direct launch to Neptune would?
For the slingshot, set up the geometry. Jupiter is itself moving, and the probe is arranged to pass on the side that lets the two motions add. Then ask what is conserved in Jupiter's frame and what is conserved in the Sun's frame, and how the answers differ.
The space probe is placed in an orbit at an altitude of $188\,\mathrm{km}$ above Earth. Given Earth has a radius of $6380\,\mathrm{km}$, calculate the period of this orbit.
The altitude is measured from the surface of the Earth, so add the Earth's radius to it to get the orbital radius before using any orbital formula.
Use $T = 2\pi\sqrt{r^{3}/GM}$ with every quantity in SI units. The mass of the probe does not appear in the expression, so it is not needed.
Convert your final answer to minutes and check it against the 10 minutes mentioned in part (c): the probe should reach its orbit in somewhat less than one revolution.
It takes 10 minutes for the space probe to reach its orbit around Earth and it remains in orbit for several hours. Sketch a graph on the axes showing the changes in gravitational potential energy for the first 40 minutes.
Gravitational potential energy is defined as zero at infinite distance from the Earth, so it is negative everywhere else. That convention fixes the sign of your entire curve before you draw anything.
Split the 40 minutes into two regimes: the 10 minutes during which the probe is still climbing, and the 30 minutes of circular orbit that follow.
A constant orbital radius means a constant potential energy, so the second part of your graph is a horizontal line, and it must sit below the axis. The rising part should flatten as the probe approaches its final orbit, since it is slowing as it climbs.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / Electromagnetism / Charged Particles, Conductors and Electric and Magnetic Fields / acceleration, perpendicular to the field, of charged particles
questions.text:
Thomson's measurement of the charge/mass ratio of the electron and the circular motion of an electron in a magnetic field are considered in this question.
Thomson's experiment measures the charge/mass ratio of an electron. Use an annotated diagram to show how Thomson's experiment can be performed.
Sketch a long evacuated glass tube with a cathode at one end and an anode containing a slit to accelerate and collimate the electrons into a narrow beam travelling along the axis.
Place charged plates inside or between the magnetic field coils so that the electric and magnetic effects can be compared, and end the tube with a curved screen where the beam lands.
Annotate the sequence of operations as well as the apparatus: first balance the electric and magnetic fields so the beam is undeflected, then use the magnetic field alone to measure the radius of the curved path.
An electron is projected at $90^\circ$ into a magnetic field of $9 \times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{T}$, at a speed of $1 \times 10^{7}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. This causes the electron to undergo uniform circular motion. Calculate the radius of the electron's path.
The electron enters the field at $90^{\circ}$, so the full magnetic force acts: $F = qvB\sin90^{\circ} = qvB$.
That magnetic force is the centripetal force for the circular path, so set $qvB = \dfrac{mv^{2}}{r}$ and simplify to $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$.
Use $m_e = 9.109\times10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}$ and $q = 1.602\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$, and sanity-check that the radius is a visible path, not a microscopic one.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / Advanced Mechanics / Projectile Motion / solve problems, create models and make quantitative predictions by applying the equations of motion relationships for uniformly accelerated and constant rectilinear motion
questions.text:
Cannonballs P and Q are fired so that they leave their barrels from the same height. Cannonball P is fired vertically upwards while cannonball Q is fired at an angle as shown. Both cannonballs take 3 seconds to reach the same maximum height.
Explain how the resulting motion of the cannonballs supports Galileo's analysis of projectile motion.
Compare the vertical motions first: the balls reach the same height in the same time, which tells you what their initial vertical velocities have in common.
Then identify what is different between the two balls — only the horizontal component of velocity — and use that to test the claim that the two motions are independent.
Reference both of Galileo's claims explicitly: the horizontal component is constant, and the resulting path is a parabola.
The position of cannonball P is plotted at the 3rd, 4th and 5th seconds of its flight. The position of cannonball Q is plotted at the 3rd and 4th seconds of its flight.
Plot the positions of the balls at each second for the remainder of their flight. Show calculations.
Take the origin of your vertical displacements at the maximum height, where the vertical velocity is momentarily zero, and time $t$ from the apex rather than from launch.
Use the plotted point one second after the apex to find $a$ from $y = \tfrac{1}{2}at^{2}$, then predict the remaining heights from that same $a$. A fall from rest gives displacements in the ratio $1 : 4 : 9$, not equal steps.
Horizontally there is no acceleration, so measure the spacing of the plotted points for $Q$ and reuse it unchanged for every later second. Work out when the flight ends before plotting any further points.
