questions.current_path: Year 11 / Dynamics / Forces / using Newton’s Laws of Motion, describe static and dynamic interactions between two or more objects and the changes that result from: a contact force; a force mediated by fields
questions.text:
Geophysics. Answer parts (a), (b) and (c) of the question in the Section II Writing Booklet.
(i) Before you draw anything, recall the convention that fixes which way the lines go: field lines leave a north pole and enter a south pole, and the north-seeking end of a compass points along the field. Get this right first or the drawing is wrong everywhere.
(ii) The evidence for sea-floor spreading is written into the rock itself: new basalt forms at the ridge and is magnetised with whatever direction the field happens to have at that moment, so reversals are recorded as stripes.
Then say what the pattern must look like on each side of the ridge - the stripes should mirror one another - and what the ages of the stripes, found by dating the rock, tell you about the rate and direction of spreading.
What happens to white light when it hits a red surface?
(i) White light is a mixture of wavelengths. Ask what happens to each wavelength at a surface that looks red, and where the energy of the absorbed wavelengths goes.
(ii) Remote sensing measures the spectrum of radiation arriving from the ground, so the question is which parts of that spectrum change when the vegetation does, and why different plants or different damage change the spectrum differently.
Then think about why a single survey is not enough: a change can only be detected by comparing surveys of the same ground taken at different times, so resolution and repeat coverage are both needed.
Describe how remote sensing can be used to monitor changes in vegetation.
Compare the use of seismic refraction and seismic reflection techniques in oil and gas exploration.
Both techniques send a wave into the ground and detect it at the surface with geophones, so start by listing what they share before you look for differences.
They differ in which part of the arriving signal they use: one exploits the very first arrivals, the other exploits later echoes from a boundary. Ask which kind of boundary and which depth each one images best.
Then say what an oil or gas reservoir looks like in the resulting data - you are looking for an anomaly against the background rather than a uniform layer, and you should say which way the anomaly appears.
A potential resource was identified near Mount Noble. The diagram shows the plan of a gravitational survey that was carried out, and the table summarises information gained from the survey.
Survey data
With reference to the diagram and the table, explain why data reduction has to be carried out on the raw data from this survey before geologists can assess the potential resource.
Work out from the table what else, apart from the resource, could be setting the gravimeter readings. Look for columns that vary from station to station - altitude is the obvious one, and so is the substrate.
A free-air correction removes the change in $g$ caused simply by being higher or lower off a datum. A Bouguer correction then removes the effect of the extra rock between the station and the datum. You need both here because the stations span a range of altitudes on the flank of a hill.
Remember too that the Bouguer correction assumes a density for the rock above the datum, so the differing densities of sandstone and granite have to be accounted for, and that the nearby topography (Mount Noble) also needs correcting. Only what is left after all of this is a candidate anomaly.
Explain how geophysical methods have benefited mineral exploration programs.
Make the general point first: geophysics looks for a physical signature of the target - a density contrast, a magnetic contrast, a radioactivity contrast, a seismic velocity contrast - and that signature is what makes the deposit findable without digging.
Then make the practical point: once the instrument can be carried on an aircraft, the survey rate rises by orders of magnitude and the cost per unit area falls, so a far larger area can be covered for the same money.
Finish by connecting both to exploration programs: many more targets are screened cheaply before drilling, so fewer dry holes are drilled and the success rate of the program rises. That is the benefit the question is asking you to justify.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Properties of the Nucleus / analyse the spontaneous decay of unstable nuclei, and the properties of the alpha, beta and gamma radiation emitted (ACSPH028, ACSPH030) | Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Properties of the Nucleus / analyse relationships that represent conservation of mass-energy in spontaneous and artificial nuclear transmutations, including alpha decay, beta decay, nuclear fission and nuclear fusion (ACSPH032)
questions.text:
Medical Physics. Answer parts (a), (b) and (c) of the question in the Section II Writing Booklet.
Part (i) is about blood, which is moving. Ask what happens to the frequency of a wave that is reflected from a moving scatterer, and what the size of that change tells you about the motion.
Part (ii) is about the scan shown. Read it as echo strength against time: it is a one-dimensional record. Think about what a computer has to do with many such records before a two-dimensional picture exists.
For part (i) you need three things: the name of the effect, the cause of the frequency change, and the quantity that the change measures. For part (ii) the key idea is that the image is assembled, not that a single scan produces it.
Part (i) is an X-ray tube. One component supplies the electrons, a second stops them, and a third controls where the radiation leaves. Ask which part of the electron's energy becomes the X-rays.
Part (ii) is a comparison, so build a two-column list: what each technique can resolve, and what each one needs from the tissues it images. Lung tissue is the awkward case - ask why.
Remember a CT scan does not use a different radiation source. It changes what is done with the information after the radiation has passed through the patient.
Describe how this transmutation is used to produce a diagnostic image.
Identify the particle in the equation first: ${}^{0}_{+1}\mathrm{e}$ is a positron, and the equation shows carbon-11 decaying by positron emission. Ask what happens when a positron meets an electron inside the body, and what happens to the energy.
Two photons are produced at that event. Momentum has to be conserved, so think about the directions in which the two photons can leave the site, and about how a ring of detectors arranged around the patient could use that to work out where the event happened.
Do not forget the delivery side of the technique: something is administered to the patient before the scan, and it does not spread evenly. Ask why it ends up concentrated in the tissue being investigated.
Describe how properties of protons in nuclei are used in the production of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
Begin with the property of the proton that allows it to interact with a magnetic field at all, and with what happens to that interaction when a very strong, uniform external field is applied.
Then ask about the frequency of the resulting motion, and about what has to be applied to the protons if energy is to be transferred to them efficiently. The keyword here is resonance, and the frequency of the applied pulse has to match the frequency of the protons.
Finally, consider what the protons do immediately after the pulse stops, and how that behaviour is picked up and turned into an image. The full chain field, alignment, pulse, relaxation, detection, image is what the top mark is for.
Assess the impact of medical applications of physics on society.
This part is an assessment, so plan two sides before you write: the benefits of the applications, and the costs they impose. Then finish with a conclusion that actually weighs the two against each other.
Support each point with a specific named application taken from earlier in the question - X-rays, CT, MRI, ultrasound, radiotherapy or endoscopy - rather than making a general claim about medicine. A general claim earns no marks here.
Read the top band of the marking criteria before you start: it asks for positive and negative effects both clearly related to the applications, an informed judgement, and organised use of appropriate terminology.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Origins of the Elements / account for the production of emission and absorption spectra and compare these with a continuous black body spectrum (ACSPH137) | Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Origins of the Elements / investigate the key features of stellar spectra and describe how these are used to classify stars | Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Origins of the Elements / investigate the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram and how it can be used to determine the following about a star: characteristics and evolutionary stage; surface temperature; colour; luminosity
questions.text:
Astrophysics. Answer parts (a), (b) and (c) of the question in the Section II Writing Booklet.
Part (i): the two views are six months apart, which is one whole orbit of the Earth, so the Earth is on the opposite side of the Sun. Ask why a nearby star and a very distant star would not shift by the same amount under that change of viewpoint.
Part (ii): use the distance modulus $m = M + 5\log\left(\dfrac{d}{10}\right)$. Work out the difference in apparent magnitude between the two distances first, then convert that magnitude difference into a ratio of brightnesses. The distance is given in parsec, which is exactly what this equation requires.
A magnitude difference is not itself a brightness: you need the second step. Make sure you express the answer as a factor, and say which distance it is the factor relative to.
Part (i): a filter is a coloured material that transmits strongly in its own band and absorbs most of the rest. Work out which part of the spectrum a class A star emits most of, then what each filter passes and how much.
Part (ii): think about why an astronomer would not trust a brightness measured with an arbitrary filter, and then about what you get if the same star is measured through two agreed standard filters.
Part (ii) has two distinct ideas to earn its three marks: making measurements comparable, and getting a new quantity out of the comparison. Name both.
An astronomer has noticed that a star has become brighter. Explain TWO possible reasons for the change in brightness.
The question asks for TWO explanations, so have two ready and make each one a real explanation rather than just a name. Each is worth about two marks.
The graph of apparent magnitude against time is the clue for one of them. Ask whether the change is a one-off or whether it repeats, and over what time scale - and what physical process in a star would produce each pattern.
For the other, ask what happens to a very massive star when it runs out of fuel, and then ask how long such an event would take compared with a few days. The timescale is what tells the two explanations apart.
A Hertzsprung-Russell (H-R) diagram of a cluster of stars and the spectral lines for stars P and Q are shown.
Explain how this data provides evidence for the evolutionary age of the stars in this cluster.
Two independent pieces of evidence are given - the H-R diagram and the two spectra - and both have to be explained. Treat them as two separate arguments.
On the diagram, the most telling feature for an old cluster is what is missing from the main sequence rather than what is present. Look for the point at which the sequence of plotted stars turns away from the sequence, and relate that to the lifetime of a star of that mass.
For the spectra, compare the widths of the lines in P and Q. Line width is a diagnostic, so ask what a larger width tells you about the density of the gas producing the lines, and therefore about whether that star has expanded.
Evaluate methods of obtaining good quality images of celestial objects using ground-based telescopes.
This is an evaluation, and the marks come from pairing each method with both its benefit and its cost, then reaching a judgement. A list of methods on its own will not score highly here.
Start by listing the problems: the atmosphere distorts and absorbs light, a large mirror deforms under its own weight, and faint objects are difficult to detect. Every method you name should be matched to one of these problems.
Note that more than one corrective optical technique is available and that they operate at very different rates. Ask yourself whether the fast techniques and the slow techniques suffer from the same drawbacks - that comparison is where the judgement in this part comes from.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Quantum Mechanical Nature of the Atom / investigate de Broglie’s matter waves, and the experimental evidence that developed the following formula: (ACSPH140) | Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Quantum Mechanical Nature of the Atom / assess the limitations of the Rutherford and Bohr atomic models | Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Quantum Mechanical Nature of the Atom / relate qualitatively and quantitatively the quantised energy levels of the hydrogen atom and the law of conservation of energy to the line emission spectrum of hydrogen using: (ACSPH136)
questions.text:
From Quanta to Quarks. Answer parts (a), (b) and (c) of the question in the Section II Writing Booklet.
Part (i): the transition is from $n = 3$ down to $n = 1$. Set $n_i$ and $n_f$ carefully, because it is easy to reverse them. Either the Rydberg equation $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\dfrac{1}{n_f^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_i^{2}}\right)$ or the energy-level route $E_n = -\dfrac{13.6}{n^{2}}$ followed by $\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{\Delta E}$ will give the answer.
Part (ii): use de Broglie's hypothesis to picture each allowed electron orbit as a standing wave fitted around the nucleus. Ask what wavelengths those standing waves can have relative to the ground state, and then ask what a photon must match in order to be absorbed.
The key idea in part (ii) is that absorption requires an exact match to a permitted energy difference, and that the ground state is the lowest state so nothing can be absorbed out of it. State both.
Part (i): compare the two forces acting between the nucleons - gravity and the electrostatic repulsion between protons. Ask which is stronger by how many orders of magnitude, and then ask what must therefore be present to hold the nucleus together at all.
Part (ii): the diagram is binding energy per nucleon against atomic number. Find where the curve is steepest and where it reaches its maximum, then use those two features to decide in which direction energy is released when light nuclei combine and when heavy nuclei split.
Part (ii) also needs the link back to mass-energy equivalence: a change in total binding energy is a change in mass, so say how the released energy is accounted for.
With reference to the properties of neutrons, describe the use of the neutron as a probe.
Build the answer property by property. The neutron is uncharged, and its mass is comparable to a proton's. Ask what each of those lets a neutron do that a charged particle cannot.
For each property, name a concrete use: scanning something you cannot see into, making a particular isotope, or studying structure at the atomic scale.
The question says 'with reference to the properties of neutrons', so every use you list has to be tied back to a property in the same sentence, or it will not earn the marks.
Describe the significance of the Manhattan Project to society.
This is a significance question, so you need consequences rather than a description of the project. Ask what was actually produced and what followed from it.
Organise the consequences into two groups: the military and political, such as the bomb, the arms race and the ever-present risk of nuclear attack, and the peaceful, such as nuclear power and radioisotopes for medicine, agriculture and industry. Include at least one clearly negative consequence, such as a reactor accident.
Finish with a statement that weighs the effects, because a significance question is not complete until the overall importance has been judged.
Assess the effectiveness of the Bohr-Rutherford model of the atom in accounting for experimental observations.
An assessment needs a strength and a limitation, each tied to a feature of the model, and then a judgement about whether the limitations were serious enough to require a new model.
Ask first what the classical Rutherford model predicted for a charged electron orbiting a nucleus, and how Bohr's quantised stationary states answered it. That is the model's biggest success, and you should be able to state why the fix worked.
Then test the model against observations beyond the hydrogen spectrum itself: the relative intensities of the spectral lines, what happens to the lines when the atom is placed in an external magnetic field, and the spectra of atoms larger than hydrogen. Each of these is a test the model has to pass or fail.

questions.current_path: Year 11 / Electricity and Magnetism / Electric Circuits / investigate quantitatively the current–voltage relationships in ohmic and non-ohmic resistors to explore the usefulness and limitations of Ohm’s Law using: (ACSPH003, ACSPH041, ACSPH043) | Year 11 / Electricity and Magnetism / Electric Circuits / investigate qualitatively and quantitatively series and parallel circuits to relate the flow of current through the individual components, the potential differences across those components and the rate of energy conversion by the components to the laws of conservation of charge and energy, by deriving the following relationships: (ACSPH038, ACSPH039, ACSPH044)
questions.text:
The Age of Silicon. Answer parts (a), (b) and (c) of the question in the Section II Writing Booklet.
Part (i): work along each branch of the circuit from the inputs, remembering what a NOT gate does, and evaluate both outputs for all four input combinations. The wire crossings shown with a small hump do not connect, which changes which input reaches which gate.
Part (ii): write the definition of an input transducer and the definition of an output transducer first, then ask what a thermistor does to its surroundings and what its surroundings do to it. Using the correct definition in each direction is what earns the top mark.
Part (i): identify each resistor by where it connects rather than by its value. One pair sets the gain of the first amplifier; look for the pair that is connected across the two supply rails and so sets a fixed potential instead.
Part (ii) has two separate calculations and you should do them in order. First the closed-loop gain of the first stage from the ratio of its two resistors. Then the potential that the divider puts on the second stage's inverting input, keeping the $15\,\mathrm{V}$ and $-15\,\mathrm{V}$ rails and the $18\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ and $12\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistors straight.
With those two numbers, the second stage is a comparator. Draw the first output, then mark on it the value at which it crosses the reference potential - that crossing is where the square wave must switch, and it happens twice in every cycle of the input.
Outline similarities and differences between transistors and integrated circuits.
Write down what the two have in common first - how each is manufactured, and what has to be provided to keep either of them safe - and only then move on to the differences.
For the differences, ask how many transistors are contained in the device, how many electrical connections it has, and what sort of circuit each is normally used for.
A similarity has to be true of both, and a difference has to be true of one and not the other. Test each of your statements that way before you write it down.
Justify the use of LEDs over traditional forms of illumination in everyday situations.
The verb here is 'justify', so every advantage must be argued rather than merely listed. Pair each feature of an LED with the loss it causes in the alternative.
Think about where the energy goes in each lamp: how much is converted into light and how much into heat, and what that means for running costs and for the temperature of the fitting.
A fair justification has to acknowledge where LEDs are the worse option as well, such as their purchase cost and their restricted operating conditions. Leaving the counter-argument out costs marks at the top band.
Explain how the development of the silicon chip has influenced the development of electronics.
Chain your reasoning rather than listing benefits: a change in the chip produces a change in the device, which produces a change in what people are able to do. Follow each link explicitly.
The physical changes worth naming are how many components can be printed onto one crystal of silicon, how close together those components can be placed, and how small and how fast each individual element can be made.
Then state what those physical changes let engineers build, and finish by saying where the trend is now running out of room and what has to take over.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / Electromagnetism / The Motor Effect / investigate qualitatively and quantitatively the interaction between a current-carrying conductor and a uniform magnetic field to establish: (ACSPH080, ACSPH081)

The diagram represents a simple DC motor. A current of $1.0\,\mathrm{A}$ flows through a square loop ABCD with 5 cm sides in a magnetic field of $0.01\,\mathrm{T}$.
Show all relevant working.
Determine the force acting on section AB and the force acting on section BC due to the magnetic field, when the loop is in the position shown.
Use $F = BIL\sin\theta$ and work out $\theta$ separately for $AB$ and for $BC$ from the direction of the field between the pole pieces.
One side has its current perpendicular to the field and the other has it parallel to the field, so one feels the full force and the other feels none because $\sin0^{\circ} = 0$.
Take the current direction from the brushes in the diagram, then apply $I\mathbf{L}\times\mathbf{B}$ or the right-hand rule to fix the direction of the non-zero force.
How is the direction of the torque maintained as the loop rotates $360^\circ$ from the position shown?
Track the loop through a half turn: the sides that experience the driving force change places, so on its own the torque would reverse.

Decide what each element of the model stands for: occupied states in the valence band, free states in the conduction band, the applied voltage, and the energy that promotes electrons between the two.
The promotion step needs a trigger you can switch on and off, so that conduction is shown to begin only once energy is supplied.
Include both kinds of charge carrier, because electrons and holes move in opposite directions and both contribute to the measured current.

questions.text:
A part of a cathode ray oscilloscope was represented on a website as shown. Electrons leave the cathode and are accelerated towards the anode.
Show all relevant working.
Explain why the representation of the path of the electron between the deflection plates is inaccurate.
The field between the plates is uniform, so the electron feels a force for the whole of the distance between the plates. It therefore cannot stay on a straight path and then bend suddenly.
An electron is negatively charged, so decide which plate repels it and which attracts it, and then check the direction of the bend drawn on the website against that.
Two separate inaccuracies earn the marks, and each needs its reason. Identify both before you start writing, and sketch the correct path as well if you can.
Calculate the force on an electron due to the electric field between the cathode and the anode.
The field strength follows $E = \frac{V}{d}$, but use the cathode-anode gap given on the diagram, not the separation of the deflection plates.
Then use $F = qE$ with the magnitude of the electron's charge, $1.6\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$, remembering that the electron's negative sign affects the direction but not the size of the force.
Calculate the velocity of an electron as it reaches the anode.
The electron starts from rest at the cathode, so $u = 0$ in $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2as$, and $s$ is the $2\,\mathrm{cm}$ cathode-anode gap from the diagram.
The acceleration is $a = \frac{F}{m}$ using the force from the previous part and the mass of an electron, $9.1\times10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}$. Take the square root only at the end, not before.
The energy relation $qV = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$ reaches the same speed and is a useful check on your arithmetic.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / Advanced Mechanics / Motion in Gravitational Fields / derive quantitatively and apply the concepts of gravitational force and gravitational potential energy in radial gravitational fields to a variety of situations, including but not limited to: the concept of escape velocity
questions.text:
Consider the following two models used to calculate the work done when a 300 kg satellite is taken from Earth's surface to an altitude of 200 km. You may assume that the calculations are correct.
Show all relevant working.
What assumptions are made about Earth's gravitational field in models X and Y that lead to the different results shown?
Model X uses $W = Fs = mgh$ with a single value of $g$. Ask what that assumes about the field over the $200\,\mathrm{km}$ of the climb.
Model Y uses $E_{p} = -\frac{GMm}{r}$ evaluated at two different radii. Ask what that assumes about the field instead.
Name the assumption for each model separately, so one mark is earned for each. Do not judge which is better here; part (b) deals with that.
Why do models X and Y produce results that, although different, are close in value?
Compare the altitude with the radius of the Earth, not with the distance the satellite travels or the work done.
A field that varies as $1/r^{2}$ changes very little over a distance that is a small fraction of $r$, so a model that treats the field as constant is a good approximation in that case.
Calculate the orbital velocity of the satellite in a circular orbit at the altitude of 200 km.
Equate the gravitational force to the centripetal force for a circular orbit: $\frac{GMm}{r^{2}} = \frac{mv^{2}}{r}$.
Cancel $m$ and rearrange for $v$. Use the orbital radius given in Model Y, not the altitude, and keep the units consistent so the answer comes out in $\mathrm{m/s}$.
Sanity check: the result should be close to the $7.9\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ of a low Earth orbit, since the altitude here is only $200\,\mathrm{km}$.

questions.current_path: Year 11 / Electricity and Magnetism / Magnetism / use magnetic field lines to model qualitatively the direction and strength of magnetic fields produced by magnets, current-carrying wires and solenoids and relate these fields to their effect on magnetic materials that are placed within them (ACSPH083)
questions.text:
— Geophysics. Answer parts (a), (b) and (c) on pages 2–4 of the Section II Writing Booklet, then parts (d) and (e) on pages 6–8. Start each part of the question on a new page.
The table shows measurements taken by a student to determine the density of two types of rocks.
Part (i): the final volume of water is not the quantity you need. What you need is the volume of the rock itself, which is the difference between the two water volumes, and you must be sure the units match the units given for the mass before you substitute.
Part (ii): the question asks for properties other than density, and for a description of each. Think about how a geophysicist measures how a rock responds to an applied force, and about how a rock's response to a magnetic field depends on what minerals it contains.
In part (ii) a bare name earns only one mark. Describe what the property is and how it is measured, and you will earn the higher marks.
Earth's magnetic field is not constant over geological time.
Part (i): the word 'long-term' fixes the timescale at millions of years, so think about what the record shows about the positions of the magnetic poles over that period, and about what rock or sediment can preserve that record.
Part (ii): a magnetic field on Earth has to be produced by moving charge, so ask what in the interior is moving and how the pattern of that motion could change with time. There is more than one mechanism.
For part (ii), three marks need three causes or one developed cause plus a second. Look at the liquid outer core and at how it rotates relative to the crust.
One method of studying Earth uses two satellites in the same orbit as shown.
Microwave signals transmitted between the satellites are used to accurately measure changes in their separation.
Explain what can be deduced about Earth by using these satellites.
The two satellites are in the same orbit at the same altitude, so as long as the field were uniform they would keep a fixed separation. Ask what would happen to that separation if one of them passed over denser material than the other.
The measurement is a timing measurement, so changes in separation are known very precisely. Ask what a long, accurate record of those changes, accumulated as Earth rotates underneath the orbit, would allow you to map.
Make sure the answer states what is deduced and then links it to something about Earth's interior. Two links are needed for the top mark, and one of them has to be the link to the satellites' motion.
Use the following information about earthquake waves to answer parts (i) and (ii).
Part (i): restrict your attention to the depth range 3500 km to 4500 km and look only at the two curves over that interval. Ask whether their gradients there are the same or different, and ignore the sharp feature at about 2900 km, which lies outside the range.
Part (ii): the ray-path diagram shows three separate features of the P-wave paths - a curved path in the mantle, a partial reflection at a boundary, and a curved path in the outer core. Match each one to a change in the medium at that depth.
For each feature, name the property of the medium that changes and then say how the wave behaves because of it. Where the change is gradual the wave bends smoothly; where it is abrupt the wave splits into a reflected and a transmitted part.
Assess the impact of applications of remote sensing on society. Support your answer using THREE examples.
The question names the number of examples: three. Plan three specific, named applications before you write, so that the judgement is supported rather than merely asserted.
For each example state what the remote-sensing data actually are - the instrument and the waveband being used - and only then the effect on society. Vague references to 'satellites' do not earn the marks.
A judgement needs both a benefit and a cost or limitation somewhere in the answer, and the whole response has to stay tied to the question's own words, 'impact' and 'assess'.

questions.current_path: Year 11 / Waves and Thermodynamics / Sound Waves / investigate and model the behaviour of standing waves on strings and/or in pipes to relate quantitatively the fundamental and harmonic frequencies of the waves that are produced to the physical characteristics (eg length, mass, tension, wave velocity) of the medium (ACSPH072)
questions.text:
— Medical Physics. Answer parts (a), (b) and (c) on pages 2–4 of the Section II Writing Booklet, then parts (d) and (e) on pages 6–8. Start each part of the question on a new page.
Ultrasound can be used to image the soft tissues of the body.
Part (i): what determines how strongly a wave is reflected at a boundary? Introduce the acoustic impedance $Z = \rho v$ and ask what has to be different between two tissues for a reflection to occur at all.
Part (ii) is two steps. First calculate the bone's impedance from the table, in which $\rho$ and $v$ are given but $Z$ is not. Then use the muscle value already supplied in the table in the expression for the reflected fraction of the intensity.
Keep the $10^{6}$ factor consistent between the two impedances - either both in units of $10^{6}\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$ or neither. Squaring the ratio at the end is easy to forget, and the final answer must be a fraction between 0 and 1.
After a patient had been treated for lung cancer, no tumours were detected in an X-ray image of the lungs.
The doctor has now recommended that the patient have a whole-body PET scan.
Part (i): write down, for each technique, the radiation used, how that radiation is produced, and where the source sits relative to the patient. The differences fall straight out of that list, and you need two of them.
Part (ii): begin from the clinical fact given in the stem - a negative X-ray does not rule out the cancer. Then give a limitation of X-rays, an advantage of PET, and one further reason a whole-body scan is specified rather than a scan of the chest alone.
For part (ii) the three marks are for the three separate pieces of justification, not for elaborating one of them at length.
Describe how the structure of an endoscope enables it to be used to detect the presence of a tumour in the stomach wall and to collect a tissue sample for analysis.
The question asks how the structure enables two different jobs: imaging the wall and taking a sample. Build a list of the parts first, then match each part to the job it does.
For the imaging job, think about what the light has to do on the way in and on the way out, and about why the two bundles of fibres have to be different from one another.
For the sampling job, think about what else has to travel down the tube besides light, and about how the operator positions and operates it from outside the patient.
A magnetic resonance image (MRI) scan uses the magnetic properties of hydrogen nuclei in the body.
Part (i): two tissues that look identical to the eye must still produce different data if they are to be distinguished. Ask what the machine actually measures about each nucleus, and what property of grey and white matter sets that measurement.
Part (ii): resonance means efficient energy transfer between two things that share a natural frequency. Work out the frequency at which the protons precess in the strong field, then ask what happens when a pulse of exactly that frequency is applied to them.
Finish by following the signal. The pulse is short, so something must change once it stops, and that change is what the receiver detects. Each of those steps is a separate mark.
Assess the impact of advances in understanding of waves on the development of imaging technologies. Support your answer using THREE examples.
Three examples are required, and the earlier parts of this question hand you exactly three: ultrasound, X-ray imaging and the endoscope. Use all three rather than substituting others.
For each one, name the specific wave property or behaviour the technique depends on - reflection and refraction at a tissue boundary, differential absorption by density, and total internal reflection in an optical fibre.
Then make the judgement the verb 'assess' demands: say whether advances in understanding waves have been the limiting factor in developing these technologies, and justify that claim from the three examples.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Origins of the Elements / account for the production of emission and absorption spectra and compare these with a continuous black body spectrum (ACSPH137) | Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Origins of the Elements / investigate the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram and how it can be used to determine the following about a star: characteristics and evolutionary stage; surface temperature; colour; luminosity
questions.text:
— Astrophysics. Answer parts (a), (b) and (c) on pages 2–4 of the Section II Writing Booklet, then parts (d) and (e) on pages 6–8. Start each part of the question on a new page.
The apparent brightness of a star depends on its absolute magnitude and its distance from Earth.
Part (i): rearrange the distance-modulus equation so that the apparent magnitude is the unknown, then substitute the absolute magnitude and the distance in parsec. Track the sign of the $5\log$ term as you go, and check that the answer is plausible for a bright star.
Part (ii): two methods are needed and each must be outlined, not just named. One measures an angle directly; the other infers the distance from the brightness only after the intrinsic luminosity has been obtained from the spectrum. State the extra step the second method needs.
If you are unsure which quantity the modulus relates, remember the defining idea: apparent magnitude measures the brightness received at Earth, absolute magnitude the luminosity the star actually emits.
The light curves of two binary systems are shown.
Part (i): these dips are eclipses, and an eclipse is a geometric accident. Ask what has to be true about the orientation of the orbital plane relative to our line of sight, and how common that is among binary systems.
Part (ii): compare the two curves feature by feature before interpreting anything. Look at the depth of each dip within a curve, whether the dips are equal to each other, and whether the bottom of a dip is flat or pointed.
Then ask, for each feature, what it tells you about the two stars - specifically their radii and their temperatures. A flat-bottomed dip means one star is completely hidden for a time; a pointed dip means the eclipse is momentary.
Explain how emission spectra and absorption spectra are produced by specific types of celestial objects.
Handle the two spectra separately rather than trying to describe them in one pass. For an emission spectrum, ask what has to happen to an electron for it to emit a photon of a particular wavelength.
For an absorption spectrum, ask what has to be happening to light as it passes through a cooler layer, and which electrons take up the energy as it passes.
The question asks for the spectra to be explained 'by specific types of celestial object', so name the kind of object as well as the process for each - hot gas for one, and a dense source seen through a cooler outer layer for the other.
The position of the Sun, star W and star Z are shown on the H-R diagram.
The curves A and B show intensity versus frequency for star W and the Sun, measured from the same distance.
Part (i): W and the Sun are both marked on the H-R diagram, so compare their positions. Spectral class tells you which is hotter, and the two curves then tell you which temperature matches which curve. Look at both the height of a curve and where its peak lies.
Part (ii): for each star read three things off the H-R diagram - its spectral type, its position relative to the main sequence, and its luminosity compared with the Sun's. Then ask what each of those implies about the size of the star and about the fusion reaction running inside it.
Watch for the combination that the question is really testing in (ii): a star that is cooler than another yet equally luminous can only be much larger, because the radiated power depends on area as well as on temperature.
Assess the impact of the development of space-based telescopes on the understanding of celestial objects.
The verb is 'assess', so relate a feature of the instrument to a gain in understanding, then weigh it against the limitations. Build the list feature by feature.
The features to look for are what the atmosphere does to light both before and after it reaches the mirror, and what can be done about combining two telescopes whose mirrors are far apart.
Do not forget the counter-argument - cost, size, and the impossibility of servicing or upgrading a telescope in orbit - and finish with an overall judgement rather than a list of benefits.

questions.text:
— From Quanta to Quarks. Answer parts (a), (b) and (c) on pages 2–4 of the Section II Writing Booklet, then parts (d) and (e) on pages 6–8. Start each part of the question on a new page.
Polonium-218 is an unstable isotope that can decay to either lead-214 by alpha decay, or astatine-218 by beta decay.
How could a Wilson Cloud Chamber, or similar device, be used to distinguish between alpha decay and beta decay?
A cloud chamber does not measure energy; it makes the track itself visible. Ask what the track looks like for each type of particle.
Alpha particles are far more strongly ionising but much less penetrating than beta particles, so the two leave tracks of different length and thickness in the same vapour.
For the calculation, write the balanced decay equation and remember that the mass defect is the mass of the starting nucleus minus the sum of the masses of the products. The masses given are nuclear masses, so no electron masses are involved.
Polonium-218 is an unstable isotope that can decay to either lead-214 by alpha decay, or astatine-218 by beta decay.
The mass of a polonium-218 nucleus is 218.00897 u, the mass of a lead-214 nucleus is 213.99981 u, and the mass of an alpha particle is 4.00260 u. Calculate the energy released by this alpha decay.
An instrument uses a beam of neutrons with a wavelength of 0.2 nm to study the structure of new materials.
Calculate the speed of the neutrons.
Start from the de Broglie relationship rather than from kinetic energy: the wavelength is given, so find the momentum from $\lambda = h/p$ and then the speed.
The obvious comparison for the penetration argument is with the charged particles in the atom, and for the resolution argument it is with the wavelength of visible light.
Do not stop after the number. The marks for the second half of this part come from naming two features of the neutron beam and saying why each one matters for a scattering experiment.
An instrument uses a beam of neutrons with a wavelength of 0.2 nm to study the structure of new materials.
Explain why this beam of neutrons is useful in determining the structure of materials.
Explain why the spectroscope was important in the development of the Bohr model of the atom.
Start by naming exactly what was missing from the Rutherford model: it could not say how the electrons were arranged, nor why they did not radiate energy as they orbited.
Then state what new evidence the spectroscope produced. Not 'more information', but the specific feature of the spectra that the model was then required to account for.
Finish by naming the change of thinking that this evidence forced: discrete lines can only be explained if the available electron energies are not continuous.
In 1927, Davisson and Germer reported the results of an experiment in which they fired electrons at a crystal of nickel and observed how the electrons were scattered.
The conclusion has to be justified by the result, so state the observation first, an interference or diffraction pattern among the scattered electrons, and then the conclusion that this observation forces.
For the significance, ask which specific weakness of the Rutherford-Bohr model the wave picture removes. The model had fixed orbits but could not explain why only those orbits were allowed.
de Broglie's idea is the link: if the electron is a wave standing in its orbit, then only orbits in which a whole number of wavelengths fits are possible.
Assess the impact of THREE advances in knowledge about particles and forces on the understanding of the atomic nucleus.
This is an assessment question: three advances, each paired with a consequence. Collect the advances first, then decide which of them changed our picture of the nucleus most.
The marks come from the pairing, not from naming the advance. A named advance with no consequence scores far less than the same advance followed by a clear 'this let scientists work out...' or 'this explained...' sentence.
Check that each of your three advances answers 'so what changed about the nucleus?'. A line that only describes the particle needs a second sentence to earn the mark.

The diagram shows a logic circuit with two inputs.
Construct a truth table for this logic circuit.
Write the logic in words before building the table. Work out what the NAND gate actually receives, and what the bubble on its output then does to that result.
A bubble on the output of a NAND gate inverts the result, and a NOT gate on an input inverts that input, so the net effect of the two inversions must be accounted for with De Morgan's theorem.
For the second sub-part, remember that logic levels are set by a voltage threshold and not by a fixed value, so each of the three measured voltages must be classified as high or low before the reading can be compared with the table.
The diagram shows a logic circuit with two inputs.

The diagram shows a circuit incorporating a positive temperature coefficient thermistor.
Calculate the range of possible voltages across the diode when the thermistor has a resistance of 10 kOhm.
The diode is connected between the top rail and the junction of the two resistors, so it is in parallel with the thermistor. That decides which of the two components the potential-divider rule is applied to.
The question asks for a range, so evaluate the divider at both extreme settings of the variable resistor, $1\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ and $20\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$, not just at one of them.

Explain an application for this circuit.
Explain how amplifiers and feedback loops are used in control systems. Support your answer with a diagram.
Define the feedback loop first, saying precisely what travels from the output back to the input, and then say what the amplifier does with the signal that arrives at the summing point.
Negative feedback is the common case: identify what is being subtracted at the summing junction, and what benefit reducing the error gives.
The question asks for a diagram, so a closed loop containing a summing junction, an amplifier, an output and a feedback path must be drawn as well as described.
Integrated circuits are used in all modern electronic devices.
Explain ONE advantage of integrated circuits compared to circuits constructed from individual components.
For the advantage, compare the two approaches on how many components have to be made, connected and assembled to perform even a simple function, not just on physical size.
For the second sub-part, ask what physically sets a floor on the size of a component. There is a limit to how small a piece of matter that performs a reliable switching function can be.
Two further brakes on the doubling are worth naming: the heat generated as more devices are packed onto the same area, and the growing number of connections that must be routed between them.

The question demands one input transducer and one output transducer, so choose them deliberately: an input transducer converts a physical quantity into an electrical signal, an output transducer does the reverse.
Each transducer must be tied to an effect on society and not just to an application. The mark is only earned once the consequence for people has been stated.

Answer the following questions about ultrasound.
Describe the piezoelectric effect and its application in ultrasound imaging.
The piezoelectric effect runs in both directions: a crystal that deforms when a potential difference is applied can also generate a potential difference when it is deformed. Both halves are needed for the mark.
For the second sub-part, write the intensity reflection expression in terms of the two impedances, then evaluate it once for each boundary. One of the boundaries has identical impedances, and that case has to be recognised before any arithmetic is attempted.
Whatever is not reflected is what enters the next medium, so quote both the reflected and the transmitted percentages for the boundary where there is a mismatch.
Answer the following questions about ultrasound.
An ultrasound pulse leaves the transducer and passes from the gel through soft tissue and bone as shown. A table of acoustic impedances is provided. Describe what happens to the intensity of the ultrasound pulse at each boundary. Use calculations to support your answer.
Contrast the use of Doppler ultrasound imaging with the use of computed axial tomography (CAT) imaging. In your answer, include an example of how each is used.
The command word is 'contrast', so the two techniques must be set against each other on the same criteria: what each one images, and what that lets a doctor do.
An example for each technology is required, and a specific use such as the motion of blood near a valve, or the detection of an abdominal tumour, earns the mark. 'It is used in hospitals' does not.
Keep the distinction sharp: one technique shows how the body is working, the other shows what it is shaped like.
Describe how positron emission tomography (PET) scanning is used in diagnosis. In your answer, refer to the interaction of positrons and electrons.
Follow the sequence in order: what is injected, what it emits, what happens to the emitted particles, what radiation results, and how that radiation is turned into an image.
The question specifically asks about the interaction of positrons and electrons, so name that interaction explicitly and state what it produces.
Then explain why the answer is diagnostically useful: the radiopharmaceutical can be chosen to concentrate in the tissue of interest, so the image is a map of function as well as of position.
Explain how principles of physics are applied in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
Start from the physical property of the nucleus that MRI exploits, the spin of the hydrogen nucleus, and state what the strong external field does to the spin directions.
'Resonance' means the applied radiation must match the precession frequency exactly, so say what happens to the nuclei when it does.
Other acceptable physics for later marks: the changing magnetic flux in the detecting coils inducing an emf by electromagnetic induction, and the field coil relying on superconductivity.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Origins of the Elements / investigate the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram and how it can be used to determine the following about a star: characteristics and evolutionary stage; surface temperature; colour; luminosity
questions.text:
- Astrophysics (25 marks)
Answer the following questions about optical telescopes.
Distinguish between the terms resolution and sensitivity as applied to optical telescopes.
Write one plain sentence for resolution and one for sensitivity, making sure that neither definition is just a rewording of the other.
Ground-based telescopes are limited by atmospheric distortion, so every improvement either compensates for the atmosphere or avoids using it at all.
Two named techniques carry the marks: active or adaptive optics, which corrects the mirror for atmospheric distortion, and interferometry, which combines light from separate collectors.
Answer the following questions about optical telescopes.
Outline ways of improving the resolution of ground-based telescopes.
Answer the following questions about determining stellar distances.
Explain how trigonometric parallax is used to determine the distance to a star.
Parallax is an apparent change of position, so the first sub-part is about how the observer's own motion, through the Earth's rotation or its orbit, supplies a measurable baseline against distant background stars.
Use the small-angle relationship to get the distance: with the parallax angle in arc seconds, the distance comes out in parsecs as the reciprocal of the angle.
For the second step, the distance modulus is $M = m - 5\log_{10}(d/10)$. Keep the logarithm in base 10 and put the distance in parsecs.
Answer the following questions about determining stellar distances.
Determine the absolute magnitude of a star which has an apparent magnitude of 4.2 and a parallax of 0.055 arc seconds.
Describe how the spectrum of a star can be used to determine its chemical composition and surface temperature.
Two different pieces of information come out of one spectrum, so treat the identification of composition and the measurement of temperature as separate steps.
For composition, the key word is absorption: the dark lines are produced by the atoms in the star's atmosphere absorbing particular frequencies of the light passing through them.
For temperature, ask which species the lines belong to: molecules, neutral atoms and ionised atoms each appear only within particular temperature ranges.
Explain how the study of different types of variable stars has increased our understanding of celestial objects.
Separate intrinsic variation, where the star itself is pulsing, from extrinsic variation, where something else in the system is changing the brightness seen from Earth.
For each type, name the measurable quantity the light curve gives and the property of the object that can then be deduced from it.
The strongest link to make is that a known standard candle lets everything near it be measured, so say how a Cepheid distance is used to find the properties of other objects.
Describe how the distribution of stars on a Hertzsprung-Russell diagram relates to the processes that occur during their evolution.
Identify the three populated regions of the diagram, the main sequence, red giants and white dwarfs, and the energy source that sustains each.
Then account for the empty space: a star passes through the transition between two processes very quickly compared with the time it spends in each group.
A sketch of the diagram with the regions labelled, together with the process for each, will pick up more marks than the processes alone.

questions.text:
- From Quanta to Quarks (25 marks)
Answer the following questions about nucleons.
Identify the TWO types of nucleon and state ONE difference between them.
Start by listing the two nucleons and picking a single clean difference between them; charge is the difference the syllabus uses.
For the second sub-part, name both forces: one acts between the protons and tends to push them apart, the other acts between all the nucleons and holds the nucleus together.
The strong force is not attractive at all separations. Its range, and the separation at which it acts most strongly, are what make the helium nucleus stable, so mention where that peak occurs.
Answer the following questions about nucleons.
Explain the stability of He-4 nuclei in terms of TWO forces.
Answer the following questions about atomic theory and the hydrogen spectrum.
Bohr's model reproduces the positions of the hydrogen lines but not everything about them, so look at the intensities of the lines and at the fine structure that more sensitive instruments reveal.
For the calculation, remember that the Rydberg formula involves the difference of two reciprocals of squares, and that the energy emitted is $hcR\left(\frac{1}{n_f^{2}} - \frac{1}{n_i^{2}}\right)$.
Set $n_f = 2$, substitute the given energy, and solve for $n_i$. The answer must come out as a whole number for the marks to be earned.
Describe how contributions to atomic theory made by Pauli and Heisenberg changed Bohr's model of the atom.
Take each scientist in turn: state the principle, then state the specific change it forced on Bohr's picture of the electron.
For Pauli, the change concerns how many electrons a shell can hold. For Heisenberg, it concerns how precisely the electron's position and its momentum can be known at the same time.
Because the question says the contributions changed Bohr's model, a change must be stated for each; naming the principle alone earns only the partial marks.
Explain how evidence from experiments involving particle accelerators and detectors has provided support for the standard model of matter.
Think about what an accelerator does to the particles involved, and about the role of a detector in turning a collision into a list of particle types and measured properties.
The question asks for evidence that supports the standard model, so the argument has to run both ways: evidence that led to the model, and evidence the model then predicted.
Each paragraph should make a measurable claim, such as a particle's charge, mass or momentum, rather than a general statement about 'supporting' the model.
How did Fermi's work in nuclear physics lead to applications that have affected society?
The question asks how Fermi's work led to applications, so the first step is what he established experimentally, namely the conditions for a controlled, self-sustaining chain reaction.
Then name the applications that depend on a controlled reaction, such as the generation of electricity and the production of radioisotopes, and give an effect on society for each.
Because this is a 'how did ... lead to' question, make the causal chain explicit in every sentence: the work, then the capability, then the application, then the effect.

Answer the following questions about analogue and digital signals and about electric and electronic circuits.
Use sketches to show how analogue and digital voltage outputs are different.
For the first sub-part, sketch voltage against time for both signals: one trace must take every value between its extremes, the other only two.
For the second, be concrete about voltage, current, size and power, and remember that an advantage has to be a benefit and not merely a description.
A good structure is: one advantage of an electronic circuit, one advantage of an electric circuit, and a clause on what each is therefore suited to.
Answer the following questions about analogue and digital signals and about electric and electronic circuits.
Describe ONE advantage of electronic circuits and ONE advantage of electric circuits.
Answer the following questions about operational amplifiers.
Build a table with one row for each property, voltage gain, input impedance, output resistance and bandwidth, and fill in the ideal value, the real value and the comparison.
For the circuit, identify which input terminal carries the signal: an inverting amplifier sends the input through a resistor to the inverting terminal, with the non-inverting terminal grounded.
The feedback resistor goes from the output back to the inverting terminal. Find the gain from the ratio of the output amplitude to the input amplitude on the two graphs, then use that gain to size the feedback resistor against the given $2.2\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$.
The logic circuit shown was constructed using a number of components.
The diagram shows acceptable input voltages for these components.
A low voltage output is required from the circuit. Determine possible input voltages for $A$, $B$ and $C$. Support your answer using a truth table.
Trace the circuit backwards from the output. The OR gate's output is low only when both of its inputs are low, and each of those inputs comes from a NOT gate.
A NOT gate is low exactly when its input is high, so work out the input conditions for each NOT gate's output to be low, remembering that the AND gate's inputs are $B$ and the output of the NOT gate on $C$.
Then complete the truth table for all eight input combinations before reading off the row that gives a low output, and remember that low and high are voltage ranges and not single values.
Explain the advantages of using integrated circuits instead of individual transistors in electronic devices.
Compare the two technologies on the same three measures: physical size, reliability, and cost or power consumption.
The strongest single argument is about how many individual components have to be made, connected and assembled to perform even a simple function.
Remember the question asks for advantages, so each point must end with 'therefore the integrated circuit version is better because...'.
A circuit is required to automatically switch on a 240 V fan when the temperature exceeds 30 degrees C. The circuit shown was designed by a student but does not operate as intended.
The graph shows the characteristic curve of the thermistor in the circuit.
Explain THREE changes that need to be made for this circuit to operate correctly.
The op amp has no negative feedback here, so it acts as a comparator: it switches when its input voltage reaches the reference set by $R_2$ and $R_3$.
Calculate that reference voltage and then the input voltage the divider actually reaches at $30^{\circ}\,\mathrm{C}$. If the two can never be equal, no component value is doing its job, and one of them must be wrong.
Then check the direction: with a PTC thermistor, does the input voltage rise or fall as the temperature rises, and is that the behaviour the fan needs?

Calculate the maximum magnetic field strength within the stationary loop during the 12-second interval.
Flux and field are related by $\Phi = BA\cos\theta$, and while the loop is stationary with the field perpendicular to its plane, $\cos\theta = 1$.
The field is largest when the flux is largest, so read the peak of the flux graph. The time axis is not needed.
Convert the $0.60\,\mathrm{m}$ diameter to a radius before you compute the area of the loop.

questions.text:
A spring is used to construct a device to launch a projectile. The force ($F$) required to compress the spring is measured as a function of the displacement ($x$) by which the spring is compressed.
The potential energy stored in the compressed spring can be calculated from $E_p = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^{2}$, where $k$ is the gradient of the force–displacement graph shown.
A projectile of mass $0.04\,\mathrm{kg}$ is launched using this device with the spring compressed by $0.08\,\mathrm{m}$. Calculate the launch velocity.
Take $k$ from the gradient of the force-displacement graph: rise over run, in $\mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$. Use the best-fit line through the points rather than a single pair.
Assume no energy is lost between the spring and the projectile, so $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^{2}$. Keep the mass on the right-hand side when you divide through; cancelling the halves does not cancel the mass.
Alternatively, the work done in compressing the spring is the area under the force-displacement graph, and that must equal the gain in kinetic energy of the projectile.
Calculate the range of a projectile launched by this device from ground level at an angle of $60^\circ$ to the horizontal with a velocity of $10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
At the highest point the vertical component of the launch velocity is zero, so the time to reach the top follows from $v = u + at$, and the time of flight is twice that.
Range is the horizontal component multiplied by the time of flight, so resolve the $10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ first rather than using the launch speed itself.

For (b)(ii) think about what happens to penetration and to resolution when the frequency changes. Higher frequency means shorter wavelength, which means both greater detail and less penetration, and the two scan types need one of each.
Explain how the application of a radio frequency wave changes the behaviour of nuclei with net spin in a strong, external magnetic field.

Movement of pointer: Towards left. Reason: Y behaves as a motor with the current flowing through it from right to left.
Movement of pointer: Towards left. Reason: For every force, there is an equal and opposite force.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / Advanced Mechanics / Motion in Gravitational Fields / determine the force of gravity between two objects
questions.text:
Compare the force of gravity exerted on the moon by Earth with the force of gravity exerted on Earth by the moon.
Compare the force of gravity exerted on the moon by Earth with the force of gravity exerted on Earth by the moon.
These two forces are the action and reaction of one single interaction, so ask how the third law relates their magnitudes.
Both marks are needed for a complete comparison: how big the forces are relative to each other, and which way each one acts.
The acceleration due to gravity on the moon is $1.6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ and on Earth it is $9.8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Quantitatively compare the mass and weight of a $70\,\mathrm{kg}$ person on the moon and on Earth.
Mass is a measure of the amount of matter, so it cannot be changed by gravity. Weight, however, is $W = mg$ and does depend on the field strength.
Use $1.6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ for the moon and $9.8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ for Earth, and report both weights in newtons so they can be compared quantitatively rather than just described.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / Electromagnetism / Electromagnetic Induction / the generation of an electromotive force (emf) and evidence for Lenz’s Law produced by the relative movement between a magnet, straight conductors, metal plates and solenoids
questions.text:
Electromagnetic induction
A drill spins a magnet above a non-magnetic metal disc which is free to rotate.
Explain the effect of the rotating magnet on the disc.
The disc is a conductor but not a magnet, so the only coupling between it and the magnet is through a changing magnetic flux.
Ask what current is induced in the disc as the magnet turns, then use Lenz's law to decide whether the magnetic field those currents produce helps the magnet's rotation or opposes it.
The diagram shows a magnet attached to an electric drill so that it can be rotated between two coils connected to a voltmeter.
The drill starts from rest and gradually speeds up, reaching its full speed after three revolutions.
Sketch a graph showing the induced emf across the coils during the time that it takes the magnet to reach its full speed.
Plot the induced emf against time, not against the number of revolutions, and remember that the magnet is stationary at the start.
Two separate features of the emf change as the drill speeds up: how large it is, which is set by the rate of change of flux, and how often it reverses sign, which is set by the rotation rate. Both must appear in the sketch, and both must level off once full speed is reached.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / Electromagnetism / Charged Particles, Conductors and Electric and Magnetic Fields / model qualitatively and quantitatively the trajectories of charged particles in electric fields and compare them with the trajectories of projectiles in a gravitational field
questions.text:
The diagram shows a cathode ray tube in a television.
Outline energy changes associated with the electrons passing through the gun, and when they strike the screen.
There are only two places to consider: inside the electron gun, and where the electrons land on the screen.
In the gun the electrons are pushed through a potential difference, so their kinetic energy increases. At the screen their kinetic energy is released. Give both transformations in words rather than naming components.
Explain the role of the components labelled Y in forming an image on the screen.
Look at how the components labelled Y are drawn: coils around the neck of the tube, so the field they produce where the beam passes is magnetic rather than electric.
A moving electron in a magnetic field experiences a force of magnitude $qvB$, so changing the current in the coils changes the field strength and therefore both the size and the direction of the deflection.

questions.current_path: Year 11 / Electricity and Magnetism / Electric Circuits / investigate quantitatively the application of the law of conservation of energy to the heating effects of electric currents, including the application of and variations of this involving Ohm’s Law (ACSPH043)
questions.text:
High-voltage transmission
Outline TWO features of high-voltage transmission lines that contribute to the safe transmission of electricity.
The question asks for features of the transmission line that make it safe. Think about what can damage or energise a high-voltage conductor, and what each piece of hardware exists to prevent.
Two marks means two features, each with a stated purpose. An unsupported list of parts earns only the first mark.
Three parallel wires X, Y and Z all carry electric currents. A force of attraction is produced between Y and Z. There is zero net force on Y.
What is the magnitude and direction of the current in X?
The force between two parallel wires varies as $\dfrac{kI_1I_2}{d}$. Since the net force on Y is zero, the attraction to Z must be cancelled by a force from X, so set the two equal with the current in X as the unknown.
Fix the direction before the arithmetic: Y and Z attract, so they carry current the same way, and a repulsive force from X means the current in X must run the other way. Then get the magnitude from the balance.

questions.current_path: Year 11 / Electricity and Magnetism / Electric Circuits / investigate quantitatively the application of the law of conservation of energy to the heating effects of electric currents, including the application of and variations of this involving Ohm’s Law (ACSPH043)
questions.text:
Superconductors
State ONE benefit and ONE limitation of the use of superconductors in the transmission of electricity through power grids.
Decide whether energy lost as heat in the transmission line counts as a benefit or a limitation, then find the cost that has to be paid to reduce that loss to zero.
One mark each: a benefit that follows from the transmission itself, and a limitation that comes from maintaining the system.
Contrast features of electrical conduction in a pure metal at room temperature with electrical conduction in a pure metallic superconductor below its critical temperature.
A contrast answer needs matching pairs of statements, one from each material. Start with how the conduction electrons move.
Then explain where the resistance in a room-temperature metal comes from, thinking about the ions in the lattice and how they are moving, and why that scattering does not occur for paired electrons in a superconductor.
Four marks means two clear contrasts, each stated for both materials.

questions.text:
Investigating projectile motion with a camera and ruler
The diagram shows a camera and a ruler set up to obtain data about a projectile's motion along the trajectory shown. The entire trajectory is visible through the camera.
Identify ONE of the errors in this set-up and describe the effect of this error on the results.
A camera records apparent size, not true size. Anything at a different distance from the camera than the trajectory, or not on the same line of sight, distorts the apparent motion.
For the effect, ask how the apparent speed of the ball near the start of the trajectory compares with its apparent speed near the end, then state which way the calculated velocity is in error.
Three marks need the error named, the effect identified, and the effect stated as a consequence for the calculated velocity.
An experiment was set up based on the method described in part (a), but conducted so that the data obtained were valid.
The graphs show data from this experiment.
Using the graphs, describe the velocity and acceleration of the ball quantitatively and qualitatively.
A straight line on a displacement-time graph means a constant velocity equal to the gradient. Use two well-separated points on the line rather than a single reading off the axes.
A straight line on a velocity-time graph means a constant acceleration equal to the gradient. Check the sign convention of the vertical axis before you state the direction of the acceleration.
Both the numbers and the words are needed: the magnitude from the gradient, then whether the quantity is constant or changing and in which direction.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / Advanced Mechanics / Circular Motion / investigate the relationship between the total energy and work done on an object executing uniform circular motion
questions.text:
The radius of the moon is $1740\,\mathrm{km}$. The moon's mass is $7.35 \times 10^{22}\,\mathrm{kg}$. In this question, ignore the moon's rotational and orbital motion.
A $20\,\mathrm{kg}$ mass is launched vertically from the moon's surface at a velocity of $1200\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
Show that the change in potential energy of the mass in moving from the surface to an altitude of $500\,\mathrm{km}$ is $1.26 \times 10^{7}\,\mathrm{J}$.
The $500\,\mathrm{km}$ is an altitude above the surface, but the denominator in $U = -GMm/r$ is the distance from the Moon's centre, so it becomes $1740 + 500 = 2240\,\mathrm{km}$.
Write the potential energy at each of the two radii before you subtract, and keep the negative sign on both of them. The change is the final value minus the initial value, and it comes out positive because the mass is moving further from the Moon.
Calculate the velocity of the $20\,\mathrm{kg}$ mass at an altitude of $500\,\mathrm{km}$.
Nothing is pushing the mass once it has left the surface, so treat the ascent as a conservation-of-mechanical-energy problem: the potential energy it gains must come out of the kinetic energy it was launched with.
Calculate the kinetic energy at launch, subtract the change in potential energy you found in part (a), then recover the speed from $E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$.

questions.current_path: Year 11 / Kinematics / Motion in a Straight Line / conduct practical investigations, selecting from a range of technologies, to record and analyse the motion of objects in a variety of situations in one dimension in order to measure or calculate: time; distance; displacement; speed; velocity; acceleration
questions.text:
The diagram shows two different cells.
How does light contribute to the flow of current in each of these two cells?
Work out, for each cell, whether an external battery is doing the collecting. In the vacuum photocell it is, so light has to do no more than start electrons moving and something else has to move them to the other electrode.
In the solar cell there is no battery, so the cell has to make its own potential difference. Ask where that comes from, and what the junction does to the electrons and the holes that the light creates in each of the two layers.
Explain how ONE advance in scientific understanding and ONE advance in technology have led to the use of semiconductors.
Answer the two halves separately and label them, because the marking guide awards the marks separately for a named development in scientific understanding and for a named development in technology.
For the understanding half, the useful ideas are how electrons can occupy different energy states in a solid, and what happens to those states when other atoms are deliberately added. For the technology half, think about what a sample has to be before those ideas can be applied to it, and about what is needed to join two layers together.
Finish by making the link explicit: say what the two advances together made possible, and name the device.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / The Nature of Light / Light and Special Relativity / investigate the evidence, from Einstein’s thought experiments and subsequent experimental validation, for time dilation and length contraction , and analyse quantitatively situations in which these are observed, for example: observations of cosmic-origin muons at the Earth’s surface; atomic clocks (Hafele–Keating experiment); evidence from particle accelerators; evidence from cosmological studies
questions.text:
Geophysics
Seismic methods are used to investigate physical properties of Earth.
The question rules out seismic methods, so start from what geophysicists can measure without sending a wave into the ground: radiation emitted by the rocks themselves, the strength of the gravitational field, magnetic properties, and heat flow.
For (a)(ii) pick ONE of the methods from (a)(i) and describe it as a chain — what is measured, what it is compared against, and what the comparison reveals about the rock.
In November 2017, a new polar-orbiting weather satellite NOAA-20 was placed in orbit. Its orbital period is $100$ minutes and it orbits Earth at an altitude of $870\,\mathrm{km}$. The average radius of Earth is $6370\,\mathrm{km}$.
Sub-part (b)(i) is about the geometry of the orbit: compare the orbital radius of NOAA-20 with that of a geostationary satellite, and think about how often the satellite returns to the same part of Earth.
For (b)(ii) the orbital radius is measured from the centre of Earth, not from the surface, so add the altitude to the radius of Earth. Convert the period to seconds before you substitute it.
Explain how both Richer and Newton independently used data obtained from experiments using pendulums to determine the shape of Earth.
Two scientists and one piece of data. Identify what Richer measured and what Newton concluded from it, and keep those two roles separate in your answer.
The link between them is a pendulum: its rate of swing depends on the acceleration due to gravity, and the acceleration due to gravity varies with latitude. Say how each scientist used that link.
How are seismic data used to provide a model of Earth's core? Support your answer with a diagram.
The whole argument rests on one material property: compare what a liquid can and cannot support mechanically, and the rest of the seismic evidence follows from it.
Your diagram has to show the shadow zones: draw Earth's cross-section with the epicentre, the boundary at about $103^{\circ}$ beyond which $S$-waves are not received, and the region beyond about $142^{\circ}$ where $P$-waves are also missing. Then state the model of the core that the evidence gives.
Explain the role of palaeomagnetic data in providing evidence that supports the theory of plate tectonics.
This is a 7-mark explanation with three threads to cover: what palaeomagnetic data actually is, what specific observations it provides, and which parts of plate tectonics each observation supports.
For each piece of evidence name the observation and the process it is evidence for — mirror-image magnetic striping about a mid-ocean ridge is evidence for sea-floor spreading, while apparent polar wander is evidence for continental drift. Then state what ties the two together.
