questions.text:
Medical Physics
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
Sub-part (a)(i) asks for specific uses, not general ones — name an organ and what is being detected in it.
Sub-part (a)(ii) is about what a very strong static field does to hydrogen nuclei before any radio frequency is applied. Consider their orientation, how many of the two possible alignments there are, and the direction of the resulting precession.
Ultrasound
Sub-part (b)(i): note that the two waves have the same frequency and strike the same boundary from opposite sides, in tissues with different acoustic impedances. Ask what is the same for both and what is different.
Sub-part (b)(ii): work in stages — get the kidney impedance first from $Z = \rho v$, then write the intensity-reflection relation with the unknown impedance $Z_{1}$ still in it, and solve algebraically rather than by trial values.
Iodine-124 is a radioactive element. The equation for its decay is shown. The symbol $e^{+}$ is sometimes shown as $\beta^{+}$.
The following is a decay table for iodine-124.
Justify the use of iodine-124 as a medical diagnostic tool. Support your answer quantitatively.
Two things have to be justified: why the decay shown in the equation is useful for imaging, and why the timing shown in the decay table is suitable for use inside a body.
For the quantitative part, read from the table the time at which the proportion remaining first reaches 0.5, then say what that number means for how long the radiation stays in the body.
Explain how the Doppler effect is used for medical imaging.
Start with the physics of reflection from a moving surface: what happens to the frequency of the reflected wave when the surface moves towards the incident beam, and when it moves away?
Then connect the size of the frequency change to the velocity of the surface, and say which body tissues move fast enough for the effect to be worth measuring.
The following image of the bones in a person's neck was produced using computed axial tomography (CAT).
Compare both the production and benefits of this CAT image with a conventional X-ray image of the same part of the person's body.
Structure the answer as two labelled halves — production and benefits — and make at least one explicit comparison in each half rather than describing the two techniques in isolation.
The key idea behind the production comparison is that a plain X-ray integrates everything in front of each point on the detector, while a CAT scan measures attenuation from many directions and reconstructs slices. The key idea behind the benefits comparison is what that does to clarity, ambiguity and soft-tissue differentiation.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Origins of the Elements / investigate the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram and how it can be used to determine the following about a star: characteristics and evolutionary stage; surface temperature; colour; luminosity | Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Origins of the Elements / investigate the types of nucleosynthesis reactions involved in Main Sequence and Post-Main Sequence stars, including but not limited to: proton–proton chain
questions.text:
Astrophysics
The parsec and trigonometric parallax
Define the parsec with the aid of a diagram.
Trigonometric parallax measures how far a star appears to shift against distant background stars as Earth moves. The largest baseline available is the diameter of Earth's orbit, $1\,\mathrm{AU}$, obtained by observing six months apart.
The definition ties an angle to a distance: draw the $1\,\mathrm{AU}$ baseline, the sight line from the star, and the small angle the baseline subtends. Work out from your diagram what happens to that angle as the star gets further away.
For the limitations, work outwards from the telescope: name everything the atmosphere does to the light on its way in, then use your diagram to state which stars can be measured at all.
The parsec and trigonometric parallax
Outline TWO limitations of using ground-based instruments to make trigonometric parallax measurements.
Variable stars
Read the shape of each light curve before writing anything. A brightness that dips and returns to the same value on a regular cycle is produced by something passing in front of the star; a smooth, rounded rise and fall is produced by the star itself.
For the distance, an apparent magnitude tells you nothing until you know the star's absolute magnitude, and the period-luminosity graph is what supplies it. Read the period off the graph in the units the axis is labelled in before you look up the magnitude.
The final step is the distance-modulus relationship $m - M = 5\log_{10}\left(\frac{d}{10\,\mathrm{pc}}\right)$ — substitute the apparent and absolute magnitudes, solve for $d$, and convert to kiloparsecs.
A H-R diagram is shown. Star X is a main sequence star of 12 solar masses.
Describe how star X will change physically and chemically as it continues to evolve.
Use the 12 solar masses rather than the marker position to locate star X: a star that massive sits far above and to the left of the Sun on the main sequence, so it is very hot, very luminous and very large.
Now trace the evolutionary path in stages. When a star this massive leaves the main sequence it swells and cools into a supergiant, and it then fuses lighter and lighter nuclei in its core in a fixed sequence.
Keep two separate lists as you write — the physical changes (radius, luminosity, temperature, state) and the chemical changes (which nuclei become which) — and finish by explaining what happens once the core has been built up to iron.
Explain how measurements made using photoelectric technologies have increased the understanding of celestial objects beyond that provided using photographic methods.
Start by contrasting what each method actually records. A photographic plate integrates the light from every star in the field at once; a CCD is an array of pixels whose readings can be summed digitally for one star at a time.
Then list what can be done to data that is already in numerical form — subtract one image from another, enhance or enlarge it, add or subtract selected colour channels — and note which of these is impossible on a developed plate.
Finish by converting each capability into a property of the star it now lets you determine, rather than listing features of the technology.
Explain how black body spectra, emission spectra and absorption spectra are used to analyse the surface temperature and chemical composition of stars. In your answer, refer to observations that can be made in a school laboratory.
Assign one job to each of the three spectra before writing. Temperature comes from the shape of the continuous (black body) curve — the position of its peak fixes the temperature by Wien's law — while the composition comes from the lines.
Make the link between the two line spectra explicit: an absorption line is a wavelength missing from the continuous spectrum, and an emission line is that same wavelength produced by a hot thin gas.
For the laboratory part, name the apparatus rather than describing it vaguely: a spectroscope, prism or diffraction grating, and the actual gas discharge tubes. Include a source that gives a continuous spectrum, such as a filament lamp.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Quantum Mechanical Nature of the Atom / assess the limitations of the Rutherford and Bohr atomic models | Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Quantum Mechanical Nature of the Atom / investigate the line emission spectra to examine the Balmer series in hydrogen (ACSPH138) | Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Quantum Mechanical Nature of the Atom / relate qualitatively and quantitatively the quantised energy levels of the hydrogen atom and the law of conservation of energy to the line emission spectrum of hydrogen using: (ACSPH136)
questions.text:
From Quanta to Quarks
The Bohr model of the atom
Identify TWO limitations of the Bohr model of the atom.
For the limitations, test the model against what is actually observed: does it hold for hydrogen alone or for every element, and does it predict how bright each spectral line is as well as where the lines fall?
For the emission spectrum, begin from the model's central postulate — the electron may occupy only certain specific energy levels — and reason forward from what must happen for an electron to change level.
Remember that the quantity released in a transition is fixed by the difference between two levels, so only particular energies can be emitted. A labelled level diagram makes this obvious and earns credit.
The Bohr model of the atom
How does the Bohr model of the atom account for the emission spectrum of hydrogen?
Chadwick's discovery of the neutron
In Chadwick's experiment three particles leave the reaction: the alpha particle, the proton and the unknown X. Their velocities are known or can be measured, so look for the conservation law that lets you solve backwards for the one property of X that is not given.
For the energy calculation, use $E = \Delta m\,c^{2}$. Add the masses on each side of the equation separately, find the difference, convert it from atomic mass units into kilograms, and only then substitute for $c$.
Sanity-check the size of your answer: a mass defect of a few thousandths of an atomic mass unit should give an energy of order $10^{-13}\,\mathrm{J}$, not of order $10^{-10}\,\mathrm{J}$.
How did Pauli infer the existence and properties of a new particle from measurements of the energies of beta particles? Support your answer with a graph.
Begin from the law of conservation of energy. If a nucleus emitted only one particle, the energies of all the emitted particles would have to add up to one fixed value.
Now look at what was actually measured and sketch the distribution: the beta-particle energies are spread over a range with a maximum, so the individual energies do not add to a fixed total and something else must be carrying the missing energy away.
Once you have inferred a new particle, use the other conservation laws to constrain it — charge in particular — and use the shape of your graph to say how much of the energy it could be carrying.
Radioactive sources, X and Y, producing two different types of radiation were placed in identical Wilson cloud chambers. The diagram shows the trails produced by each.
Describe the changes in the nuclei of X and Y which have produced these trails.
Match each track to a particle using two features: the density of the droplets along the track measures how strongly the particle ionises, and the amount the track bends in the chamber's magnetic field measures the sign and size of the particle's momentum.
Once you have named the particle, write down what it does to the parent nucleus. Treat the atomic number and the mass number separately, and remember that an electron carries almost no mass but does carry charge.
Using the standard model, analyse the roles of both forces and particles in the current understanding of the atom.
Start with the particle side: name the two families of fundamental particles and say what each one goes to make — remember that one nucleon contains three of them and the other has no constituents.
Then work through the four interactions one at a time and ask of each: what does it act between, over what range is it significant, and what happens without it? That automatically identifies the one that is negligible and the one responsible for radioactive decay.
Finish by tying each force to the structure it maintains inside the atom. That link between forces and structure is what turns a list of facts into an analysis.

questions.current_path: Year 11 / Electricity and Magnetism / Electric Circuits / investigate quantitatively and analyse the rate of conversion of electrical energy in components of electric circuits, including the production of heat and light, by applying and and variations that involve Ohm’s Law (ACSPH042)
questions.text:
The Age of Silicon
Electric and electronic circuits; optical fibres
Outline TWO differences between an electric circuit and an electronic circuit.
For the comparison, first decide what each kind of circuit is optimising for — the power it delivers or the information it carries — and then build each difference from that: the voltage and current levels, and the resistance of the components used.
For silica, list what an optical fibre needs to achieve and match each need to a property of the material: it must form into a thin flexible strand, it must transmit light with very little loss, and the light must be kept inside the core.
For the last of those, remember that total internal reflection requires the core to have a higher refractive index than the surrounding cladding, so the question to ask is whether the refractive index can be controlled.
Electric and electronic circuits; optical fibres
How do the properties of silica make it an ideal material for use in electronic communication?
Operational amplifiers
An inverting amplifier is defined by where the two resistors go: one in series from the input to the $(-)$ terminal, the other from the output back to that same $(-)$ terminal. The $(+)$ terminal goes to ground, and no connection is made to the $(+)$ terminal from the input.
For the graph, get the gain from the ratio of the two resistances before drawing anything, and remember the output can never exceed the supply rails however large the input becomes.
Find the input voltage at which the straight line would produce exactly the rail voltage, draw the linear section up to that point, and flatten the response at the rails out to the full input range.
The graph shows the average number of transistors incorporated into integrated circuit chips from 1970 to 2015.
Relate information in the graph to the evolution of computer technology.
Read the axes before drawing any conclusion. The vertical axis is logarithmic, so the straight rising line means the count is increasing exponentially — work out roughly how many years each tenfold step takes.
Now convert the rate of growth into consequences: more transistors on a chip means more memory and more processing, so trace the effect on the size, cost and range of uses of computers since 1970.
Treat the dashed forward prediction separately, and say what eventually limits the trend rather than assuming the straight line continues indefinitely.
Explain how an electronic circuit can use a relay to switch high-power devices. In your answer, refer to the roles of the components of the relay.
Begin with the problem: state why the electronic circuit cannot itself carry the high voltage or current without being destroyed.
Then separate the relay into its two sides — the low-power input side containing the electromagnet, and the high-power side containing the switch contacts — and state how energy gets from one to the other without an electrical connection between them.
Name the components and their roles individually: coil and soft iron core, armature or lever, pivot, and the contacts. A well-labelled diagram will earn credit here.
The diagrams show a circuit and the characteristic curve of the thermistor used.
Explain the operation of this circuit. Support your answer with a truth table and data from the thermistor characteristic curve.
Solve the sensor first. Work out the reference voltage set by the two fixed resistors, then find the thermistor resistance at which the input equals it. Because this is an NTC thermistor, resistance falls as temperature rises, which fixes a temperature threshold.
Read that threshold off the thermistor characteristic curve rather than assuming a value, and keep the figure consistent with the divider arithmetic.
Then identify each gate in turn and work out the logic from the isolation switch, the temperature signal and the smoke signal. Finish with a truth table covering every combination and state the single condition under which the alarm sounds.

questions.text:
Calculate the wavelength of light emitted by an electron moving from energy level 3 to 2 in a Bohr model hydrogen atom.
Use the Rydberg formula $\frac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\frac{1}{n_f^{2}} - \frac{1}{n_i^{2}}\right)$ with $R = 1.097\times10^{7}\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}$.
For an emission the electron starts on the higher level, so $n_i = 3$ and $n_f = 2$. Calculate $1/\lambda$ first, then invert it.
Describe the behaviour of electrons in the Bohr model of the atom with reference to the law of conservation of energy.

questions.text:
A capsule travelling at $12\,900\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ enters Earth's atmosphere, causing it to rapidly slow down to $400\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
During this re-entry, the capsule reaches a temperature of 3200 K.
What is the peak wavelength of the light emitted by the capsule?
Use Wien's law, $\lambda_{max} = \frac{b}{T}$, with $b = 2.898\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m\,K}$ and the temperature in kelvin.
The constant is in $\mathrm{m\,K}$, so report your answer in metres with a sensible number of significant figures.
Outline TWO limitations of applying special relativity to the analysis of the motion of the capsule.
Special relativity is a theory of inertial frames moving at speeds that are close to the speed of light. Test both of those conditions against the capsule's situation during re-entry.
You need two distinct limitations. One concerns how fast the capsule is going; the other concerns the kind of motion the capsule is undergoing.

questions.text:
Describe the difference between the spectra of the light produced by a gas discharge tube and by an incandescent lamp.
Do not describe the light source or the colour of the light. Describe what the spread of wavelengths reaching the observer looks like for each source, and say which one contains every wavelength and which one contains only a few.
The difference is ultimately a difference in the state of the emitting material: a hot dense solid radiates at all wavelengths, whereas excited atoms in a gas emit only at the wavelengths set by their energy-level differences.
The graph shows the curves predicted by two different models, X and Y, for the electromagnetic radiation emitted by an object at a temperature of 5000 K.
Identify an assumption of EACH model which determines the shape of its curve.
Compare where the two curves go at the short-wavelength end before you commit to an answer. One of them leaves the top of the graph still heading upwards as the wavelength decreases, which means the model behind it predicts more and more intensity as the wavelength falls. Ask what assumption about energy exchange produces that behaviour, and then ask what the other model must assume instead to keep the intensity finite at short wavelengths.
You need one assumption for each model, not two assumptions for one of them, and each should be a statement about how energy is exchanged rather than about the shape of the graph.
The diagram shows the radiation curve for a black body radiator at a temperature of 5000 K.
On the same diagram, sketch a curve for a black body radiator at a temperature of 4000 K and explain the differences between the curves.
Sketch it in the unused part of the grid, keeping the same axes, and get three features right: where the peak sits along the wavelength axis, how high the peak is, and where the curve lies relative to the printed one at short wavelengths.
The cooler body must still be a black body, so the curve keeps the same general shape: starting from zero at very short wavelengths, rising to a single maximum, then falling away slowly at long wavelengths. Do not draw a taller or a sharper curve.

questions.current_path: Year 11 / Kinematics / Motion in a Straight Line / conduct practical investigations, selecting from a range of technologies, to record and analyse the motion of objects in a variety of situations in one dimension in order to measure or calculate: time; distance; displacement; speed; velocity; acceleration
questions.text:
A metal rod sits on a pair of parallel metal rails, 20 cm apart, that are connected by a copper wire. The rails are at $30^{\circ}$ to the horizontal.
The apparatus is in a uniform magnetic field of 1 T which is upward, perpendicular to the table.
A force, $F$, is applied parallel to the rails to move the rod at a constant speed along the rails. The rod is moved a distance of 30 cm in 2.5 s.
Show that the change in magnetic flux through the circuit while the rod is moving is approximately $5.2\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{Wb}$.
The circuit is a loop whose area grows as the rod slides, so the quantity you need is a change in area multiplied by the component of the field perpendicular to the loop. Decide what that angle is before using $\cos\theta$.
Two dimensions of the loop change the area: the distance the rod travels along the rails and the distance the rails are apart. Both go into the area, and the travel time is not needed for this part.
Calculate the emf induced between the ends of the rod while it is moving, and state the direction of flow of the current in the circuit.
The emf is the rate of change of the flux found in the previous part, so that flux change is the numerator and the time interval from the stem is the denominator. An equivalent single-step form is $\varepsilon = Blv$.
For the direction, first decide whether the flux through the loop is increasing or decreasing, then use Lenz's law to work out which way the induced current must circulate to oppose it, and describe that direction from above rather than from one particular rail.
The experiment is repeated without the magnetic field.
Explain why the force required to move the rod is different without the magnetic field.
Compare the demands on the applied force with and without the field. In both cases the rod is being lifted up the rails, and in one of those cases something else is also consuming energy. Identify that second consumer and say what happens to the required force when it is removed.
The same conclusion can be reached two ways: through an energy accounting, or through Lenz's law applied to the force on the rod. Either is acceptable, but the force is still needed afterwards, so explain why the answer is a smaller force rather than no force.

A satellite is launched from the surface of Mars into an orbit that keeps it directly above a position on the surface of Mars.
Mass of Mars $= 6.39 \times 10^{23}\,\mathrm{kg}$. Length of Martian day $= 24$ hours $40$ minutes.
Identify TWO energy changes as the satellite moves from the surface of Mars into orbit.
Compare the satellite's energy on the surface with its energy in orbit. Work out how fast it has to be moving in orbit to keep falling around Mars instead of dropping to the ground, and how much further it is from the centre of Mars.
Two changes are required here, so name two separate quantities rather than one.
Calculate the orbital radius of the satellite.
Convert the length of the Martian day into seconds. It is $24\,\mathrm{h}$ plus $40\,\mathrm{min}$, and that total is the satellite's period $T$.
The satellite obeys the same law of periods as a moon around a planet, $r^{3} = \frac{GMT^{2}}{4\pi^{2}}$. Substitute $T$, the mass of Mars and $G$, then take the cube root.

questions.text:
A student performs an experiment to measure Planck's constant, $h$, using a device that emits specific frequencies of light when specific voltages are applied.
The voltage, $V$, needed to produce each frequency, $f$, is given by
where $q_e$ is the charge on an electron. Data from the experiment is shown.
Graph this data on the axes provided. Include a line of best fit.
Label both axes first: voltage in volts on the vertical axis, frequency in units of $10^{14}\,\mathrm{Hz}$ on the horizontal axis. Plot the frequency values exactly as tabulated, so $3.5$ goes at 3.5 units, not at $3.5\times10^{14}$.
Pick a scale that uses most of the grid and still has room for the whole line, then mark the four points carefully before drawing anything.
Draw one straight line of best fit that passes close to all four points. Because $V = \frac{hf}{q_e}$ has no constant term, a good fit should pass close to the origin, so a line with a large intercept means a point or a scale is wrong.
The student proposes using data point 1 to calculate a value for Planck's constant.
Justify a better method to calculate Planck's constant from the experimental data provided.
A value of $h$ taken from data point 1 alone carries the full random error of that one pair of readings. Ask how you could use the other three points at the same time.
Look back at the graph from part (a): one quantity that can be read off it is built from all four points at once, and once you rearrange $V = \frac{hf}{q_e}$ into $h = \frac{q_e V}{f}$ that quantity becomes $h$ directly.
Your justification needs a reason as well as a method, so state explicitly what using four points instead of one does to the random error.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / Electromagnetism / The Motor Effect / investigate qualitatively and quantitatively the interaction between a current-carrying conductor and a uniform magnetic field to establish: (ACSPH080, ACSPH081)
questions.text:
A student is considering how to levitate a thin metal rod in a strong magnetic field of $1.2\,\mathrm{T}$. The current flowing through the rod will be $2.3\,\mathrm{A}$.
Use a labelled diagram to show a suitable orientation of the current and the magnetic field to achieve this outcome. Include relevant forces in your diagram.
Levitation means the net force on the rod is zero, so the magnetic force must act vertically upwards to oppose the weight $mg$, which acts vertically downwards.
For that force to be as large as possible the current-carrying rod must be perpendicular to the field, i.e. $\theta = 90^{\circ}$. Choose which of $B$ or $I$ points out of the page and which lies along the rod, then check $\boldsymbol{F} = I\boldsymbol{L}\times\boldsymbol{B}$ with the right-hand rule.
Your diagram needs all four things labelled: $B$, $I$, the upward magnetic force and the downward weight, otherwise the orientation cannot be judged.
Explain why the maximum mass per unit length of the rod cannot exceed $0.282\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}}$. Support your answer with a calculation.
Levitation is an equilibrium condition, so start by writing the magnetic force equal to the weight.
Both $mg$ and $BIL$ contain the length of rod $L$, so divide the whole equation by $L$; the mass per unit length then appears on its own.
For the word 'maximum': the angle between the rod and the field can only be chosen so that $\sin\theta \le 1$, so the value you obtain with $\sin\theta = 1$ is the largest the field and current can support.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / The Nature of Light / Light and Special Relativity / investigate the evidence, from Einstein’s thought experiments and subsequent experimental validation, for time dilation and length contraction , and analyse quantitatively situations in which these are observed, for example: observations of cosmic-origin muons at the Earth’s surface; atomic clocks (Hafele–Keating experiment); evidence from particle accelerators; evidence from cosmological studies
questions.text:
A spaceship travels to a distant star at a constant speed, $v$. When it arrives, 15 years have passed on Earth but 9.4 years have passed for an astronaut on the spaceship.
What is the distance to the star as measured by an observer on Earth?
Set the Earth time equal to the spaceship's proper time dilated: $15 = \frac{9.4}{\sqrt{1 - v^{2}/c^{2}}}$, where the 9.4 years is the time measured where the astronaut is at rest.
Solve for $v$ as a fraction of $c$ before doing anything else, then use $s = ut$ with the Earth-frame time of 15 years. Expressed in light years the answer is just $\frac{v}{c}\times 15$.
Check your answer: it must be smaller than 15 light years, because the spaceship travels at less than the speed of light.
Outline how special relativity imposes a limitation on the maximum velocity of the spaceship.
Classical momentum $mv$ is not the whole story at these speeds. Write the relativistic expression $p = \frac{m_0v}{\sqrt{1 - v^{2}/c^{2}}}$ and examine its denominator as $v$ approaches $c$.
Newton's second law ties a rate of change of momentum to a force, so consider what force would be needed to keep increasing that momentum once it becomes very large.
An outline needs both halves: the behaviour of the momentum as $v \to c$, and the resulting restriction on the velocity of a massive object.

questions.text:
In an experiment, a proton accelerates from rest between parallel charged plates. The spacing of the plates is 12 cm and the proton is initially positioned at an equal distance from both plates, as shown. Ignore the effect of gravity.
The electrical potential energy of the proton is recorded in the following graph for the first 5 cm of its motion.
On the graph, sketch the corresponding kinetic energy of the proton over the same distance.
The electric field does the work, so every joule of potential energy lost appears as kinetic energy: $KE$ at any point equals the drop in $PE$ up to that point.
Remember the proton starts from rest, so its $KE$ is zero at $0\,\mathrm{cm}$, where the printed line is at its highest.
Because the field between the plates is uniform, both energies change linearly with distance. So the $KE$ curve must be a straight line whose gradient has the same size as, but the opposite sign to, the gradient of the printed line.
The experiment is repeated using an electron in the place of the proton.
Explain how the motion of the electron would differ from that of the proton.
Compare the two particles in the same uniform field with $F = qE$. The magnitude of the charge is the same for a proton and an electron, so compare their masses and the sign of their charges.
Then use $a = \frac{F}{m}$. The electron's mass is roughly 1836 times smaller than the proton's, so work out how much larger its acceleration becomes even though the force is unchanged.
Two of the three marks come from describing how the motion differs; the third comes from explaining why it differs.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / Advanced Mechanics / Projectile Motion / solve problems, create models and make quantitative predictions by applying the equations of motion relationships for uniformly accelerated and constant rectilinear motion
questions.text:
A $3.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ mass is launched from the edge of a cliff.
The kinetic energy of the mass is graphed from the moment it is launched until it hits the ground at X. The kinetic energy of the mass is provided for times $t_0$, $t_1$ and $t_2$.
Account for the relative values of kinetic energy at $t_0$, $t_1$ and $t_2$.
Read the cliff diagram before the graph: the ball leaves the edge on an upward path, so at $t_0$ it has a horizontal component and an upward vertical component.
Between $t_0$ and $t_1$ gravity is reducing the upward vertical velocity to zero, so the $KE$ falls, but it does not fall to zero because the horizontal component is unaffected. Check that against the shape of the curve.
For the final comparison, think about gravitational potential energy: how does the height of the mass at $t_2$ compare with its height at $t_0$, and what does conservation of energy then imply for the $KE$?
The horizontal component of the velocity of the mass during its flight is $13.76\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
Calculate the time of flight of the mass.
You need the vertical velocity of the mass at launch and again at the ground; the given $13.76\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ horizontal component is the same at both moments, since gravity does not change it.
At $t_0$ and at $t_2$ the tabulated $KE$ is the TOTAL kinetic energy, so use $KE = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$ to get the total speed at each time, then use Pythagoras with the $13.76\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ component to extract the vertical part.
The whole flight is one uniformly accelerated vertical motion, so finish with $v_y = u_y + at$ over the full interval from $t_0$ to $t_2$, taking care with the sign of the initial upward component.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Properties of the Nucleus / analyse the spontaneous decay of unstable nuclei, and the properties of the alpha, beta and gamma radiation emitted (ACSPH028, ACSPH030) | Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Properties of the Nucleus / predict quantitatively the energy released in nuclear decays or transmutations, including nuclear fission and nuclear fusion, by applying: (ACSPH031, ACSPH035, ACSPH036) | Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Properties of the Nucleus / the law of conservation of energy | Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Properties of the Nucleus / mass defect | Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Properties of the Nucleus / Einstein’s mass–energy equivalence relationship
questions.text:
A spacecraft is powered by a radioisotope generator. Pu-238 in the generator undergoes alpha decay, releasing energy. The decay is shown with the mass of each species in atomic mass units, u.
Show that the energy released by one decay is $9.0 \times 10^{-13}\,\mathrm{J}$.
Write the mass balance for the decay: initial mass minus (final mass plus alpha particle mass) is the mass that has been converted into released energy.
That difference is very small, so subtract with enough decimal places kept; rounding the masses too early is the usual trap here.
Convert the mass deficit with $1\,\mathrm{u} = 1.66\times10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}$ before applying $E = \Delta mc^{2}$, otherwise the result will be wrong by many orders of magnitude.
At launch, the generator contains $9.0 \times 10^{24}$ atoms of Pu-238. The half-life of Pu-238 is 87.7 years.
Calculate the total energy produced by the generator during the first ten years after launch.
Turn the half-life into a decay constant with $\lambda = \frac{\ln 2}{t_{1/2}}$, and keep the time in years so that it matches the ten-year interval and the units cancel.
The number of nuclei still present after time $t$ is $N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}$; the quantity you want is the difference $N_0 - N$, not $N_0$ itself.
Finally multiply the number of decays by the energy released in ONE decay, which you found in part (a).

questions.current_path: Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Properties of the Nucleus / examine the model of half-life in radioactive decay and make quantitative predictions about the activity or amount of a radioactive sample using the following relationships:
questions.text:
The radioactive decay curve for americium-242 is shown.
Use the graph to find the half-life of Am-242 and hence show that the decay constant, $\lambda$, is $0.043\,\mathrm{h^{-1}}$.
Read the initial mass from the curve where it crosses the vertical axis, halve that value, then read horizontally across the grid to where the curve reaches the halved mass and drop down to the time axis.
The grid is ruled every $10$ micrograms vertically and every 8 hours horizontally, which makes the halving easy to locate to within a small fraction of a division.
Convert the half-life you read into a decay constant with $\lambda = \frac{\ln 2}{t_{1/2}}$, and check that the units come out as an inverse time rather than a time.
Calculate how long it takes until the mass of Am-242 is 8 micrograms.
Eight micrograms is one tenth of the mass present at $t = 0$, so write the surviving mass as one tenth of the initial mass in the decay equation.
Take natural logarithms to remove the exponential, giving $\ln\left(\frac{N}{N_0}\right) = -\lambda t$, then rearrange for $t$.
Use the decay constant in $\mathrm{h^{-1}}$ from part (a) so that $t$ comes out in hours, and be aware that carrying an extra decimal place in $\lambda$ moves the final answer by about an hour.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / Advanced Mechanics / Circular Motion / investigate the relationship between the total energy and work done on an object executing uniform circular motion
questions.text:
A rocket is launched vertically from a planet of mass $M$. After it leaves the atmosphere, the rocket's engine is turned off and it continues to move away from the planet. From this time the rocket's mass is $200\,\mathrm{kg}$. The rocket's speed, $v$, at two different distances from the planet's centre, $R$, is shown.
Show that the magnitude of the change in kinetic energy from point 1 to point 2 is $2.2 \times 10^{9}\,\mathrm{J}$.
Apply $KE = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$ at each point separately and then subtract; because the mass is the same at both, $m$ can stay outside the bracket and cancel nicely.
Keep the numbers manageable by working in scientific notation: $5500^{2} = 3.03\times10^{7}$ and $2900^{2} = 8.41\times10^{6}$.
The kinetic energy is larger at the closer point, so going from point 1 to point 2 the change is negative. Quote the magnitude, which is what the question asks for.
Determine the mass $M$ of the planet using the law of conservation of energy.
Set the change in kinetic energy equal to the change in gravitational potential energy, using $U = -\frac{GMm}{R}$ with $M$ the unknown mass of the planet.
Write the potential energy change between the two radii explicitly as $GMm\left(\frac{1}{R_2} - \frac{1}{R_1}\right)$. Because $R_2$ is the larger radius the bracket is negative, which correctly represents a gain in potential energy.
Every quantity in that expression is known except $M$, so rearrange to isolate it with $G = 6.67\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{N\,m^{2}\,kg^{-2}}$.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / Electromagnetism / Charged Particles, Conductors and Electric and Magnetic Fields / acceleration of charged particles by the electric field | Year 12 / The Nature of Light / Light: Quantum Model / analyse the photoelectric effect as it occurs in metallic elements by applying the law of conservation of energy and the photon model of light, (ACSPH119)
questions.text:
Light of frequency $7.5 \times 10^{14}\,\mathrm{Hz}$ is incident on a calcium metal sheet which has a work function of $2.9\,\mathrm{eV}$. Photoelectrons are emitted. The metal is in a uniform electric field of $5.2\,\mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$, perpendicular to the surface of the metal, as shown.
Show that the maximum kinetic energy of an emitted photoelectron is $3.2 \times 10^{-20}\,\mathrm{J}$.
Use $K_{max} = hf - \phi$, and convert the work function from electronvolts to joules using the charge on an electron, $1\,\mathrm{eV} = 1.602\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$.
Both terms must be in the same units and of comparable magnitude, so check the size of each before you subtract; if they differ by several orders of magnitude a conversion has been missed.
Use $h = 6.626\times10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\,s}$ and $f = 7.5\times10^{14}\,\mathrm{Hz}$; the photon energy will be of order $5\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$.
Calculate the maximum distance, $d$, an emitted photoelectron can travel from the surface of the metal.
Ask where the photoelectron moves fastest and where it stops: at the maximum distance $d$ above the sheet its kinetic energy is zero.
So the magnitude of the work done against the field, $W = qEd$, must equal the maximum kinetic energy found in part (a).
Substitute $E = 5.2\,\mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$ and $q = 1.602\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$ and solve for $d$. keeping the unit consistent with the field strength.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / The Nature of Light / Light: Wave Model / conduct investigations to analyse quantitatively the interference of light using double slit apparatus and diffraction gratings (ACSPH116, ACSPH117, ACSPH140)
questions.text:
A laser producing red light of wavelength $655\,\mathrm{nm}$ is directed onto double slits separated by a distance, $d = 5.0 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m}$. A screen is placed behind the double slits.
Newton proposed a model of light. Use a labelled sketch to show the pattern on the screen that would be expected from Newton's proposed model.
Sketch only what the particle model allows. Every particle of light travels in a straight line from the source through one of the two openings to the screen, so the pattern on the screen is built from the light passing through each opening on its own. The model you are drawing has no superposition principle, so ask what the particles arriving by the two different routes can do to each other.
Label your sketch: mark where light from each opening lands on the screen, how wide that image is, and any part of the screen that receives no light at all. Keep in mind which model you are drawing, since a different model of light would predict a different pattern on the same screen.
When the laser light is turned on, a series of vertical bright lines are seen on the screen.
Calculate the angle, $\theta$, between the centre line and the bright line at A.
Count the fringes outwards from the central maximum before choosing a value for $m$: the central bright line is $m = 0$ and each bright line beyond it adds one to the order. The marked line is not the first one away from the centre.
The condition you want is the one for constructive interference, so the path difference must be a whole number of wavelengths. Since $\lambda$ is much smaller than $d$, the resulting angle is small, so it can be left in radians or converted to degrees, but the conversion must be done if the answer is quoted in degrees.
The laser is replaced with one producing green light of wavelength $520\,\mathrm{nm}$. Explain the difference in the pattern that would be produced.
Nothing in the arrangement changes except the wavelength, so ask what that single change does to the quantity that sets the position of each fringe. Comparing the spacing of the bright lines is far more useful than comparing their brightness or width.
For the explanation, connect the change in wavelength to the change in the angle of each fringe before saying anything about the appearance of the screen, and note what stays unchanged at the centre of the pattern.

questions.text:
In a thought experiment, light travels from X to a mirror Y and back to X on a moving train carriage. The path of the light relative to an observer on the train is shown.
Relative to an observer outside the train, the path of the light is shown below, at three consecutive times as the train carriage moves along the track.
Describe qualitatively how the constancy of the speed of light and the thought experiment above led Einstein to predict time dilation.
The two observers do not disagree about the speed of light; they disagree about how far the light travelled. Compare the path in the first figure with the path in the second.
In the second figure the carriage has moved horizontally between the outward and return legs, so the outside observer's path is a zig-zag and is longer overall.
Combine that longer distance with $t = \frac{d}{c}$ to explain why the outside observer assigns the longer time to the identical journey.
The train is travelling with a velocity $v = 0.96c$. To the observer inside the train, the return journey for the light between X and Y takes 15 nanoseconds. How long would this return journey take according to the observer outside the train?
The 15 nanoseconds is the time measured in the train's own frame, because both the emission and the return happen at the same place in that frame. It is therefore the proper time $t_0$.
Use the time-dilation relation $t = \frac{t_0}{\sqrt{1 - v^{2}/c^{2}}}$ with $v$ written as a multiple of $c$ so that $c$ cancels out of the square root.
Convert the result into seconds at the end, or leave it in nanoseconds, but state the unit either way.

questions.current_path: Year 11 / Electricity and Magnetism / Magnetism / use magnetic field lines to model qualitatively the direction and strength of magnetic fields produced by magnets, current-carrying wires and solenoids and relate these fields to their effect on magnetic materials that are placed within them (ACSPH083)
questions.text:
One type of stationary exercise bike uses a pair of strong, movable magnets placed on opposite sides of a thick, aluminium flywheel to provide a torque to make it harder to pedal.
Explain the principle by which these magnets make it harder to pedal.
The flywheel is a conductor moving through a non-uniform magnetic field, so think about which induction effect occurs inside a bulk conductor rather than in a circuit.
Use Lenz's law: the induced effect always opposes the change in flux that produced it, never reinforces it.
For the final link, a force acting on the rim of the wheel about its axis is a torque, and a torque opposing the rider's pedalling is exactly what makes the bike harder to turn.
The bike rider wants to increase the opposing torque on the flywheel. Justify an adjustment that could be made to the magnets to achieve this.
The size of the induced eddy currents depends on how rapidly the magnetic flux through the wheel changes, so ask how the field strength at the wheel depends on the distance of the magnets from it.
By Lenz's law the braking force is then proportional to those induced currents, and the braking torque follows because the force acts out at the rim of the flywheel.
Your justification must name the adjustment and give the whole chain of reasoning from flux change to induced current to force to torque. Consider how the field at the wheel varies with distance from the axis as well as with distance from the magnets.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / Advanced Mechanics / Projectile Motion / solve problems, create models and make quantitative predictions by applying the equations of motion relationships for uniformly accelerated and constant rectilinear motion | Year 12 / Advanced Mechanics / Circular Motion / solve problems, model and make quantitative predictions about objects executing uniform circular motion in a variety of situations, using the following relationships:

Show that the vertical component of the projectile's velocity at P is $14.2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
The hammer is in uniform circular motion of radius $1.6\,\mathrm{m}$ with period $0.50\,\mathrm{s}$, so start from $v = \frac{2\pi r}{T}$.
That $v$ is the full speed at P; the velocity there makes $45^{\circ}$ with the horizontal, so resolve it to obtain the vertical component.
The mass is not needed for the speed, because the period alone determines how fast the hammer is moving.
Calculate the horizontal range of the projectile from point P.
Split the flight into two parts: from P up to the top of the trajectory, and from the top down to the ground. The horizontal velocity stays at the value found in part (a) for the whole flight.
For the rise, use $v_y = u_y - gt$ to get the time to the top, then $s_y = u_y t - \frac{1}{2}gt^{2}$ to get the height gained.
Add the release height of $1.2\,\mathrm{m}$ to get the height of the top above the ground, find the fall time from rest with $s_y = \frac{1}{2}gt^{2}$, add the two times and multiply by the horizontal velocity.

Spectra provide information about the stars that produce them.

Two things must come out of this spectrum: which atoms are present, and how hot the surface is. Ask what each feature of the spectrum is telling you - a dark line is made when a particular atom in the star's atmosphere absorbs that wavelength, and a bright line when a particular atom emits it.

The diagram represents one hydrogen emission line from the spectrum of a star.

questions.text:
A $400\,\mathrm{kg}$ satellite is travelling in a circular orbit of radius $6.700 \times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{m}$ around Earth. Its potential energy is $-2.389 \times 10^{10}\,\mathrm{J}$ and its total energy is $-1.195 \times 10^{10}\,\mathrm{J}$.
At point P, the satellite's engines are fired, increasing the satellite's velocity in the direction of travel and causing its kinetic energy to increase by $5.232 \times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{J}$. Assume that this happens instantaneously and that the engine is then shut down. The satellite follows the trajectory shown, which passes through Q, $6.850 \times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{m}$ from Earth's centre.
Analyse qualitatively the energy changes as the satellite moves from P to Q.
No calculation is needed. Use two facts: the engine is now off, so nothing is doing work on the satellite; and the engines pushed it faster along its direction of travel at P, so it now has more total energy than it did in the circular orbit.
Between P and Q the radius is increasing. Decide which of the two energy stores must grow as the satellite climbs further from Earth, and use conservation to say what happens to the other one. The total tells you nothing about the split, so do not use it to argue the two stores are unchanged.
Show that the kinetic energy of the satellite at Q is $1.194 \times 10^{10}\,\mathrm{J}$.
Two quantities have to be in hand before the kinetic energy can be found: the total mechanical energy of the satellite at Q, and its gravitational potential energy at Q. Remember that the engine's contribution is added to the total, not to the kinetic energy directly.
The potential energy at Q needs the radius of Q, not the radius of the original circular orbit, and it needs the Earth's mass, which is not in the stem and must be taken from the data sheet. Then use $E = U + K$ with the total at Q.
Explain the motion of the satellite after it passes through Q.
Convert the kinetic energy at Q into a speed with $K = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}$, then work out what speed a circular orbit at that same radius would require using $v_{\text{orbit}} = \sqrt{GM/r}$ and the Earth's mass from the data sheet. The comparison of those two numbers settles the question.
Keep the two speeds clearly labelled, because the whole argument turns on which is larger. A satellite whose speed exceeds the circular value at its radius has too much energy to be captured into that circle, so its distance from Earth continues to increase rather than staying constant.

questions.text:
Development of models of the atom has resulted from both experimental investigations and hypotheses based on theoretical considerations.
A key piece of experimental evidence supporting the nuclear model of the atom was a discovery by Chadwick in 1932. An aspect of the experimental design is shown.
What was the role of paraffin in Chadwick's experiment?
Follow the path of the unknown radiation in the diagram and ask what the last block it strikes is for. Paraffin is hydrogen-rich, so the question is what a hydrogen-rich material does when fast neutral particles arrive, and what happens to the hydrogen nuclei afterwards.
A full response to this part needs three things in order: what the paraffin contains, what the unknown radiation does to it, and what is then done with the particles that come out. Missing the last one loses the point of the part.
How did Chadwick's experiment change the model of the atom?
Write this answer in two steps. First, the properties Chadwick was able to infer about the radiation itself from the behaviour of the particles he measured — how it interacts with matter and how its mass compares with a particle whose mass was already known. Second, the single change in the model of the atom that those properties force.
Explain how de Broglie's hypothesis regarding the nature of electrons addressed limitations in the Bohr–Rutherford model of the atom.
There is more than one way in which the Bohr–Rutherford model fails, and an answer that deals with only one of them cannot score full marks. Find them by asking what the model predicts for (i) an electron that is moving in an orbit and (ii) the range of orbits that is permitted, then treat each as a separate argument.
The second limitation is resolved by a condition on the orbit itself: something must decide which orbits are allowed. Find that condition in de Broglie's hypothesis before you write about the second limitation.

questions.text:
An absorption spectrum resulting from the passage of visible light from a star's surface through its hydrogen atmosphere is shown. Absorption lines are labelled W to Z in the diagram.
Determine the surface temperature of the star.
You do not need the labelled lines W to Z for this part. What you need is the wavelength at which the broad intensity curve reaches its maximum, and the constant that links that wavelength to an absolute temperature.
Read the peak position to the resolution the grid allows, convert it to metres, and check the order of magnitude of the answer: a star's surface temperature should come out in the thousands of kelvin, not the tens.
Absorption line W originates from an electron transition between the second and sixth energy levels. Use $1/\lambda = R\left(\frac{1}{n_f^{2}} - \frac{1}{n_i^{2}}\right)$ to calculate the frequency of light absorbed to produce absorption line W.
The formula supplied gives a wavenumber, not a frequency, so a conversion is needed after the substitution. Keep track of which quantity is on the left-hand side at each step rather than writing $1/f$ or similar.
The stem gives the transition as between the second and the sixth level; the lower level is the final one because the electron is being promoted upwards when the photon is absorbed. Once you have the wavelength, convert it to a frequency and compare the result with the position of line W on the graph.
Explain the physical processes that produce an absorption spectrum.
Build the explanation in two stages and make sure both appear: where the continuous spectrum comes from, and then what happens to particular frequencies as the light crosses the atmosphere. The bridge between the two stages is $E = hf$.
Be precise about what is missing from the transmitted light. It is not that the photon changes colour or that it is scattered; it is that the photons of those particular frequencies are absorbed by the gas and never reach the observer, which is why those wavelengths show up as dips.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Properties of the Nucleus / predict quantitatively the energy released in nuclear decays or transmutations, including nuclear fission and nuclear fusion, by applying: (ACSPH031, ACSPH035, ACSPH036) | Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Properties of the Nucleus / the law of conservation of energy | Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Properties of the Nucleus / mass defect | Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Properties of the Nucleus / binding energy | Year 12 / From the Universe to the Atom / Properties of the Nucleus / Einstein’s mass–energy equivalence relationship
questions.text:
The simplified model below shows the reactants and products of a proton–antiproton reaction which produces three particles called pions, each having a different charge.
There are no other products in this process, which involves only the rearrangement of quarks. No electromagnetic radiation is produced. Assume that the initial kinetic energy of the proton and antiproton is negligible.
Protons consist of two up quarks (u) and a down quark (d). Antiprotons consist of two up antiquarks ($\bar{u}$) and a down antiquark ($\bar{d}$). Each of the pions consists of two quarks. The following tables provide information about hadrons and quarks.
Identify the quarks present in the $\pi^{-}$, $\pi^{+}$ and the $\pi^{0}$ particles.
Use the quark-charge table and the sign of the charge on each pion, and nothing else: each pion is two quarks, so add two entries from the table and find the pair that gives the right total. The trick is that the antiquark entries carry the opposite charge to the corresponding quark.
Check each answer by adding the two charges you have chosen: the pair must total $+1$, $-1$ or zero to match Table 1, and the two charged pions cannot come out as the same pair of quarks because their charges are opposite.
The energy released in the reaction is shared equally between the pions. Calculate the energy released per pion in this reaction.
The energy released is a loss of rest mass, since the stem says the initial kinetic energy is negligible and no radiation is produced. So add the rest masses on the reactant side and on the product side and take the difference; charge conservation and the speed of the pions are not part of this calculation.
The stem tells you the energy is shared equally between the three pions, so the number of pions is the divisor at the end. Work in the units of Table 1 throughout and state your result as an energy, remembering that $E = mc^{2}$ means the mass in $\mathrm{MeV}/c^{2}$ becomes an energy in MeV.
Calculation of the pions' velocities using classical physics predicts that each pion has a velocity, relative to the point at which the proton–antiproton reaction occurred, which exceeds $3 \times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Explain the problem with this prediction and how it can be resolved.
Answer this in two parts: state which quantity cannot be exceeded and by what, and then state which quantity the classical calculation wrongly treated as constant. A complete response says what the energy would otherwise have become, since that is what the resolution changes.
Be careful with the wording: the resolution does not claim that the speed limit is wrong, and it does not claim the pions are light. It has to explain why the same energy produces less speed than the classical calculation predicts, so ask which quantity that calculation held fixed.

questions.text:
An electron gun fires a beam of electrons at $2.0 \times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ through a pair of parallel charged plates towards a screen that is $30\,\mathrm{mm}$ from the end of the plates as shown. There is a uniform electric field between the plates of $1.5 \times 10^{4}\,\mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$. The plates are $5.0\,\mathrm{mm}$ wide and $20\,\mathrm{mm}$ apart. The electron beam enters mid-way between the plates. X marks the spot on the screen where an undeflected beam would strike. Ignore gravitational effects on the electron beam.
Show that the acceleration of an electron between the parallel plates is $2.6 \times 10^{15}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.
Nothing in the stem gives the force, so two relationships have to be combined. Write the electric force on a single electron in terms of the field strength and the charge, set it equal to $ma$, and solve for $a$.
Keep the electron's charge and mass in standard form as you substitute. Their ratio is of order $10^{12}$, so it is worth checking that the order of magnitude of your answer is plausible before moving on.
Show that the vertical displacement of the electron beam at the end of the parallel plates is approximately $8.1\,\mathrm{mm}$.
Between the plates the beam keeps its horizontal speed, so the time spent there is the distance travelled along the beam divided by that speed. Use the width of the plates for that distance and the plate separation for something else.
The vertical motion starts from rest, because the beam enters the plates travelling along the beam and gains its vertical velocity entirely from the field. So the vertical displacement is $\tfrac{1}{2}at^{2}$ with the time you have just found.
How far from point X will the electron beam strike the screen?
The field exists only between the plates, so once the beam is past them the vertical motion is uniform at whatever speed it had at that moment. Find that speed first, from the acceleration and the time already calculated.
The journey from the plates to the screen is at an angle, so the time to cross the gap is not the gap divided by the vertical speed; use the unchanged horizontal speed for that. Then remember to add the displacement already accumulated inside the plates.

questions.text:
Two horizontal metal rods, A and B, of different materials are resting on a frictionless table. Initially they are at rest in position 1. Both rods are then connected to a battery using wires. After the switch is turned on, currents of different magnitude flow in each rod. The rods move to position 2 after time, $t$. In position 2, B has a larger displacement than A from position 1. The masses of the wires are negligible.
Position 1 is reproduced below. Draw wires to show how the battery must be connected to the ends of the two rods in order for the magnitude of the current in each rod to be different, and for position 2 to be reached. No components, other than the wires, are required.
Two requirements must be satisfied at once: the magnitude of the current in each rod must be different, and the rods must move from position 1 to position 2. Work out what each one says about how the rods are wired.
If both rods share a single path around the circuit, one current flows in both of them, so the rods cannot be in series. Each rod must form its own branch across the battery.
Antiparallel currents repel, while currents in the same direction attract. Position 2 shows the rods farther apart, so check the sense of the currents that your connection produces and reverse one rod if necessary.
When the switch is turned on, the current in rod A is greater than the current in rod B. Consider this statement. Position 2 results from the larger current in rod A, causing a larger force to act on rod B. Evaluate this statement with reference to relevant physics principles.
Write down the expression for the force between two parallel current-carrying conductors, $F = \mu_0 I_1 I_2 l/(2\pi r)$, and notice that it is symmetric in the two currents.
The rods interact only through this magnetic force, so apply Newton's third law: what does it say about the force on A compared with the force on B?

A student conducts an experiment to determine the work function of potassium. The following diagram depicts the experimental setup used, where light of varying frequency is incident on a potassium electrode inside an evacuated tube.
For each frequency of light tested, the voltage in the circuit is varied, and the minimum voltage (called the stopping voltage) required to bring the current in the circuit to zero is recorded.

The starting position of a simple AC generator is shown. It consists of a single rectangular loop of wire in a uniform magnetic field of $0.5\,\mathrm{T}$. This loop is connected to two slip rings and the slip rings are connected via brushes to a voltmeter.
The loop is rotated at a constant rate through an angle of $90$ degrees from the starting position in the direction indicated, in $0.1$ seconds.
Calculate the magnitude of the average emf generated during this rotation.
Over a quarter turn the flux goes from its largest possible value to zero (or the other way round), so find the flux in the starting position and the flux in the position after $90^{\circ}$ and use the change between them.
The average emf is that change in flux divided by the time the rotation takes, so convert the loop dimensions into an area in square metres before substituting.
The same coil was then rotated at $10$ revolutions per second from the starting position. The voltage varies with time, as shown in the graph.
Two things have changed: the rotational speed and the direction of rotation. Take them one at a time instead of describing the new curve in a single step.
A change in rotational speed acts on both axes at once. Check what happens to the time for one complete cycle, and check separately what happens to the size of the peak voltage, because the peak emf depends on how quickly the flux is changing and not only on the period.
Finally ask what the voltage is doing at the instant the graph starts. The coil is at the same starting position as before, so look at how quickly the flux is changing there - fastest or not at all - and remember that reversing the rotation swaps the sign of the voltage.

Show that the wavelength of the electrons in this experiment is $182\,\mathrm{nm}$.
The beam speed is given, so the wavelength follows from the de Broglie relationship using the mass of an electron from the data sheet. Nothing about the slits or the screen is needed for this part.
Watch the powers of ten carefully: a speed of only a few thousand metres per second gives a wavelength of the order of hundreds of nanometres, not of metres or micrometres. Converting your result to nanometres is a good final check.
An interference fringe occurs on the screen where constructive interference takes place. Determine the distance from the central bright spot on the screen to the centre of the next interference fringe.
Constructive interference requires the path difference to be a whole number of wavelengths, so begin by establishing the fringe order $m$ for the first bright line away from the central maximum, then use the small-angle form of the condition with the slit separation and the screen distance both in metres.
Be especially careful with the slit separation. The printed paper gives it in micrometres, and this copy's stem reads $1\,\mathrm{mm}$; the data note on the question records the discrepancy, and a thousand-fold error in $d$ changes the answer by a thousand.
Determine the potential difference acting in the electron gun to accelerate the electrons in the beam from rest to $4 \times 10^{3}\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
An electron accelerated from rest through a potential difference has gained kinetic energy equal to the work the field does on it. Write that relationship down, then rearrange it for $V$ rather than for the kinetic energy.
The velocity has to be squared and halved, and the magnitude of the electron's charge goes in the denominator. A result of order $10^{-5}\,\mathrm{V}$ is expected, because the electrons are moving slowly rather than at relativistic speeds.

questions.current_path: Year 12 / The Nature of Light / Electromagnetic Spectrum / conduct investigations of historical and contemporary methods used to determine the speed of light and its current relationship to the measurement of time and distance (ACSPH082)
questions.text:
The diagram shows a model of the orbits of Earth, Jupiter and Io, including their orbital direction and periods of orbit. In this model, it is assumed that the orbits of Earth, Jupiter and Io are circular.
A method to determine the speed of light using this model is described below. When Earth was at position P, the orbital period of Io was measured, and the time that Io was at position R was recorded.
Six months later, Io had orbited Jupiter $10^{3}$ times, and Earth had reached position Q. The orbital period of Io was used to predict when it would be at position R. Assume that Jupiter has not moved significantly in its orbit around the Sun.
The time for Io to reach position R was measured to be $1.000 \times 10^{3}\,\mathrm{s}$ later than predicted, due to the time it takes light to cross the diameter of Earth's orbit from P to Q.
Use the measurements provided in the model to calculate the speed of light.
The light travels from P to Q, which are diametrically opposite on Earth's orbit, so the distance is the diameter of the orbit, not the radius. Convert the radius from kilometres into metres and double it.
The measured delay is the time the light takes to make that crossing, so divide the distance by that time. The number of Io orbits is not needed - it only explains how accurately the arrival time at R can be predicted.
Consider a modification to this model in which the Earth's orbit is elliptical.
Explain how this modification will affect the determination of the speed of light.
Hold the delay fixed and ask what an elliptical orbit does to the distance the light has to cross. A circle has only one radius, whereas an ellipse has a short axis and a long axis, and the two give different crossing distances.
Because the calculation is a distance divided by a time, decide separately for each axis which way the calculated speed moves, and be ready to say why. You do not need a new value for the time in order to argue this.
